Funnel Playbook Version 20 October 2026

The FINTECH Circle Funnel Playbook

The operating manual for the FINTECH Circle funnel: how a senior financial-services leader goes from a cold invite to a registration, a live webinar, an application, a call and a paid Board Programme place, and exactly what to do at every step.

For the operator and anyone hired to run the funnelContains no passwords or keys. Dated readings of live systems sit in one part, with their read time

  • 28PartsFrom planning an event to how it is wired
  • 199Task cardsEach with an owner and a safety level
  • 6Funnel stagesFrom a cold lead to a paying member
  • 3Safety levelsRead, Go, Send now. A typed word releases anything that reaches people

    Start Here

    Start Here

    The path every buyer walks, the problem this fixes, the whole funnel on one page, the funnel in motion, and how to use this playbook.

    The Path Every Buyer Walks

    STATUS: TEACHING FRAME FROM THE REVOPS REFERENCE, MAPPED TO THIS FUNNEL   AS OF: 2026-10-19

    Every buyer walks the same seven steps. Marketing counts leads, sales counts deals, and nobody counts what happens in between. That handoff is where revenue leaks. RevOps is the decision to run all seven steps as one system, with one owner and one set of numbers. Seven steps give seven counts and six rates between them.

    The tools behind the path (the calendar tool, the inbox, WebinarGeek, the CRM, the payments) all have an API. That is why Claude can do the reading, writing and measuring across all seven steps through one connector. The strategy, the offer and what ships stay with people.

    The Problem This Playbook Fixes

    Here is the problem this fixes. The funnel is made of a dozen tools, three automation layers and two outreach channels, and the knowledge of how it fits together has lived in a few people's heads and a few scattered documents. When a person is added, a campaign is changed, or a number looks wrong, nobody has one place to look.

    This playbook is that place. It explains each stage in plain language, then gives a task card for every step that has to be done, in the same shape every time: why it matters, what Claude does, what a person does, every step, what good looks like and the common mistakes. Where a step can be run by typing a request into the Claude Project chat, the exact request is given.

    What the reader takes away

    • A clear picture of the six stages, the tool behind each one, and which tool is the system of record for every number.
    • A step by step cycle for running a webinar, from picking the date to reading the results, with the safety level of every step.
    • A content engine for the operator's LinkedIn presence that keeps the operator in the editor's chair and the production off the operator's desk.
    • A funnel equation that says which number to fix first, and where each input is read.
    • The rules, traps and open decisions, written down once so nobody has to rediscover them.

    Who this is for. the operator, who needs to understand and approve; the operations team, who run the cycle; and anyone hired later, who needs to be productive in days. Where a step needs a person, the card says so. Where Claude can do it, the card shows the request to type.

    The Lessons in This Section

    • One funnel, six stages. Everything is a step in one of them.
    • Every step has an owner and a safety level, so nothing that reaches people happens by accident.
    • Live numbers are never written in a document. They are read from the system that did the work, on the day.

    The Whole Funnel, End to End

    Each stage has exactly one system of record. When two tools disagree, the one in the last column wins, and the number is quoted with the time it was read.

    #StageWhat happensSystem of record
    1Find and clean leadsApollo search on the persona, dedupe by email, keep nine financial industries, remove engaged people and other clients' contactsMaster Outreach Sheet (one tab per webinar)
    2TrafficCalendar invites from 20 warmed mailboxes, cold email from a separate set, LinkedIn posts and adsTantra · Instantly · LinkedIn and Metricool
    3Landing and registerOne branded page captures the registration and sends it to four places at onceWebinarGeek (the registration), then GHL (the contact)
    4NurtureConfirmation and reminder emails, WhatsApp join link and four timed WhatsApp remindersWebinarGeek (email) · GHL (WhatsApp)
    5The live webinar60 minutes with the operator, polls, three calls to action, an offer, live Q&A, then a replayWebinarGeek
    6Apply, call, payApplication, a 15-minute call, payment, onboarding, then the 52-week follow-upGHL (CRM and payments) · Work Tracker (applications)

    Across all six stages, the live dashboard reads every system once a day, and Claude (through the Claude Project and the connector) answers questions and runs tasks behind plan cards. Part 10 explains what the dashboard reports, and 17.1 lists what Claude can change.

    The First Week of a New Operator

    STATUS: CURRENT   AS OF: 2026-10-19

    A new operator can learn the funnel in five working days by reading and by planning, without sending anything. Every item below is a read or a plan. Nothing reaches people until the operator types send now in a later week.

    How to Use This Playbook

    How This Playbook Is Organised

    It answers four different questions, kept in four different places so that none of them goes stale because of another. Anything dated sits in the second, the third holds placeholders only, and the fourth is history.

    Master PlaybookHow the system works. Evergreen. Parts 1 to 24 and the reference.Current StateWhat it looks like today. Every row dated, sourced and re-read before quoting.Event RunbookHow to run one webinar. Placeholders, never a real date.Event and Performance LogWhat happened at each webinar. One record each, append-only.Decision RegisterDecisions, actions and open questions, kept apart.

    Reading the Labels

    A small label appears only where a reader could mistake one kind of statement for another.

    • RULE What FINTECH Circle normally does. It holds until a decision changes it.
    • EXAMPLE Shows how a mechanism works. Not a record of what happened.
    • CURRENT STATE How something is configured now. Carries a date. Re-read before quoting.
    • HISTORICAL Was true on the date given. Not re-read. Never quote it as current.
    • DECISION A choice that was made, with its date where known.
    • PROPOSAL Suggested, not decided. Nothing here is built unless a badge says so.
    • VERIFIED Read from the system itself on the date given.
    • UNVERIFIED Recorded or expected, but not read. Do not state it as fact.

    Square-Bracket Placeholders

    A word in square brackets, such as [WEBINAR DATE], stands for a value that changes with every event. It is never a real value. The Event Runbook (26.2) says where each is read.

    The three roles

    WhoRole
    The operatorAsks any question about the funnel and the numbers. Is the source and the face of the content. Signs off every LinkedIn post. Sets Accepted or Rejected on Board Programme applications.
    The operations teamRuns every task in this playbook, through the chat and the connector where it can, by hand where it cannot. Designs and schedules approved content.
    ClaudeAnswers from live data. Plans, drafts and checks. Runs the tools, always behind a plan card, and never acts on its own.

    The three safety levels

    Every task card carries one of these on its first line. The level is a promise about what the step can do to a real person.

    LevelTyped wordWhat it covers
    ReadnoneNumbers, lists, status, previews, drafts. Changes nothing.
    Go"go"Creating a draft, a tab, a tag, a broadcast, a template. Editing a draft or paused campaign. Blocking a domain.
    Send now"send now"Sending invites, activating a campaign, enrolling contacts in a live workflow, registering a person, cancelling a wave, editing an active campaign. Irreversible, so never assumed.
    The Truth Rules
    1. A claim about a live system is valid only in the turn it was read. Re-read before saying a campaign is paused, a draft or finished.
    2. Vendor counters are not delivery. Confirm at the system that did the work: calendar RSVPs for invites, WebinarGeek for attendance, GHL payments for revenue.
    3. Procedure belongs in the tools, not in reminders. A step that says "remember to" is a bug waiting to happen, so the tool itself enforces it and this playbook says where.
    4. A dated document carries STATUS and AS OF on its first lines, and is corrected the moment the status changes.

    How to read this playbook

    • First time: read Start Here and Part 1, then skim the card titles in Parts 2 to 10 to see the cycle.
    • Running a webinar: go to the Event Runbook (Part 26). It sends you into Parts 2 to 10 for the detail. The timeline below shows the order.
    • What is configured today: Part 25. Every row carries the date it was read.
    • What happened at a past webinar: Part 27.
    • An open question or a decision: Part 28.
    • Producing content: go straight to Part 5.
    • Something looks wrong: Part 17 has the known traps and the tool list.
    • What to run next, after the funnel is steady: Part 13 covers other funnel shapes, and Part 14 covers the later stage.
    • Prompts to paste: the prompt library is in 17.4. Each prompt also sits inside the card it belongs to.

    FINTECH Circle runs a free live webinar for senior financial-services leaders who want board, non-executive, advisory or fractional roles in UK fintech. The webinar leads to an application, a call and, for those accepted, enrolment in the Board Programme.

    The webinar headline in use: The Insider Roadmap to Access Top UK Fintech Board Seats in 2026, hosted by the operator. It teaches a 6-step insider board roadmap, then invites attendees to apply or book a call.

For cohorts after 1 October, read the Consolidated Document tab "Monthly Webinars for April 2026 to April 2027", the Work Tracker or the dashboard. If none has a date, say so.

    The pricing principle behind the ladder

    The reference playbook says the load-bearing rung is the entry offer. Price it so the revenue it produces covers the cost of the traffic that produced it, and the top of the funnel becomes free. Every rung above it is then margin. Almost nobody buys the expensive thing first: they buy something small, it works, and they climb.

    This is a test to run, not a verdict. For FINTECH the webinar is the free rung and the traffic cost is not yet recorded, so the honest answer today is "not known". Recording the cost is the first step.

    1. The Fintech Advisory and NED Landscape
    2. Regulatory Accountability and Personal Risk (FCA, SMCR, fiduciary exposure)
    3. Portfolio Career Strategy Design
    4. Advisory vs NED vs Fractional Roles

    DIFFERENT VERSIONS, read 20 October 2026. This is the offer file's list (25 September 2026). The live registration page says "8 structured modules" and a Digital Course quiz workbook holds six assessed modules. Whether these describe different products is UNVERIFIED, and the count to quote is an open decision (D1 in 28.4). No count is quoted as fact in this playbook. The 12-hour figure is consistent across three sources.

    The buyer: "UK Portfolio Finance Leader"

    • Who: 15 to 30+ years in banking, insurance, asset management, fintech or top-tier consulting and audit. Current or former C-suite, board member, NED or partner, often moving away from a full-time role after a redundancy or reorganisation.
    • Wants: paid part-time strategic work, a meaningful title, to give back to younger CEOs and boards, intellectual engagement.
    • Fears: regulatory and legal risk, reputational damage, and paying for courses that do not lead to roles.
    • Core problem: UK board seats are mostly filled through networks and headhunter shortlists before they are ever advertised.
    • Compares against: the FT NED Diploma, NED on Board, the Institute of Directors and university NED courses.

    Illustrative journeys from the brief: Ben, 55, an ex-C-level executive made redundant who wants a fractional or board role for the next ten years; Anna, 60, one unpaid charity board seat who needs two more roles; Tom, 50, an audit partner who expects AI to reduce his role and wants a first board seat. These are teaching examples, not data.

    The Lessons in This Section

    • The webinar is the entry point. The programme is the product. Every stage exists to move one person one rung up the ladder.
    • The buyer fears wasting money and reputation more than they want a title, so credibility beats persuasion everywhere.
    • The operator's own board experience is the proof. It is the source of the content, never something to be claimed for the operator.

    Why This Funnel Fits This Audience

    STATUS: STANDING RULES FROM THE ANALYSIS; THE EVIDENCE AND COUNTS ARE IN THE EVENT LOG   AS OF: 2026-09-18

    The insider angle works because it matches how the market really runs: boards fill seats through networks. Every piece of copy, invite title and post should make that reader feel seen. A message that could be about "leadership" in general has failed.

    What the Analysis Has Taught

    The rules below come from an analysis of the calendar channel across the first nine webinars. They hold until the analysis is re-run. The counts, the per-segment findings and the charts are a historical result: see 27.4 Pooled Analysis: Webinars 1 to 9.

    QuestionStanding ruleDecision it supports
    GeographyThe UK is the strongest market and the only one that beat the average in every webinar of the analysis. A few markets were consistent losers.Weight volume toward the UK and away from consistent losers.
    Seniority"Head of" titles perform at least as well as C-suite. Partner was below average.Buy Head of alongside C-suite. Drop Partner, VP and Manager.
    Company sizeHeadcount has no predictive value.Do not filter on headcount.
    CopyOne of the five invite titles (V2) was the best and two were below average.Weight the next wave toward the best title.
    FatigueYield fell as volume rose, because the same people were reached again.Fresh leads and warm re-invites matter more than any copy change.
    Read Segments Honestly

    A pooled lift is not evidence. A segment must win consistently across webinars. A market can read above average when pooled yet win only one or two webinars, so it stays excluded. Always check per-webinar consistency before moving volume.

    The Lessons in This Section

    • The UK, Head of titles and the best-performing invite title are the proven combination.
    • The real problem is fatigue, not copy. The cure is new people and warm re-invites.
    • Never move volume on a pooled number. Check it wins webinar by webinar.

    The Funnel Equation

    A funnel is a chain of rates multiplied together. If one is weak, it drags every later number down, and improving a strong stage changes almost nothing. The equation below names every link and says where it is read, so the next experiment goes to the weakest link and not the favourite one.

    No rate is quoted here. They change with every webinar. Read each from the source shown, and quote the time it was read.

    The whole funnel

    OC = (PV × RR + AR) × SUR × BR × CR

    The tree at the top of this part shows the same line, open by branch.

    OC
    Onboarded customers: people who paid and were onboarded
    PV
    Page visits to the registration page
    RR
    Registration rate: sign-ups divided by page visits
    AR
    Auto-registrants: people registered without the form, mainly calendar Yes or Maybe replies bridged into the broadcast
    SUR
    Show-up rate: attendees divided by registrants
    BR
    Booking rate: applications plus booked calls divided by attendees
    CR
    Close rate: onboarded customers divided by applications and calls

    Stage 1: Traffic

    Metric: VR = page visits ÷ people reached, across every channel
PV = CIS × VRCI + PE × VRCE + PI × VRP + AI × VRA
VRCI = IDR × ICR      (calendar invites)
VRCE = EDR × ELCR     (cold email; opens are not tracked)
VRP  = PLCR           (LinkedIn posts: link clicks ÷ impressions)
VRA  = ACTR           (LinkedIn ads: clicks ÷ impressions)
    InputMeaningRead at
    CISCalendar invites sentTantra campaigns and the Outreach Sheet. Tantra under-reports; use the calendar RSVPs for outcomes.
    IDR, ICRInvite delivery and link-click ratesNot currently measured by channel. Calendar links carry ?utm_source=cal, so page analytics can count them.
    PE, EDRPeople emailed, email delivery rateInstantly analytics. Bounce rate is the signal; opens are off.
    PI, PLCRPost impressions, link-click rateMetricool or LinkedIn analytics. Webinar posts keep the link in the first comment.
    AI, ACTRAd impressions, click-through rateLinkedIn Campaign Manager. Lead-gen forms use ?utm_source=lg_form, ads ?utm_source=linkedinad.
    A Measurement Gap Worth Closing

    Channel attribution is not available today: UTM fields on WebinarGeek registrations are empty and the CRM does not record the lead channel. Until registration links are tagged end to end, the funnel can say how many registered but not which channel each came from. Closing this gap is an open action (28.4).

    Stage 2: Landing and Registration

    Metric: PAR = attendees who signed up on the page ÷ page visits
PAR = RR × PSSR
R = PV × RR + AR
PSSR = NASR × (1 - TAR) + ASR × TAR
    InputMeaningRead at
    RRRegistration rateLanding page analytics (Tag Manager and Stape) against WebinarGeek subscribers
    ARAuto-registrantsTantra to WebinarGeek bridge. These count as interest, not self-registration.
    TARThank-you action rate: share who ask for the WhatsApp join linkGHL inbound WhatsApp messages against registrants
    ASR, NASRShow rate of those who did, and did not, take the thank-you actionWebinarGeek attendance split by tag

    Stage 3: Reminders and Nurture

    Metric: SUR = attendees ÷ registrants
SUR = DJR + EJ + WJ
EJ = REDR × REOR × EJCR      (WebinarGeek email reminders)
WJ = WOR × WDR × WRR × WJCR  (GHL WhatsApp reminders)
A  = R × SUR
    InputMeaningRead at
    DJRDirect join rate: joined without clicking any reminderWebinarGeek
    EJEmail joinsWebinarGeek email statistics
    WORWhatsApp opt-in rate: registrants who asked for the join linkGHL conversations
    WJWhatsApp joinsGHL workflow records and WebinarGeek attendance

    Stage 4: The Live Webinar to Application or Call

    Metric: BR = (applications + calls booked) ÷ attendees
BR = LBR + (1 - LBR) × FUCR × BCR + NSA × RWR × RCR × BCR
LBR  = OSR × OCTR × BCR       (acted during the event)
NSA  = (R - A) ÷ A            (no-shows per attendee)
CB   = A × BR
    InputMeaningRead at
    OSR, OCTROffer stay rate and click-through at slide 41WebinarGeek viewer minutes. CTA clicks are UI only, entered by hand after the event.
    FUCRClick rate on the follow-up emailsWebinarGeek emails today, GHL as they move
    RWR, RCRReplay watch and click ratesReplay page records to the Work Tracker Replays tab
    BCRBooking completion: calls booked ÷ offer clicksCalendly and GHL calendar

    Stage 5: The Sales Pipeline

    Metric: CR = onboarded customers ÷ (applications + calls booked)
CR = CHR × QR × PR × WR × PCR × OCR
OC = CB × CR
    InputMeaningRead at
    PRProposal rate: offers sent ÷ qualifiedApplication sheet approval column and the accepted decision
    QRQualified rate. Rule: 15 or more years and a Yes answer is Pre-Qualified, 10 or more is Under Review, otherwise Not Qualified.Work Tracker tab Programme Applicants
    CHRCalls held, including rebooked ones ÷ calls bookedCalendly, GHL calendar
    RBRNo-shows who rebooked ÷ no-shows, with follow-ups straight away, then 3 days, 3 days, 3 days and a week laterGHL tags and bookings
    WRWin rate: accepted ÷ offered, with deal follow-ups on day 3, day 7 and day 12Approval column on the application sheet
    PCRPayment completion: paid ÷ acceptedGHL payments transactions
    OCROnboarding completionGHL contact records and the cohort WhatsApp group

    Stage 6: The Next 52 Weeks

    Metric: YRR = calls booked from follow-up messages ÷ people on the list
LS  = R - OC                  (everyone who registered and did not buy)
YCB = LS × YRR
YRR = RMB + CEB + DSB         (re-marketing, cohort emails, downsell)
    InputMeaningRead at
    RMBBookings from warm re-invites to past no-shows and registrantsTantra and Instantly campaigns for that list
    CEBBookings from the seven cohort emails to attendeesWebinarGeek, moving to GHL
    DSBBookings from the Digital-tier downsell to declined applicantsDraft sequence, not yet running

    One metric per stage, in all three shapes

    The reference playbook gives each shape its own metric at stages 2 and 3, and the same metric at stages 1, 4, 5 and 6. Stages 3 to 6 of the other two shapes are listed for completeness. They matter only if that shape is adopted.

    Funnel Equation Model

    Type Other Numbers

    Teaching model, not FINTECH results. The starting numbers only show how the chain works. Replace them with figures read from the sources named under each row. The model finds the step that moved most against the last webinar, which is where the week's work goes.

    The Lessons in This Section

    • The funnel is a chain of rates. Fix the weakest link, not the favourite.
    • Every input has a named place where it is read, and some have none yet. The gaps are listed, not hidden.
    • Post-webinar stages have the most untracked inputs. Entering CTA clicks and applications by hand after each event is what keeps the equation alive.

    Reading Results Without Fooling the Team

    Several obvious-looking numbers in this funnel are wrong. These cost real time when they are trusted.

    TrapRealityDo instead
    Tantra campaign listReturns only campaigns that still exist, which was roughly half of the invites actually sent when it was last compared. Deleted campaigns' invites are invisible. sentCount is always 0 for calendar campaigns.Read calendar RSVPs: yes, maybe, no, waiting. Never derive Pending.
    Instantly analyticsReply counts under-report badly. Open counts are 0 because tracking is off.Do not quote either as real. Read replies in the inbox.
    Day-1 resultsRSVPs accrue over days.Judge at day 3 to 4.
    Early master sheets (WEB #1 to #6)Lead lists with an empty tracking scaffold. They show who was targeted, never what was sent.Use Tantra contacts as the record of who was contacted.
    Applications and paid customers filesStale exports.Read revenue live from GHL payments.
    Reversed namesSome raw lists store first and last names swapped for lastname.firstname addresses.Check the first name against the email before personalising.
    Calendar campaign linkThe WebinarGeek link and auto-register field are create-only. A campaign made without them can never be linked.Create waves only through the tool that sets them.
    Campaign name vs statusA name can say DRAFT while the status is active.Trust the status field, never the name.
    GHL not-watched tagWatched equals false is not the same as no-show. Attendance tags under-count.Build no-show lists from WebinarGeek.

    The Lessons in This Section

    • Counters from tools that did not do the work are not outcomes.
    • Time matters: a number read on day 1 is not the same number on day 4.
    • If a number looks too good or too bad, check it at its source before acting.

    • Approve the data policy and any purchase.
    • Approve the cleaned list.

    After

    Turn attention into applications, calls, payments and members.

    Layer 1 Understand

    Objective. Every interested attendee and no-show gets a clear next step.

    What
    Follow-ups, an application, a decision, a call, payment and onboarding.
    How
    Send the follow-ups. Tag no-shows. Enter the manual numbers. Process applications. Book calls. Take payment.
    With what
    WebinarGeek, the CRM, the application sheet, Gmail, Calendly, GHL Payments and Courses.
    What else
    • Skip-the-wait door.
    • Downsell for declined applicants.
    • A GHL calendar as an alternative to Calendly.
    Layer 2 Operate
    Process
    • Follow up.
    • Retarget no-shows.
    • Decide on applications.
    • Hold the call.
    • Take payment.
    • Onboard.
    Human actions
    • Decisions, calls, tiering.
    Automated actions
    • Decision emails, course access.
    AI actions
    • Drafts follow-ups. Prepares call notes.

    Part 9 9.1 9.4 9.6

    Layer 3 Understand the system
    Inputs
    Attendance and clicks.
    Tools
    CRM, sheets, Gmail, Calendly, payments.
    Outputs
    Members and revenue.
    Handoff
    Review and the next cycle.
    Metrics
    Applications, calls, payments, revenue by tier.
    Failure points
    • Stale application counts presented as live.
    • Tier not recorded on payers.

    Where to look things up for this stage.

    How to Read the Layers

    Every stage opens in five layers. Layer 1 is the short answer and a picture. Layer 2 is what to do. Layer 3 is how the system is wired. Layer 4 points to the reference centre (Part 17). Layer 5 is what else could be done. Current Available Potential Alternative

    Safety on every action: Read no real-world change. Go a draft or a configuration not yet released. Send now releases something to people or makes a consequential change.

    Funnel Economics

    The path from traffic to revenue as one formula, and the quantities behind it.

    Customers = Pool reached x Registration rate x Attendance rate x Application rate x Acceptance rate x Payment rate
Cost per registrant = Total acquisition cost / Registrants
Cost per attendee = Total acquisition cost / Attendees
Cost per qualified lead = Total acquisition cost / Applications
Cost per customer (CAC) = Total acquisition cost / New customers
Revenue per lead = Revenue / Registrants
Payback = CAC / Monthly contribution per customer
LTV = Average revenue per customer x Gross margin x Expected lifetime
Channel ROI = (Revenue from channel - Cost of channel) / Cost of channel

    Attendance rateWebinarGeek attendance over registrantsViewer events arrive one to two hours late Documented

    Revenue, customersGHL paymentsA stale paid-customers file must never be shown as live revenue Documented

    Funnel Model Write-Ups

    One entry per model, with the same fifteen headings. Only Current is in production; the rest are hypotheses, and any FINTECH example under them is a possibility, not a result.

    Webinar funnel Current
    What it is
    A free live masterclass that every channel points at, followed by an application and a call.
    Use when
    The audience needs education and trust before a high-ticket decision, and a live session can be run.
    Avoid when
    The offer is simple and low-commitment, or no host is available on the date.
    Prerequisites
    A cleaned pool, sending domains, a registration page, WebinarGeek, the CRM, and a host.
    Journey
    Invite, registration, confirmation, reminders, live session, offer, application, call, payment.
    Conversion points
    Registration, attendance, application, call booked, payment.
    Metrics
    Reach, registration rate, show rate, applications, calls, accepted, paid.
    Strengths
    Education and trust at scale; the one funnel with a full set of tools behind it.
    Weaknesses
    Low acceptance from cold invites; show rate depends on reminders; revenue arrives weeks later.
    Risks
    Deliverability, consent, wrong dates, a registration that fails.
    Human work
    Hosting, the offer, the calls, approving every send.
    AI opportunities
    Drafting copy, reading results, finding the worst step.
    Automation opportunities
    Waves, reminders, tags, follow-up, the daily dashboard.
    FINTECH Circle relevance
    This is the funnel in production. Parts 2 to 9 document it.
    Alternatives
    Application funnel only; call-first; content-led.
    Application funnel Current
    What it is
    A selective programme where the applicant is screened before a call or a place.
    Use when
    Fit matters more than volume, and places are limited.
    Avoid when
    Open enrolment with no screening.
    Prerequisites
    A written screening rule, a form, a reviewer and a decision record.
    Journey
    Interest, application, review, call, decision, payment.
    Conversion points
    Application submitted, call booked, accepted, paid.
    Metrics
    Applications, acceptance rate, time to decision.
    Strengths
    Protects the cohort quality; filters before a human call.
    Weaknesses
    Adds a step that some good buyers skip.
    Risks
    Slow review; stale rows in the application sheet.
    Human work
    Reviewing and deciding.
    AI opportunities
    Summarising answers and flagging gaps.
    Automation opportunities
    Form to sheet, tags, call reminders.
    FINTECH Circle relevance
    Used after the webinar. Elite requires an application and interview; Flagship and Digital differ (Part 9).
    Alternatives
    Call-first; a short qualification quiz.
    Call-first funnel Possible
    What it is
    A booking page is the first ask, with little or no education before it.
    Use when
    A small, high-value audience that will take a call, and enough call capacity.
    Avoid when
    A large cold list with no prior trust, or no one to take calls.
    Prerequisites
    A booking route, a call script and a qualification rule.
    Journey
    Invite, booking, reminder, call, decision.
    Conversion points
    Booking, show, decision.
    Metrics
    Calls booked per contact, call show rate, acceptance.
    Strengths
    Short path; fast learning on the offer.
    Weaknesses
    Every call costs human time; weak for cold contacts.
    Risks
    Low show rate; call capacity exhausted.
    Human work
    Every call.
    AI opportunities
    Call prep notes, summaries, follow-up drafts.
    Automation opportunities
    Booking, reminders, tags.
    FINTECH Circle relevance
    Hypothesis: a warm re-invite list of past attendees could be tested here (13.4). Not run today.
    Alternatives
    Webinar funnel; application funnel.
    Content-led funnel Possible
    What it is
    Authority posts that carry people to the registration page, with no direct ask first.
    Use when
    Trust has to be built before any ask, and there is time.
    Avoid when
    A near deadline.
    Prerequisites
    The content engine, a content owner and tagged links.
    Journey
    Post, click, registration page, webinar.
    Conversion points
    Click, registration.
    Metrics
    Reach, engagement, clicks, registrations from content.
    Strengths
    Compounds; builds authority at low marginal cost.
    Weaknesses
    Slow; hard to attribute without tags.
    Risks
    Voice drift; a claim without a source.
    Human work
    Voice, approval, proof.
    AI opportunities
    Ideas, drafts, design briefs, critique.
    Automation opportunities
    Scheduling, the content view.
    FINTECH Circle relevance
    The content engine is described in Part 5, but most of its tool connections are UNVERIFIED and its funnel contribution is not measured. Not run as a measured funnel.
    Alternatives
    Webinar funnel with content as a channel.
    Lead magnet funnel Possible
    What it is
    A useful asset is exchanged for contact details, then nurtured.
    Use when
    The audience is cold and needs warming before a webinar.
    Avoid when
    There is no asset worth giving.
    Prerequisites
    An asset, a delivery page and a nurture sequence.
    Journey
    Click, download, nurture, webinar invitation.
    Conversion points
    Download, then registration.
    Metrics
    Downloads, downloads to registration.
    Strengths
    Builds a warm list that is owned.
    Weaknesses
    Low intent if the asset is weak.
    Risks
    Consent for the follow-up.
    Human work
    Asset quality.
    AI opportunities
    Drafting the asset and the sequence.
    Automation opportunities
    Delivery and nurture.
    FINTECH Circle relevance
    A board-readiness checklist is a hypothesis. Not built.
    Alternatives
    Content-led; reverse squeeze.
    Reverse squeeze Possible
    What it is
    A call or application is offered first, and a smaller path is offered to those who do not take it.
    Use when
    Two price points exist and call capacity is limited.
    Avoid when
    There is no smaller offer.
    Prerequisites
    A video or page, a booking route and a smaller product.
    Journey
    Page, choose a call or the smaller path, nurture.
    Conversion points
    Call booked, or small-path purchase.
    Metrics
    Calls booked, small-path sales, upgrade rate.
    Strengths
    Captures buyers who would not take a call.
    Weaknesses
    Needs two offers to maintain.
    Risks
    Cannibalising the higher tier.
    Human work
    Calls and offer design.
    AI opportunities
    Segmenting the nurture.
    Automation opportunities
    Routing by choice.
    FINTECH Circle relevance
    The Digital tier at its listed price (Part 1) could act as the smaller path. Hypothesis, see Part 13.
    Alternatives
    Call-first; webinar with a downsell.
    Workshop funnel Possible
    What it is
    A hands-on session that needs practice and time.
    Use when
    The learning cannot be done in a talk.
    Avoid when
    No one can facilitate.
    Prerequisites
    A facilitator, materials, a cap on attendees.
    Journey
    Register, prepare, attend, follow up.
    Conversion points
    Register, attend, apply.
    Metrics
    Attendance, completion, applications.
    Strengths
    Strong proof of value.
    Weaknesses
    Costly to run.
    Risks
    Low attendance.
    Human work
    Facilitation.
    AI opportunities
    Prep and summaries.
    Automation opportunities
    Reminders and tagging.
    FINTECH Circle relevance
    Listed only as an option. The playbook holds no workshop content by design.
    Alternatives
    Webinar funnel.
    Event funnel Possible
    What it is
    A summit or in-person day with speakers and guests.
    Use when
    An audience of record already exists.
    Avoid when
    No event team.
    Prerequisites
    Venue or platform, speakers, an invitation list.
    Journey
    Invite, register, attend, follow up.
    Conversion points
    Register, attend, apply.
    Metrics
    Registrations, attendance, applications.
    Strengths
    High trust and networking.
    Weaknesses
    Fixed cost; one-off.
    Risks
    Low turnout.
    Human work
    The whole event.
    AI opportunities
    Agenda drafting, follow-up.
    Automation opportunities
    Registration, reminders.
    FINTECH Circle relevance
    A summit has been run before (tags exist). A repeat is a hypothesis (13.8).
    Alternatives
    Webinar series.
    Video or replay first Possible
    What it is
    A recorded session is the first thing people see.
    Use when
    A strong recording exists and live capacity is low.
    Avoid when
    The offer needs live questions.
    Prerequisites

    26.5 The New-Event Checklist

    • Date chosen and in the cohort calendar
    • Broadcast created on 575538, duration 60 minutes
    • Operations repointed the event configuration
    • Landing page shows the new date; fallback broadcast id current; replay link current
    • WebinarGeek and LinkedIn descriptions and banners updated
    • Reminder subject times match the event time
    • Deck dates, cohort and offer updated; DM slide numbers aligned
    • Application form cohort wording current
    • Lead pool sufficient for the planned volume
    • Suppression sweep done
    • Calendar wave plan read and approved
    • Instantly campaign duplicated, date swapped, activated only after 'send now'
    • Follow-up sequences scheduled for attendees and no-shows
    • Manual post-event figures entered

    How to Do Each Item

    The checklist above is the tick-list. This is the procedure behind it: for each item, how it is done, who does it, and how it is verified. Do the items in this order, because each one is a dependency of the next. "Go" and "send now" mean the same here as in 17.1: a plan card first, and nothing that reaches people without the typed word.

Claude reads the live state first and shows one plan card: the latest broadcast on webinar 575538 and whether one already exists on that date, the next webinar number, the sheet tabs that exist, the Instantly and Tantra campaigns that exist, the unused leads left on the latest tab, and the cohort the event feeds.     Part 2

    Plan the Event

    From four weeks out: the date, the broadcast, the sheet tab, the copy and the checks that make every later step safe. Then the five things set once and revisited when the offer changes.

    Master Playbook

    10 task cards2 sectionsReviewed by Operator as runner

    Before Starting

    The first five cards are done once per webinar, three to four weeks before the event. Nothing in them reaches people, so most steps are reads or low-risk changes. They are also where most late errors are born, so they are worth doing in order.

    2.1 Pick the Date From the Cohort Calendar

    Owner The operator and operationsTime 20 minSystem Consolidated DocumentSafety Read

    Why It Matters

    The webinar is not a standalone event. It feeds a cohort application deadline, so the date decides how long the follow-up window is. A webinar about ten days before month end gives the cohort emails time to run before applications close.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Reads the Consolidated Document tab "Monthly Webinars for April 2026 to April 2027" and the dashboard's list of past and planned webinars.
    • Finds the next webinar number: the last number in the Outreach_Webinars tab plus one.
    • Reports which cohort the date feeds and how many days of follow-up that leaves.
    What the Operator Does
    • Choose the date and the start time. The default is 12:00 Europe/London; some events run at 11:00.
    • Confirm which cohort deadline it feeds.

    Every Step

    1. Ask the chat: "What is the next webinar number, which cohort does the [WEBINAR DATE] webinar feed, and how many follow-up days does that leave?"
    2. Check the date does not clash with the previous webinar's follow-up sequence.
    3. Write the date, time and cohort in the change log for this event (see 26.5, the new-event checklist).
    4. Tell the operations team, so the broadcast and sheet tab are created (next card).

    Done When The date, time, webinar number and cohort are recorded in one place.

    What Good Looks Like

    • The date is chosen from the calendar, not from memory.
    • The time is stated in Europe/London, because that is the audience time zone.

    Common Mistakes

    • Choosing a date and only later discovering it leaves three days of follow-up.
    • Stating a time without a time zone.

    2.2 Create the Broadcast and the Sheet Tab

    Owner Operations, ClaudeTime 10 minSystem WebinarGeek, Master Outreach SheetSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    Everything downstream hangs off two objects: the WebinarGeek broadcast, which is what people register for, and the sheet tab, which is the queue of who to invite. A missing or duplicated broadcast sends invites to the wrong event.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Looks up the latest broadcast on the existing webinar. If one already exists on that date, it is reused, never duplicated.
    • Shows a plan card, then on "go" creates the broadcast on webinar 575538 (60 minutes, Europe/London). A new webinar is never created.
    • Lists the sheet tabs, and on "go" creates WEB #<n> <Mon D> with the header row copied from the latest tab.
    • Counts unused leads on the tab and says plainly whether the pool is big enough.
    What the Operator Does
    • Type the request in the chat and read the plan card.
    • Reply "go" only if the card shows what is expected.

    Every Step

    1. Type: "New webinar on [WEBINAR DATE] at [WEBINAR TIME]. What exists already and what is missing?"
    2. Read the plan card. It lists what it found (existing broadcast, tab, Instantly campaign, Tantra campaigns), what it will create, and what it will not touch.
    3. Reply "go". Claude creates the broadcast and the tab, then reads them back to verify.
    4. Note the broadcast id. It goes into the event configuration (card 2.5).

    Done When One broadcast and one tab exist for the event, each verified by reading it back.

    What Good Looks Like

    • The duration reads 60 minutes. A wrong duration makes every calendar entry and reminder wrong.
    • The tab header matches the previous tab: column A is the date, B the owner, C the sender, and lead data starts in column D.

    Common Mistakes

    • Creating a new webinar instead of a new broadcast on 575538.
    • Editing the broadcast time after invites have gone out. Invites keep the old time.

    2.3 Update the Page Copy, Banners and Deck

    Owner OperationsTime 2 hoursSystem WebinarGeek, LinkedIn, CanvaSafety Person

    Why It Matters

    Anyone who clicks through from an invite sees the registration page, the WebinarGeek description, the LinkedIn event page and the banners. A stale date on any of them costs registrations and creates confusion on the day.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Drafts the updated text for each surface from the Consolidated Document tabs: WebinarGeek Description, WebinarGeek Page Banner, LinkedIn Event Description, LinkedIn Event Page Banner.
    • Updates banners and the deck through the Canva connector where it is connected.
    What the Operator Does
    • Paste the text into WebinarGeek and LinkedIn by hand, because those edits are login only.
    • Update the deck: dates, the cohort, the offer slide, and align the live DM slide numbers with the current deck.

    Every Step

    1. Ask for the new copy: "Draft the WebinarGeek description and LinkedIn event text for the [WEBINAR DATE] webinar."
    2. Paste the WebinarGeek description and replace the banner.
    3. Update the LinkedIn event page and banner. Treat it as a secondary channel (2.5 explains why).
    4. Open the deck. Change dates, the next cohort, and the offer slide. Check the three call-to-action slides still point to the right links.
    5. Tick each item in the new-event checklist as it is verified.

    Done When No surface shows a previous date, a previous price or the wrong cohort.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Every price matches the current price list in Part 1.
    • The cohort wording matches the next cohort. The application form and older copy still mention a May cohort and need updating.

    Common Mistakes

    • Leaving an old price from earlier copy in a description.
    • Updating the page but not the banner, so the image still shows the old date.

    2.4 Check the Landing Page, the Replay and the Emails

    Owner OperationsTime 45 minSystem Cloudflare Worker, WebinarGeekSafety Read

    Why It Matters

    The registration page reads the upcoming broadcast from the backend. If the date is wrong there, every invite sends people to a page that contradicts it. The replay page is hard-coded in places, and the WebinarGeek reminder subject lines carry the time as text.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Checks the page shows the new date and that the fallback broadcast id is current.
    • Runs the landing page check through the monitoring tool and reports what failed.
    What the Operator Does
    • Open the page in a private window and submit a test registration with a test email.
    • Open the WebinarGeek emails and change the hard-coded time in the subject lines if the event is not at 12:00.

    Every Step

    1. Open webinar.fintechcircle.com in a private window and read the date.
    2. Submit a test registration. Confirm a confirmation email arrives from WebinarGeek, and the registration appears in the webinar's subscriber list and the Work Tracker Registrants tab.
    3. Open the replay page and check its link points to the current broadcast. It has been hard-coded to an old broadcast before.
    4. In WebinarGeek, open Emails and check the confirmation, the one-day reminder, the one-hour reminder and the live-now email. Fix "12PM" in subject lines if needed.
    5. Ask Claude for the landing page check. It reads the live page and the broadcast it points at, and reports pass or fail.

    Done When A test registration completes end to end, and no email or page shows the wrong time.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Page and Worker both use Europe/London. Nothing enforces this, so it is checked whenever the schedule changes.
    • The test registration uses a fresh email address each time.

    Common Mistakes

    • Checking the page only, not the replay link.
    • Assuming reminder subject lines update themselves when the broadcast time changes.

    2.5 Repoint the Event Configuration

    Owner OperationsTime 10 minSystem Event configurationSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    The wave sender refuses to plan or send if the broadcast date and its configuration disagree. That is deliberate: it stops invites going out against the wrong event. The configuration must be updated to the new broadcast before any wave is planned.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Reports the broadcast id and the start and end times that the wave sender currently holds.
    • Compares them to the new broadcast and says whether they agree.
    What the Operator Does
    • Give operations the new broadcast id, start and end.
    • Operations repoints the configuration, and the next wave preview then passes the date check.

    Every Step

    1. Send the brief: broadcast id, start time and end time in Europe/London.
    2. Operations updates the event configuration and confirms.
    3. Ask the chat to preview a wave. It must not stop at the date check.

    Done When A wave preview runs without a broadcast date refusal.

    What Good Looks Like

    • The change is made once and read back.
    • The date check is treated as a safeguard, not an annoyance.

    Common Mistakes

    • Overriding the date check. It exists because a wave built against a stale date was once the failure.

    Set Once, Revisit When the Offer Changes

    The next five cards are not repeated every webinar. They fix the offer, the buyer, the brand rules, the size of the list and the event line, which every webinar then reuses. Revisit them when the offer, the price or the audience changes, and after any webinar that shows a weak link in the funnel equation. Claude drafts each one from the facts already in this playbook and marks what it cannot source, so the person only answers the open notes.

    2.6 Write the Offer Sentence and Score It

    Owner Operator, ClaudeTime 50 minSystem Strategy documentSafety Person

    Why It Matters

    Every page, email and invite repeats one sentence about the offer. If a stranger cannot say it back correctly, no channel will fix that. And no headline rescues a weak offer, so it is scored on the value equation before any copy is written. Do this once, then again whenever the offer or the price changes.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Drafts each of the six slots from the offer and buyer facts in Part 1, and writes [check] wherever it cannot source an answer.
    • Scores the four value levers out of 10, with one concrete change beside each.
    • Rewrites the sentence with the two lowest levers fixed, in the same template.
    What the Operator Does
    • Answer every [check] note. The time slot and the guarantee slot are the open ones today.
    • Score as hard as a sceptical buyer would, and keep only the changes that can be delivered.
    • Read the final sentence aloud to someone outside the business. If they ask a follow-up question, rewrite it.

    Every Step

    1. Ask the chat: "Draft the six-slot offer sentence for the current webinar offer, mark what cannot be sourced, and score it on the value equation."
    2. Fill the six slots. They join into: I help [who] go from [before] to [after] using [mechanism], in [time], or [guarantee].
    3. Working draft from facts already in Part 1, for the operator to correct: I help senior financial-services leaders with 15 to 30 years in banking, insurance, asset management, fintech or consulting go from a market where board seats fill through networks before they are advertised to a first or next UK fintech board, NED or advisory seat, using the 6-step insider board roadmap, in [time: to confirm], or [guarantee: to confirm].
    4. Score each lever out of 10 and write one change beside each: a number and a deadline for the outcome, proof a sceptic sees in ten seconds, a win in week one, one step done for the buyer.
    5. Make the changes to the two lowest scores, then update the slots.
    6. Place the sentence on the ladder, and name and price the rung above it, built or not.
    7. Under the sentence, list the price, the guarantee, what is included and what is not.

    Done When A stranger repeats the sentence back correctly, two rungs are named and priced, and the two lowest levers are changed.

    What Good Looks Like

    • The tool or method goes in the mechanism slot, never in the outcome. Buyers pay for the after state.
    • The after state is a number with a unit and a period.
    • A guarantee names who carries the risk, and nothing is promised that cannot be honoured for every buyer.

    Common Mistakes

    • A buyer named as a market, such as founders, instead of a size, an industry and a role.
    • An outcome with no number, which no dashboard can count.
    • Leaving out what is not included, so it surfaces later as an objection on the call.

    2.7 Define the Buyer in Ten Fields

    Owner Operations, ClaudeTime 60 minSystem Sheet, Apollo filtersSafety Read

    Why It Matters

    A guessed buyer builds a list of the wrong people, and every later step then works perfectly on people who never buy. FINTECH already has a buyer description in Part 1. This card is how to check it against the real customers, and how to rebuild it if the offer changes.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Reads the paying customers live from GHL payments and the applicant sheet, and lists what more than half of them share.
    • Drafts the ten fields and the exclusions, and marks assumptions [check].
    • Turns role, geography, size and industry into the search filters used in Apollo.
    What the Operator Does
    • Quote the deal-killing objection word for word.
    • Write at least three exclusions from the worst customers.

    Every Step

    1. Ask the chat for the best customers by revenue, retention and ease to serve. Fewer than 20: use them all. None yet: use the 10 best sales conversations and mark each value assumed.
    2. Fill fields 1 to 4 for each of them. Any value shared by more than half goes into the buyer description.
    3. Fill fields 5 to 10 from real conversations, not from imagination.
    4. Quote the objection that kills deals exactly. Do not paraphrase it. That sentence is what the page and the session must answer.
    5. List what the worst five customers share. Those are the exclusions. Write at least three.
    6. No recent conversations? Ask five customers: which number is each judged on this quarter, and what is in the way?

    Done When Every value is traced to a real customer, the objection is quoted, and three exclusions are written.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Bands, not labels: 11 to 50 employees is a filter, SMB is not.
    • The role is someone who can say yes alone. A champion who needs a committee slows every deal.
    • The trigger is an event visible from outside, so it says who to reach first.

    Common Mistakes

    • Describing the customer wanted instead of the ones that exist.
    • Paraphrasing the objection.
    • Skipping exclusions, so the list fills with companies too small, too big or out of reach.

    2.8 Write the Brand Rules Sheet

    Owner Operator, operationsTime 30 minSystem Strategy documentSafety Person

    Why It Matters

    Every page, email, post and invite that Claude drafts follows one written set of rules. Without it, drafts leave gaps in tone, numbers and claims, and each gap is fixed by hand afterwards. Two prices or two speaker titles across assets is what a sceptical buyer notices first.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Drafts every rule from the brand guidelines, logos and sample pieces that are attached.
    • Writes [check] wherever the documents are silent, instead of guessing.
    • Applies the colours, fonts and anonymity choice to everything it drafts afterwards.
    What the Operator Does
    • Answer every [check].
    • Decide who approves numbers and which customers may be named.
    • Choose whether cold outreach is branded or anonymous. Cold email already sends from separate domains and never from the main brand domain.

    Every Step

    1. Attach the brand guidelines, the logo files and a few pieces that sound right.
    2. Check each drafted answer against what would be signed off.
    3. Names: brand, product, method and offer names exactly as they must appear. The brand is written FINTECH Circle.
    4. Voice: three words that sound like the brand, three that never do, and the words always used. The never list does most of the work.
    5. Colours as hex codes, the fonts, and a link to the logo files.
    6. Claims: where each number comes from and who signs it off, written before anyone writes copy.
    7. Legal lines, and what stays unbranded now, because the cold landing page is built from that choice.
    8. One version of each fact: one speaker title, one set of numbers, one call to action.

    Done When Every rule is written once and the open [check] notes are answered.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Colours are hex codes. A page cannot use the word navy exactly.
    • The banned words list is not empty.
    • A guarantee or a customer name is only used if legal or the customer has approved it.

    Common Mistakes

    • Colours named as words.
    • An empty banned words list, so drafts use the very phrases the brand dislikes.
    • A customer name or a guarantee in copy that nobody approved.

    2.9 Size the List Backwards and Approve the First 25 Rows

    Owner Operations, ClaudeTime 40 minSystem Sheet, ApolloSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    Buying a list by budget instead of by target means finding out weeks later that the funnel could never reach the number. Sizing starts from the revenue wanted and works back. Then a person reads 25 names before anything is bought in bulk, because one bad filter would otherwise fill the whole list with people who never buy. Buying leads spends money, so it follows the plan card rule.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Divides the monthly target by the offer price to give the buyers needed, then divides by each rate that has evidence behind it.
    • Builds the first 25 rows from the buyer filters, deduplicated by email, without customers, opt-outs, excluded industries and left-out countries.
    • Checks each email is well formed and sits on the company domain, then pauses until a person approves the 25.
    What the Operator Does
    • Enter only rates that can be evidenced from own records.
    • Read each of the 25 and ask whether that person would be invited.
    • Approve only when the sample looks like the best customers.

    Every Step

    1. Ask the chat: "Size the list backwards for a target of [amount] a month at the current price. Use only rates that can be evidenced, and say which are unknown."
    2. Read the answer. A blank rate reads unknown, will measure. Never borrow a benchmark from a blog post.
    3. If the number of people to invite is absurd, change the price, the offer or the funnel now, before any data is bought.
    4. Ask for the first 25 rows from the filters, with the customers' email domains and the left-out countries removed.
    5. Read all 25. A pattern of misses points at one field: wrong titles mean field 5, wrong companies mean fields 1 to 4.
    6. Approve. Claude then fills the full list the same way, inside the credit budget on the plan card.

    Done When The number of people to invite is known, or the first rate to measure is named, and the first 25 rows are approved.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Work backwards from revenue, one evidenced rate at a time.
    • The 25 are judged against the best customers, not against the filters.
    • The cold-pool cleaning rules in Part 3 still apply to every row.

    Common Mistakes

    • Copying an industry conversion rate into a rate field.
    • Keeping a target the price can never reach, then buying the list anyway.
    • Approving without reading the 25.

    2.10 Set the Event Line, Test the Title and Fix the Replay Expiry

    Owner Operator, operationsTime 20 minSystem Strategy document, WebinarGeekSafety Person

    Why It Matters

    One line carries everything people see: title, date, time with zone, length and platform. It is set once so nothing is rewritten, and every invite, reminder and page repeats it. A vague title gives a busy buyer no reason to give up an hour. A replay that never closes removes the reason to come live.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Drafts titles from the buyer's outcome and the method name, and joins the answers into one event line.
    • Reads the current replay setting in WebinarGeek before a decision is made.
    • Uses the date, time and zone in every invite and reminder it drafts.
    What the Operator Does
    • Pick a date the invites can meet, and an hour the audience is at work in their zone.
    • Set a replay expiry that will be kept.

    Every Step

    1. Topic: the buyer's outcome plus the method's name. The title now in use is The Insider Roadmap to Access Top UK Fintech Board Seats in 2026.
    2. Title test: would the buyer give up an hour for it? Outcome first, method name second, no wordplay, short enough to read in a calendar notification.
    3. Date: any upcoming day. Check public holidays in the buyers' countries. Further out is safer than sooner.
    4. Time: in the audience's zone, which is Europe/London. Current events run at 12:00.
    5. Length and replay: 60 minutes, then a recording that stays up for a stated time.
    6. Write it as one line and paste it in the change log for this event.

    Done When One line with title, date, time with zone, length and platform, and a replay expiry that is written down.

    What Good Looks Like

    • The title leads with the outcome the buyer wants.
    • The follow-ups tell people when the replay closes, and it actually closes.

    Common Mistakes

    • Stating the time in the operator's zone when the audience sits in another.
    • A title about the offer instead of the buyer's outcome.
    • A replay that never closes.

    The Lessons in This Section

    • Do the first five in order, three to four weeks out.
    • The broadcast and the sheet tab are the two objects everything else hangs off.
    • A stale date on any surface costs registrations. Check them all.
    • The offer sentence, the buyer, the brand rules, the list size and the event line are set once and reused.
    Part 3

    Leads

    The persona, the cleaning rules and the steps that turn a list into a safe queue.

    Master Playbook

    LeadTrafficLandingNurtureLiveAfter

    8 task cards1 sectionReviewed by Operator as runner

    The Rules Behind Every List

    STATUS: TARGETING SPEC CURRENT   AS OF: 2026-09-24

    Leads are the fuel for the two outreach channels. The persona and the cleaning rules below are fixed. Claude applies them every time, and a person approves anything that reaches people.

    RuleSetting
    Industries (exactly nine)Accounting · Banking · Capital Markets · Financial Services · Insurance · Investment Banking · Investment Management · Venture Capital and Private Equity · Management Consulting
    Geographies (eighteen)United Kingdom, Ireland, Netherlands, Sweden, Norway, Switzerland, Germany, UAE, Jersey, Guernsey, Cyprus, Malta, Singapore, Hong Kong, France, Denmark, Finland, Monaco. Germany has been excluded from sends since 25 August 2026 by operator decision.
    SeniorityDirector to C-suite. Head, Director, Chief and Partner are kept. Title words excluded: intern, student, recruiter, assistant, retired, professor, trainee.
    Company size1,000 or more employees, but size does not predict conversion, so it is not a filter that earns its place.
    Dedupe keyEmail, lowercased and trimmed. Never phone: company switchboards cause false merges.

    The owned universe (a dated snapshot; read it live before relying on it):

    STATUS: SNAPSHOT, RE-READ BEFORE USE   AS OF: 2026-09-22

    • 153,925 unique people had been contacted by Tantra by 4 September.
    • The qualified cold pool after the persona and exclusions was 61,587 at two or fewer prior touches, 44,595 after dropping low-converting geographies, 35,811 of them in the UK. Only 1,915 qualified people had never been touched.
    • Apollo showed about 742,000 buyable in the eighteen geographies, with the UK best covered. The latest buy overlapped the owned pool by only 2.5%, so buying is a real refill channel.

    What this means: the local pool is mostly recycled. Each additional touch yields less, so fresh people and warm re-invites matter more than copy.

    3.1 Check Whether the Pool Is Big Enough

    Owner Operations, ClaudeTime 5 minSystem Master Outreach SheetSafety Read

    Why It Matters

    Planning a wave without knowing how many unused leads exist is how a wave comes up short at the last minute. The question is answered in seconds from the sheet, and it decides whether a refill is needed.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Counts unused leads on the latest tab: never stamped on any tab, never contacted in Tantra or Instantly, minus suppressed people, blocked domains and excluded countries and titles.
    • States plainly whether the planned volume is covered, and proposes a refill if it is not.
    What the Operator Does
    • Decide the planned volume for the event.
    • Decide whether to refill, reuse or send smaller waves.

    Every Step

    1. Type: "Is there enough unused list for another wave of 5,000?"
    2. Read the answer. It will show counts by country and the reason for each exclusion.
    3. If short, go to the next card. If enough, go to Part 4.

    Done When The unused count is known and compared to the plan.

    What Good Looks Like

    • The count excludes everyone who must not be contacted, not just unstamped rows.
    • The answer comes with the time it was read.

    Common Mistakes

    • Counting unstamped rows without excluding people already contacted by Tantra. The sheet's stamps under-record real sends by tens of thousands.

    3.2 Decide Whether to Buy New Data

    Owner OperatorTime 15 minSystem ApolloSafety Person

    Why It Matters

    Reused data loses deliverability and conversion with every touch. The current decision is to stop buying new cold names and work with the pool already owned. That decision has a cost, and the cost should be seen before the next wave is planned.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Reads the Apollo availability tab on the dashboard and reports headroom by country.
    • Shows how many reusable leads remain at one touch or fewer, and the segments that have never converted.
    What the Operator Does
    • Decide: work only from the owned pool, or keep buying small amounts of fresh data to protect the sending domains.
    • If buying, name the segments: Head of and C-suite titles in the UK, and under-covered markets only where they have converted.

    Every Step

    1. Read the headroom and the touch counts on the dashboard.
    2. Decide the policy for this quarter and record it in the change log.
    3. If buying, write a search order: industries, geographies, title list, and the exclusion of companies already owned.
    4. Operations buys and cleans the list (next card). Apollo searching is free to read; buying spends money.

    Done When The data policy for the next wave is recorded.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Buying is framed as a deliverability decision, not only a volume one.
    • A buy is judged by yield, not by row count: the last buy produced 20,687 usable rows from 27,106.

    Common Mistakes

    • Stopping all buying and leaving the sending domains to carry second and third touches indefinitely.
    • Buying titles and geographies that have never converted because they are cheap.

    3.3 Clean a New List

    Owner Operations, ClaudeTime 1 to 2 hoursSystem Cleaning checks in the chatSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    A bought list is not persona filtered. The raw 110k Apollo list was 70% non-financial: pharma, machinery, law. It also contained other clients' contacts and swapped first and last names. Sending to it unchecked damages the domains and the reputation.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Reads the attached list and reports: row count, duplicate emails, missing emails, off-industry rows, other-client rows, suppressed and previously contacted people.
    • Writes an operations brief from the findings (see 17.7).
    What the Operator Does
    • Attach the list in the chat, or share the Google Sheet link for very large lists.
    • Operations checks the brief and loads the result.

    Every Step

    1. Attach the list and type: "I am attaching a new list. Check it and tell me what is usable."
    2. Read the counts. Compare the expected clean count to the row count.
    3. Cleaning order: dedupe by email, keep the nine industries, remove engaged people (WebinarGeek registrants, attendees, RSVP responders, applicants, paying customers, opt-outs, blocked domains), strip other clients' contacts, normalise countries.
    4. Check first names against the email before personalising. Lists for BCG and BNP Paribas have had first and last swapped.
    5. Join the LinkedIn URL back in by email if it is needed. It exists only in the raw lists.

    Done When A clean count, an operations brief, and a list that has been checked against every exclusion.

    What Good Looks Like

    • The brief states the source, the date, and every count removed and why.
    • Other clients' contacts are removed. Three other companies' lead lists have been found inside the pool before. If a source column names another company, flag it and remove it.

    Common Mistakes

    • Deduping by phone number.
    • Trusting a source column that names another client.

    3.4 Run the Suppression Sweep

    Owner Operations, ClaudeTime 15 minSystem Instantly, TantraSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    Any company that replies asking to be removed, or replies with hostile text, is blocked as a whole domain, not just that address. Without a sweep before each wave, a complainant's colleagues are invited again. Example (historical, September 2026): one large bank with three complainants and thousands of records was blocked whole, and so was a consultancy after a consent complaint.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Reads the replies and classifies each one as a removal request, hostile, or an auto-reply, using the first-person request rule so legal footers do not cause false positives.
    • Shows the list of what it would block, and changes nothing yet.
    • On "go", adds the domain to the Instantly block list and marks every Tantra record at that domain as unsubscribed, through the connector's suppression tool.
    What the Operator Does
    • Read the list and say "go" only if nothing important would be blocked by mistake.
    • Handle any GDPR deletion request separately: blocking is not erasure.

    Every Step

    1. Type: "Check the replies for removal requests and show me what would be blocked."
    2. Read the list. Check nothing important is being blocked by mistake.
    3. Reply "go". Claude blocks the domains and updates the suppression list the next wave will filter against.
    4. For a deletion request, also remove the row from the sheets and files, and send a reply to the person.

    Done When The Instantly block list and the Tantra unsubscribed flags are updated, and the suppression list is current.

    How Invite Replies Are Handled

    Replies to calendar invites land in the 20 sender mailboxes and are not read by a person. Instead, a reply that says stop or unsubscribe is being wired to move the person onto Tantra's unsubscribe list automatically, so the next wave leaves them out. This is in progress; until it is live, run the suppression check in 3.4 before every wave. Other replies are not read.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Free email providers, security gateways and the team's own sending domains are never domain-blocked.
    • Every record per email is patched in Tantra, because contacts are duplicated per list.

    Common Mistakes

    • Blocking only the address. The next person at that company is invited again.
    • Treating a block as a deletion. It is not one.

    3.5 Load the Tab

    Owner OperationsTime 30 minSystem Master Outreach SheetSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    A wave can only invite people who are in the Master Outreach Sheet. The chat can read the sheet and create tabs, but it cannot yet add lead rows, so loading is done by operations from the brief.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Reads the tab after loading and reports the new unused count.
    • Previews the wave with all exclusions applied, which doubles as a check that the load worked.
    What the Operator Does
    • Operations loads the cleaned rows into the tab: date in A, owner in B, sender in C, lead data from column D.

    Every Step

    1. Operations loads the rows using the brief.
    2. Ask the chat: "What is the unused count on the WEB #[N] tab now?"
    3. Compare to the expected clean count in the brief. A mismatch is investigated before any wave.

    Done When The tab holds the expected number of clean, unstamped leads.

    What Good Looks Like

    • The sheet is owned by the operations Google account and shared to the team, because the connector's Google access cannot act as the team's own Workspace address.
    • Column A stays empty until a wave is confirmed ready.

    Common Mistakes

    • Stamping column A before the campaign is verified. A stamp means consumed, so stamping a wave that then fails burns those leads.

    3.6 Keep a Do-Not-Contact Tab

    Owner Operations, ClaudeTime 15 minSystem Master Outreach SheetSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    Available Suppression lives in the Instantly block list, the Tantra unsubscribed flags and the suppression list. A visible tab in the outreach sheet is one more safety net: one row per person who must never be contacted again, with the reason and the date. The reference playbooks keep exactly this, and an agent reads bounces and unsubscribes into it every day.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Reads the Tantra and Instantly campaigns for bounces and unsubscribes and adds each address once, with the reason and the date.
    • Never deletes or reorders a row.
    What the Operator Does
    • Share the sheet with the right access: Editor, not Viewer, for anything that must write.
    • Never delete the tab to tidy up.

    Every Step

    1. Decide the tab name and columns: address, reason, date, source.
    2. Share the sheet at Editor level with the account that will write to it.
    3. Ask Claude: "Add every bounce and unsubscribe from the last wave to the do-not-contact tab."
    4. Check the tab before the next wave and make selection exclude every address on it.

    Done When Every bounce and opt-out has one row on the tab, and the next wave excludes them.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Each address appears once, with a reason and a date.
    • The tab is a record, not a replacement: the block list and the Tantra flags stay in place.

    Common Mistakes

    • Deleting the tab. Those addresses then have no record outside Tantra.
    • Sharing as Viewer, which lets the reader see the sheet but not write to it.

    3.7 Gate a List Before It Is Loaded

    Owner Operations, ClaudeTime 10 minSystem Cleaning checks in the chatSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    Available A list can pass the persona filter and still be unsafe. Two numbers decide whether a list is fit to send: how many duplicates it holds, and how likely its addresses are to bounce. The reference playbooks reject a purchased list with more than 2% duplicates and keep a cold email list below 1% bounce. These are reference starting points; FINTECH's own bounce history shows why the second one matters.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Counts duplicate addresses in a new list and reports the percentage.
    • Reads the bounce rate of the previous use of any reused list, per campaign, from Instantly.
    • Recommends hold, verify first, or go, and shows the numbers.
    What the Operator Does
    • Decide whether to verify the addresses first, send smaller, or drop the list.
    • Do not reuse a list whose last campaign bounced badly without checking it.

    Every Step

    1. Attach the list and ask: "What is the duplicate rate, and what did this list bounce last time?"
    2. Compare to the starting points: duplicates above 2% means reject; bounce above 1% means verify before using.
    3. Decide and record the decision on the operations brief.

    Done When The list has a recorded duplicate rate, a bounce history and a decision.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Bounce rate is judged per campaign, not as one overall figure that hides the bad lists.
    • The decision is written on the brief, so the next person sees why.

    Common Mistakes

    • Looking only at the overall rate. 1.72% looks healthy while the lists behind it ranged from 5.6% to 35.0%.

    3.8 Keep Test Contacts Out of the Counts

    Owner Operations, ClaudeTime 10 minSystem CRM, dashboardSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    Available Every rehearsal creates a real-looking contact: a test registration, a test booking, a test payment. If those contacts stay unmarked they inflate registrations, skew the cost per registration and may even be invited to a wave. A single tag, applied at creation, keeps them out.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Creates test contacts with a test tag and an address on a test domain.
    • Excludes the tag from the dashboard counts, from wave selection and from every audience upload.
    What the Operator Does
    • Use only the test addresses for rehearsals.
    • Approve the tag name once so every tool uses the same one.

    Every Step

    1. Agree one tag name, for example test.
    2. Ask Claude to create the test contacts with that tag before any rehearsal.
    3. Run the rehearsal: registration, booking, payment as needed.
    4. Ask Claude to confirm the dashboard and the next wave preview exclude every tagged contact.

    Done When Tagged test contacts exist, and none of them appears in a count, an audience or a wave plan.

    What Good Looks Like

    • The tag is applied when the contact is created, not afterwards.
    • Counts are checked once with and once without the test contacts to prove the exclusion works.

    Common Mistakes

    • Tagging after the fact, after the contact already counted.
    • Using a real colleague's address for a test and then wondering why they were invited.

    The Lessons in This Section

    • The nine industries, the exclusions and the opt-out guard are not preferences. They are what keeps the sending domains alive.
    • Count the real unused pool before planning, not the unstamped rows.
    • A stamp means consumed. It is written only after the campaign is verified.
    • A list must pass its duplicate and bounce gates, and test contacts must never reach a count.
    Part 4

    Traffic: Calendar, Email, LinkedIn and More

    The order of channels, the sending rules and limits, the weekly gate, and cards for the channels FINTECH runs and the ones it could add.

    Master Playbook

    LeadTrafficLandingNurtureLiveAfter

    22 task cards1 sectionReviewed by Operator as runner

    The Order of Channels and the Rules

    Several channels run side by side on purpose, because one channel alone is a risk. The order is fixed: cold outreach validates the funnel quickly, organic content builds the reputation and shows what resonates, and the best posts are then promoted with paid ads. The long-term direction is to make organic content the largest share of traffic.

    ChannelBest forCost of running itStatus
    Organic content (LinkedIn)Reputation, steady registrations, learning what resonatesTime and quality control. No media spend.Current
    Paid ads (LinkedIn retargeting)Scaling the posts that already workMedia spend. Needs proven creative first.Current
    Calendar invites (Tantra)The largest channel, fast traffic before an eventWarmed mailboxes, fresh data, domain upkeepCurrent
    Cold email (Instantly)Fast traffic, A/B testing of anglesDomain rotation, deliverability monitoringCurrent
    Meta paid adsCold audiences beyond the contact listMedia spend, pixel and conversion trackingAvailable
    LinkedIn outreach, lead forms, event pageNamed buyers and a second free path to the pageSafe pace, one profile, and token upkeepAvailable
    Blog, SMSSlow compounding traffic; time-critical nudgesWriting time; consent and sender approvalPotential

    Outreach is the quick fix. The infrastructure is hard to maintain and deliverability decays with every reuse of the same names, which is why the long-term direction is toward content and ads. The first seven cards in this part cover what runs today. The cards from 4.8 on add the limits, the weekly gate and the channels FINTECH could add, each badged Available or Potential. Content production has its own part (Part 5).

    Sending Rules, Every Wave
    • Balanced distribution across mailboxes, never fill-first.
    • Event time in the audience time zone, Europe/London.
    • About 1,000 invites per campaign; capacity is about 250 per mailbox per day, roughly 5,000 a day, but the shared Google quota (about 1,500 invites per service account per day) is the real limit.
    • Send 3 to 7 days before the event. Judge results at day 3 to 4.
    • The invite location is always https://webinar.fintechcircle.com/?utm_source=cal, never the WebinarGeek page (operator rule, 2 September 2026).
    • One tag only: variationN. No first-name placeholders in titles, because an unfilled name leaves a title that starts with a stray comma.

    4.1 Plan a Calendar Wave (Tantra)

    Owner Operations, ClaudeTime 15 minSystem Tantra, Master Outreach SheetSafety Read

    Why It Matters

    Creating a calendar campaign is the send. There is no draft and no pause. So the plan is where every mistake is caught, and the plan card is the whole safety net.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Selects leads: unused only, never stamped on any tab, never contacted in Tantra or Instantly, minus RSVPs, attendees, suppressed people, blocked domains, excluded countries and titles.
    • Shows the plan card: counts per wave, the invite variation per wave, the schedule, the geographic mix, and why leads were skipped. The plan is saved for 48 hours.
    What the Operator Does
