    8.1 Prepare the Polls, Calls to Action and Chat Prompts

    Owner OperationsTime 1 hourSystem WebinarGeekSafety Person

    Why It Matters

    Anything not set before going live is lost. A call to action that is not loaded, a poll that is not created, or a replay that is not enabled cannot be fixed during the session in front of the audience.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Drafts the poll text and chat prompts from the Consolidated Document, and checks the slide timings against the run of show above.
    What the Operator Does
    • Sign in to WebinarGeek, open the webinar and the broadcast's interaction settings, and set the polls and the three call-to-action buttons with their links and slide timings.

    Every Step

    1. Open the broadcast's interaction settings.
    2. Create the polls from the "Chat prompts and polls" tab. Check the wording.
    3. Create the three call-to-action buttons with their links: the 15-minute call, the application, the Personal Board Career Review.
    4. Check the registration form is short, and that replay is set up now, not after the event.
    5. Test everything in a preview.

    Done When Polls, three buttons and replay all work in a preview.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Replay is set before the event.

    Common Mistakes

    • Setting the call to action after the event has started.

    8.2 Run the Dry Run

    Owner Operations, OperatorTime 1 hourSystem WebinarGeekSafety Person

    Why It Matters

    Every failure in the session is found while it costs nothing, with the team, the slides and a test attendee on a second device. Anything untested, such as a muted presenter, a poll that will not start, or a dead offer link, surfaces live in front of the audience.

    How It Works

    What the Operator Does
    • Run the whole session on the same computer, network and slides that will be used live.
    • Agree every hand-off between roles out loud.
    • On the morning, name a second person as a co-presenter fallback.

    Every Step

    1. Two to three days before, run the full session with the team and a second device as a test attendee.
    2. Walk every poll, the three call-to-action buttons, the offer and the Q&A close.
    3. Join from the second device. Check what an attendee sees.
    4. Test the recording with a short real session that only the team registers for.
    5. Fix every unknown the run finds.

    Done When A full dry run with no unknowns left.

    What Good Looks Like

    • The offer minute and the Q&A close are rehearsed most. They are the ones that decide conversion.
    • The dry run is not on the night before. That leaves no time to fix what it finds.

    Common Mistakes

    • Rehearsing on a different laptop or network from the live one.
    • Skipping the poll and button starts because they seem simple.

    8.3 Run the Live Session

    Owner Operator, operationsTime 60 minSystem WebinarGeekSafety Person

    Why It Matters

    The session is the highest-value hour in the funnel. The operator teaches. The team runs everything else so the operator never has to touch a control.

    How It Works

    What the Operator Does
    • The operator presents. A moderator runs the chat, polls and direct messages on the run-of-show timings.
    • A second person watches the join link and the reminder emails for problems.

    Every Step

    1. Start as the run of show says. Open with the moderation guidelines in the chat.
    2. Run each poll and call to action on its slide.
    3. Send the direct messages at their minutes.
    4. At minute 40, collect questions and use the seeded ones if the room is quiet.
    5. Show the offer on slide 41, then close with the Q&A.
    6. Log the attendee count every five minutes. That curve is the retention data for the next review.
    7. Repeat the call to action link in the chat every five minutes after the offer.

    Done When The session runs on time and every poll and call to action fires.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Every call to action is a click on a button and also a link in the chat.

    Common Mistakes

    • Presenting and moderating at the same time.

    8.4 Test Zoom for the Mid-November Webinar

    Owner Operator, operationsTime 2 days of setupSystem Zoom, GHLSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    WebinarGeek reminder deliverability has been falling across the coaching network this guidance comes from, and the coaching cohort has moved to Zoom over the last two months. Zoom is better known, so it carries brand recognition. The test costs one webinar: the Friday event stays on WebinarGeek and the mid-November end-of-year event runs on Zoom.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Writes the Zoom setup plan card: registration path, reminders, recording, reporting, and what it changes in this setup.
    • After the event, compares registration to attendance, reminder delivery and call-to-action clicks between the two platforms.
    What the Operator Does
    • Decide whether to proceed after reading the plan card.
    • Pause the WebinarGeek subscription for the month of the test only if the comparison is clean.

    Every Step

    1. Read the plan card. Decide if the Zoom test goes ahead for the mid-November webinar.
    2. Set up the Zoom event: registration, polls, cloud recording, the offer link ready for the chat.
    3. Switch on the native reminders and follow-up emails in the Zoom Webinar, schedule the two timed ones through the connector, and keep the GHL WhatsApp reminders pointing at each person's own Zoom join link.
    4. Run the dry run (8.2) on Zoom.
    5. After the event, compare registration to attendance, reminder delivery and call-to-action clicks for the two platforms, then decide.

    Done When A recorded decision: stay on WebinarGeek, or move.

    STATUS: TEST AGREED ON THE 14 OCT CALL; SETUP DETAILS BELOW ARE FROM THE GROWTHCLUB WORKSHOP PLAYBOOK AND NEED CHECKING AGAINST THE FINTECH ZOOM PLAN   AS OF: 2026-10-17

    QuestionWebinarGeekZoom
    Reminder deliverabilityReported to be falling across the coaching network this guidance comes fromBetter reported
    Brand recognitionLowerHigher
    On-screen call-to-action popupYes. This is why FINTECH moved to it.No. Use a link in the chat and a QR code in the deck.
    Chat and Q&AFullerBasic chat, limited Q&A
    Reminder emailsSent by the platformZoom Webinars can send native reminders and attendee and absentee follow-up emails. A standard Zoom meeting sends none. Two timed reminders Zoom cannot send natively (a "we have started" and a "three hours to go") are sent separately by the connector.

    What Changes in This Setup if the Test Goes Ahead

    • The registration service returns a WebinarGeek watch link. A Zoom event needs its own registration path and join link.
    • The Worker listens to WebinarGeek events. A Zoom event needs its own attendance and recording source.
    • The connector's wave tools link calendar campaigns to a WebinarGeek broadcast, and auto-register Yes and Maybe into it.
    • The dashboard and the connector read WebinarGeek. Zoom reporting must be added before it can sit in the funnel.

    Zoom Setup Notes From the Workshop Playbook

    • Account settings beat meeting settings. Check passcode, authentication and cloud recording settings in the Zoom account first.
    • Register everyone, so each person gets their own join link, and keep the recording on.
    • Create the polls on the meeting. A poll does not start itself: the moderator opens Polls and launches each one.
    • There is no offer button in a standard meeting. Have the moderator paste the offer link in the chat the moment the offer slide appears, with ?src=live added so the click is attributed.
    • Run a 15-minute test session first with two devices and fresh test emails.

    What Claude Can Already Do on Zoom

    • Create a Zoom Webinar with registration set to auto-approve, cloud auto-recording, a practice session, Q and A, and the native reminder and follow-up emails switched on.
    • Register people through Zoom's connection and return a unique join link for each. It shows a plan first and only registers after a go.
    • Pull true join and leave durations, so engaged attendees can be counted honestly, which WebinarGeek's drop-in counting hid. Only totals are kept, no names or emails.
    • Send the two reminders Zoom cannot send natively, from a verified sending domain.
    • Every default title and name from the method must be replaced with FINTECH's own before anything runs. Claude lists them in the plan card.

    What Good Looks Like

    • The test is judged on the same measures as every other webinar.
    • If organic traffic becomes the main source, the registration-to-attendee rate improves anyway and the deliverability worry matters less.

    Common Mistakes

    • Switching without a reminder path. Check the native reminders are on and the two timed ones are scheduled, or the show rate suffers.

    8.5 Run the Offer Minute and Close the Replay

    Owner Tech moderator, chat moderatorTime LiveSystem WebinarGeekSafety Person

    Why It Matters

    The offer is where the hour pays for itself. In a live webinar the button does not appear by itself. Someone has to start it, someone has to paste the link, and someone has to follow up the people who said yes within the hour. The deadline then has to be real, or the whole session loses its pull.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Prepares the list of poll 4 yes answers from the studio results and the personal message for each person to approve.
    What the Operator Does
    • The tech moderator starts the button. The chat moderator pastes and repeats the link. The DM operator sends the personal booking messages.

    Every Step

    1. When the offer slide appears, the tech moderator opens Interactions in the studio and starts the call to action. Choose End manually so it stays up.
    2. Add a source tag to the link so the click is credited to the session.
    3. Paste the same link in the chat and pin it. Repeat it every five minutes.
    4. Anyone who answered yes to poll 4 gets a personal message with the booking link within the hour.
    5. Name one deadline. It is the same one on the slide and in every email.
    6. Make the replay expire, then actually close it. No expiry means no reason to watch today.

    Done When The button ran at the offer minute, the link was repeated, and every poll 4 yes got a personal message inside an hour.

    What Good Looks Like

    • The deadline in the slide, the emails and the replay page agree.

    Common Mistakes

    • Showing the button during teaching.
    • A replay that never closes.

    8.6 Build the Deck to the Ten-Section Arc

    Owner Claude drafts, the operator approvesTime Half a daySystem DeckSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    Most hosts spend a week on slides and five minutes on the moments that make money. Strong webinar decks tend to run the same arc in the same order. Compared with that arc, a deck's weak point is usually the order, not the content.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Maps each slide of the live deck to the ten sections and flags missing or out-of-order ones.
    What the Operator Does
    • The operator decides what to change. Any change to the offer slides needs a new plan card.

    Every Step

    1. Read the ten sections and their minute ranges below.
    2. Map the live deck's slides to the sections.
    3. Check each poll sits where the arc puts it.
    4. Check the offer, objections and call to action sit between minute 39 and 46.
    5. Check Q and A has the next step on screen.
    6. On a 45-minute session, keep the order on a shorter clock.

    Done When Every section is present, in order, with its poll or prompt.

    What Good Looks Like

    • The offer appears once.

    Common Mistakes

    • Teaching past minute 45.
    • A call to action with no link in the chat.

    8.7 Know the Zoom Connect Rules and Room Lock

    Owner OperationsTime 2 hoursSystem ZoomSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    The Zoom test goes ahead in mid-November. The traps are not in the product. They are in the account: a setting at account level silently overrides the meeting. This card holds the rules in one place so the test is not found out on the day. Reference rules

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Reads the account settings the connector can reach and lists any that disagree with the rules.
    What the Operator Does
    • Make the account switches. Make co-hosts inside the meeting on the day.

    Every Step

    1. Check account settings first. Meeting passcode on and embedded in the invite link, only authenticated participants off, focus mode on, request permission to unmute on, co-host and cloud recording on. If a switch is greyed out, change it at account level.
    2. Build a server-to-server app with only the scopes needed (14 in the connector reference, recount in the Zoom app), activate it, and keep its credentials with the connector.
    3. Know error 1001: registrants refused on joining. Authenticated-only is on. Turn it off.
    4. Know error 429: Zoom allows three registrations per person per day. Use a fresh email for every test.
    5. Plan for the 100-seat cap on a Pro room. It counts the host and co-hosts, so staff take a few seats. Joining after it is full is refused.
    6. At the start open Security and untick Unmute Themselves and Start Video. Focus mode alone does not stop people unmuting.
    7. Make co-hosts inside the meeting: Participants, hover a name, More, Make Co-Host. Alternative hosts set in advance must be licensed users on the account.
    8. A standard Zoom meeting sends no reminder emails. Every reminder comes from the funnel, with each person's own link.

    Done When The test passes with a fresh email, two devices, the lock applied and the recording arriving.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Settings are changed at account level first.

    Common Mistakes

    • Trusting the meeting settings over the account.
    • Reusing one email for repeated tests.

    The Lessons in This Section

    • Five named roles run the room. The host only teaches.
    • Poll 4 yes gets a personal message within the hour.
    • Polls, buttons and replay are set before going live, never after.
    • The dry run proves every hand-off. It is not the night before.
    • A platform switch changes the registration, reminder and reporting paths. Plan all three.
    Part 9

    After the Event: Follow-Up, Applications, Calls and Payment

    Most of the revenue is decided in the first week after the webinar. These cards cover follow-up, applications, the call and the payment.

    Master Playbook

    LeadTrafficLandingNurtureLiveAfter

    18 task cards1 sectionReviewed by Operator as runner

    From Webinar to Paying Member

    The webinar does not close anything on its own. The sale is made in the weeks after it: an application, a short call, an acceptance, a payment. Most of the revenue is decided by how well the first week after the event is run, and by whether the people who did not attend are followed up.

    Apply, call, pay, onboard. The path for one person is below. Each step has one system of record.

    StepWhat happensWhere it lives
    ApplyThe application form: name, email, phone, title, company, years of experience, LinkedIn, cohort commitment. 15 or more years and a Yes answer is Pre-Qualified; 10 or more is Under Review; otherwise Not Qualified.Work Tracker tab Programme Applicants, and an email to the applications address
    DecideThe operator sets Approval to Accepted or Rejected. A trigger sends the matching email and writes the send to a log column.Application sheet (columns Q and R)
    CallA 15-minute Board Positioning Call or a Personal Board Career Review.Calendly, connected to GHL, or a GHL calendar
    PayDeposit or full payment in GBP on a payment page. Acceptance emails carry the links.GHL Payments
    OnboardWelcome email, the joining link and the cohort WhatsApp group on the payment-success page.GHL, the payment-success page

    9.1 Send the Attendee and No-Show Follow-Ups

    Owner OperationsTime 1 hourSystem WebinarGeek (moving to GHL)Safety Person

    Why It Matters

    People who attended have already shown they are interested. People who did not attend are a registered audience who still got a reminder. Both groups convert better than cold leads, and both are ignored if the sequences are not scheduled before the event.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Drafts or refreshes the sequence text from the Consolidated Document tabs "Cohort Emails" and "Follow up Emails", with the date, price and cohort corrected.
    What the Operator Does
    • Check the sequences are scheduled in WebinarGeek, with the right audience for each.
    • Replace any historical price still in older copy.

    Every Step

    1. Attendees, from the day after until the cohort deadline: seven cohort emails. Replay and apply; why profiles get shortlisted; reviewing applications today; extension; final day; closed; the next webinar.
    2. No-shows, at +1 day, +1 week, +2 weeks and +1 month: book a call; the replay; "From Executive Career to Board Portfolio"; "See the Programme in Practice".
    3. Next webinar: the warm re-invite to no-shows and past registrants (4.4) and the remarketing email.
    4. Declined applicants: a Digital-tier downsell sequence exists as a draft in two versions. It is not running.
    5. Check the replay page gates on name, email and company, and that its link points to the current broadcast.
    6. Make the replay expire and then close it on the day. An expiry that is never enforced gives no reason to watch today.

    Done When Both sequences are scheduled before the event, for the right audiences.

    What Good Looks Like

    • The attendee and the no-show lists are built from WebinarGeek, not from GHL's watched tag.

    Common Mistakes

    • Sending the same sequence to attendees and no-shows.
    • Leaving the replay link on last month's broadcast.

    9.2 Tag the No-Shows for Retargeting

    Owner Operations, ClaudeTime 15 minSystem GHL, WebinarGeekSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    A no-show list that is wrong either misses people or contacts attendees by mistake. GHL's watched equals false is not the same as no-show, and its attendance tags under-count. The only reliable source for who did not attend is WebinarGeek.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Builds the no-show list from WebinarGeek attendance, tags them in GHL, and first lists any published workflow the tag would trigger.
    What the Operator Does
    • Reply "go" for the tag. Enrolling people in a live workflow that sends WhatsApp or email needs "send now".

    Every Step

    1. Type: "Tag last webinar's yes and maybe no-shows for retargeting."
    2. Read which workflows the tag would fire.
    3. "go" to tag. "send now" only if enrolling in a live workflow.
    4. Use the tagged list for the retarget campaign and the LinkedIn audience (4.6).

    Done When Tagged, with no accidental workflow firing.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Tag writes are additive and a tagged person is never removed by the chat.

    Common Mistakes

    • Tagging more than a few dozen people without checking what the tag triggers.

    9.3 Enter the Manual Numbers

    Owner OperationsTime 20 minSystem WebinarGeek, Work TrackerSafety Person

    Why It Matters

    Call-to-action clicks, applications and calls have no API. They are entered by hand after each webinar, and until they are, those tiles on the dashboard read "awaiting input". That makes the post-webinar stages of the funnel equation blank.

    How It Works

    What the Operator Does
    • Open WebinarGeek statistics and read the call-to-action clicks.
    • Count applications and booked calls from the Work Tracker and the calendar.
    • Enter them in the place the dashboard reads.

    Every Step

    1. Within a day of the event, open the broadcast statistics.
    2. Record clicks on each of the three buttons.
    3. Record applications and booked calls.
    4. Check the dashboard shows them the next day, with the badge "operator".

    Done When The dashboard no longer shows "awaiting input" for the event.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Each number is badged live, operator, derived or awaiting input. A blank means not available, never zero.

    Common Mistakes

    • Leaving it for a week. The follow-up decisions are made in the first three days.

    9.4 Process the Applications

    Owner Operator, operationsTime 10 min per applicationSystem Application sheetSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    The application is the first moment a prospect commits something. A slow decision loses the buyer. The sheet's automation handles the email, so the only manual step is the decision itself.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Reads the application rows and summarises each: years of experience, the qualification rule result, and any note.
    What the Operator Does
    • The operator reads the application and sets Approval, column Q, to Accepted or Rejected.

    Every Step

    1. Open the Programme Applicants tab. Read the new rows.
    2. Set Approval to Accepted or Rejected.
    3. The sheet's automation sends the matching email from the team address, copies the team, and writes the send in the log column.
    4. Check the log column. Any non-empty value counts as handled, which prevents a duplicate send. An hourly sweep catches anything missed.
    5. For an accepted applicant, the email carries the payment link.

    Done When Every decided application has an email and a log entry.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Three forms feed sheets: the FINTECH one, a partner (CISI) form with its own sheet and Calendly, and a future-cohort form.

    Common Mistakes

    • Never reset the application sheet's set-up on a live sheet.
    • Saving a change to the sheet's automation is not the same as publishing it.
    • The form still mentions the May cohort. That wording needs updating.

    9.5 Book the Call: Calendly or a GHL Calendar

    Owner Operator, operationsTime Setup 2 hoursSystem Calendly, GHLSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    Two ways to book the call both work. Calendly is already connected to GHL, so a booking made there reaches GHL as a contact update and an appointment. GHL also has its own calendar, which keeps the booking, the contact and the reminders in one tool and can rotate bookings between team members. The team can use either, or one for each type of call. What matters is that every booking ends up on the contact in GHL.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Writes the test plan and checks that a test booking from either option creates the right contact activity and stage.
    What the Operator Does
    • Choose the option for each type of call.
    • Test a booking from each option before switching any link in a slide or an email.

    Every Step

    1. Option A, Calendly: open the Calendly connection to GHL and check which event types it covers. Book a test call and check the contact is created or updated, the appointment appears and the pipeline stage moves to Call Booked.
    2. Option B, a GHL calendar: in GHL open Calendars and create a calendar for the call. Add team members for a rotating calendar. Book a test call and check the same three things.
    3. Pick which option each link uses: the acceptance email, the slides, the thank-you page and the chase emails (9.15 lists every door).
    4. Switch a link only after its test passes, and keep the other option's link live until the first week of real bookings has no problems.
    5. If one option is later retired, cancel it last, after every link that used it has been replaced.

    Done When A test booking from each option in use creates the contact activity and the Call Booked stage in GHL.

    STATUS: BOTH OPTIONS AVAILABLE. CALENDLY IS CONNECTED TO GHL. BUILD STEPS FOR A GHL CALENDAR IN 9.15   AS OF: 2026-10-19

    What Good Looks Like

    • Either option is fine; the test decides, not the preference.
    • Every booking is visible on the contact in GHL.

    Common Mistakes

    • Switching a link before its test.
    • Retiring an option while links to it are still in sent emails or on slides.

    9.6 Take Payment and Onboard

    Owner OperationsTime 15 min per customerSystem GHL PaymentsSafety Read

    Why It Matters

    Revenue lives in GHL payments, not in the Opportunities pipeline, which is empty. A customer is a person, not an order. A deposit plus its balance is one customer, and one person who paid from two email addresses is merged.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Reads revenue and customers live from payment transactions and states which of the three counts is meant: total, webinar-attributed or outreach-sourced.
    What the Operator Does
    • Check the payment page and the acceptance email carry the current price.
    • Check the payment-success page sends the welcome email, the joining link and the cohort WhatsApp group.

    Every Step

    1. Ask: "What is revenue and the number of customers, and which are webinar-attributed?"
    2. Check the figure comes with the time it was read.
    3. For a new customer, check the welcome email and the group link were sent.
    4. Never mark a customer paid by hand or from a thank-you page. Payment is confirmed only by a server message from the payment system.

    Done When Revenue and customers are read live, onboarding checked.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Owner and test payments and duplicate orders are excluded. Each customer is credited to the last webinar whose outreach list held them before they paid.

    Common Mistakes

    • Quoting the old paid-customers file. It is a stale export.
    • Marking a deal paid by hand or from the thank-you page.

    9.7 Use the GHL Pipeline and Conversation View

    Owner Operator, operationsTime Setup half a daySystem GHLSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    GHL is the source of truth for contact data and offers more than is used. Pipelines show each applicant as a card from application to payment. A conversation view puts email, SMS and WhatsApp messages in one thread beside the contact's activity. When volume grows, one person can set appointments while another takes the calls.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Designs the pipeline stages and the conversation set-up as a spec, then reads the result.
    What the Operator Does
    • Build the pipeline in GHL from the spec. Decide who sets appointments and who takes calls.

    Every Step

    1. Write the stages for the Board Programme: application received, pre-qualified, under review, call booked, accepted, deposit paid, paid in full, onboarded.
    2. Build the pipeline in GHL and add the cards from the application sheet.
    3. Check the conversation view shows messages and form submissions for a test contact.
    4. Once tracking (6.4) is on, add page visits to the view.

    Done When Every applicant has a card in a stage.

    What Good Looks Like

    • At the last read (October 2026) tier was not recorded reliably. A tier field and a dedicated customer tag give clean lists.

    Common Mistakes

    • Starting the pipeline without deciding who owns each stage.

    9.8 Give Every Pipeline Stage an Entry Event, an Owner and a Clock

    Owner OperationsTime 1 hourSystem GHLSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    A stage that nobody can name the entry event for should be deleted. If a card moves only when someone remembers to drag it, the pipeline will lie. Ten honest stages beat twenty aspirational ones. This is the reference eleven-stage board, with No Show and Unqualified as exits. Reference board

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Writes the entry event, owner and clock beside each stage in the spec, and checks a test contact moves on its own.
    What the Operator Does
    • Build the board in GHL from the spec. Put a name on each owner role.

    Every Step

    1. Write the entry event beside each stage before building a single automation. If no event exists, delete the stage.
    2. Name three roles, even if one person plays all three: setter, closer and coordinator.
    3. Set the clocks: setter first response within 24 hours, and a call within 5 minutes for an enquiry during working hours; closer sends the proposal within 24 hours of a good call; coordinator fixes missing data within 6 hours and reviews anything stuck in Follow-Up for more than 7 days.
    4. Put an owner and a next action date on every open deal. A deal without a next action is a deal nobody is working.
    5. Colour the two exits so No Show and Unqualified stand out on the board.
    6. Test with a fake lead: book a call as a test contact with a source tag on the link and check the contact, the stage and the confirmation. Mark the appointment no-show and check the missed-call tag and stage appear on their own. Rebook, mark it showed and walk it to a test payment. If any step needed a hand, that move is not wired yet.

    Done When Every stage names its event, owner and clock, and a fake lead walks the whole board without a hand on it.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Unqualified today is not unqualified forever.

    Common Mistakes

    • A stage with no entry event.
    • A deal with no next action date.

    9.9 Add the Extra Tags and Fields

    Owner Operations, ClaudeTime 1 hourSystem GHLSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    The webinar tags are not enough once calls and proposals begin. Fourteen extra tags and nine fields let every chase, review and report read the same record. They are created before the stages and the workflows that use them, because a tag that does not exist silently breaks every workflow that listens for it. Reference set

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Creates the tags and custom values the connection allows, after a plan card, and reads the list back.
    What the Operator Does
    • Create any field the connection cannot create, in the GHL settings, with the exact name and type.

    Every Step

    1. Create the fields first, because every stage and workflow reads them. Name them exactly as in the table.
    2. Create the tags. Type a tag once and it exists everywhere. Spell them exactly.
    3. Keep the existing webinar tags unchanged. Never rename them.
    4. Read the tag list and field list back and compare with the tables below.

    Done When All fourteen tags and nine fields exist with these exact names.

    The Fourteen Extra Tags

    TagSet whenWhat it does
    call-no-showA booked sales call is missedStarts the recovery run. Kept separate from a missed session.
    enquiryA person asks without bookingStarts the two-hour chase
    ghostedSilent at day seven of recoveryHands the person to the 52-week engine
    nurtureA not-now answerParks the deal in Nurture-Back
    deal-lostThe deal is closed as lostStarts the door-open email
    referralA lead comes from a referralCredits the advocate
    reactivatedA dormant contact repliesReturns the person to the main board
    confirmedThe WhatsApp confirmation went outStops the confirmation resending
    webinar-completedThe attendance sync has finishedStarts the follow-up
    next-step-takenThey booked or boughtStops every nudge
    bookedA call is bookedStops attended and no-show chasers
    proposal-sentA proposal goes outStarts the proposal watchdog
    proposal-acceptedThe proposal is acceptedStops the proposal chase
    proposal-declinedThe proposal is declinedStops the chase, starts the lost path

    The Nine Extra Fields

    FieldTypeUsed for
    next_action_dateDateEvery open deal. A deal without one is not being worked.
    lost_reasonDropdownSet when a deal closes lost. Timing feeds Nurture-Back.
    reengage_afterDateSet when someone says not now
    score_bandDropdownTop, middle or bottom, from the qualification rule
    diagnostic_scoreNumberThe score behind the band
    priorityDropdownRouting: first, second or third priority
    deal_valueNumberThe value of the open deal
    proposal_sent_atDate and timeStarts the 48-hour chase
    proposal_expires_atDateExtend once or close as lost with reason timing

    What Good Looks Like

    • Tag writes are additive.

    Common Mistakes

    • A typo in a tag name, which silently breaks every workflow that listens for it.

    9.10 Run the Four Extra Pipelines and the Weekly Review

    Owner OperationsTime 15 min a weekSystem GHLSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    The main pipeline forgets four kinds of people: missed calls, the not-nows, happy customers who could refer, and contacts who went quiet. Four small pipelines beside it track them like deals, each with one owner and one way back into the main board. None of them is a dead end. Reference set

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Reads the cards in each pipeline and lists those with no next action, those that have not moved in two weeks, and anyone who replied and was never answered.
    What the Operator Does
    • Give each pipeline one owner. Do the fifteen-minute weekly review.

    Every Step

    1. Create the four pipelines beside the main one, with the stages below.
    2. Give each one entry trigger and one exit that lands in the main board or the 52-week engine.
    3. Each week give each pipeline fifteen minutes. Look for cards with no next action date, cards that have not moved in two weeks, and anyone who replied but was not answered.
    4. Move or close every card that is touched. Do not leave a card to read next week.

    Done When Each extra pipeline has an entry trigger, a weekly review and an exit.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Every card has a next action date.

    Common Mistakes

    • Treating an exit as a dead end.

    9.11 Recover a Missed Sales Call

    Owner Setter, closerTime Setup 2 hoursSystem GHL, calendar, messagingSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    A booked call that nobody turns up to is the most expensive miss in the funnel, because everything before it was paid for. Recovery starts inside minutes, runs for seven days, and stops the moment the person rebooks. A person who misses the webinar and a person who misses a booked call are different people with different messages. They never share a tag.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Drafts the text, the short email and the seven-day mix from the call's original booking answers, for approval.
    What the Operator Does
    • Approve the copy. Make the two calls the same day. Build the workflow from the spec.

    Every Step

    1. Add a missed-call tag that is different from the webinar not-watched tag.
    2. Within five minutes: a text with new time slots.
    3. Within fifteen minutes: an email under 80 words, saying what they would have got and giving the rebook link.
    4. The same day: two call attempts, from a task and an alert to the contact owner.
    5. Across seven days: a mix of email, text and calls. Any rebooking stops everything.
    6. No reply by day seven: tag ghosted and hand the person to the 52-week engine.

    Done When A test no-show gets its tag, the text, the email and the task without a hand on it.

    What Good Looks Like

    • A rebook link goes out inside the hour.

    Common Mistakes

    • Sharing one tag for two kinds of miss.
    • Letting a missed call wait.

    9.12 Set the Chase Timings

    Owner Operations, ClaudeTime 1 hourSystem GHL, emailSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    A follow-up that comes too late loses the buyer, and one that never stops irritates them. Four chase clocks cover the gaps in the funnel. Each stops the moment the person books or pays.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Writes each chase email for approval and checks that each one stops on a booking or payment.
    What the Operator Does
    • Approve the copy and the timings. Check a test contact receives none after booking.

    Every Step

    1. Enquiry not booked: email after 2 hours.
    2. Attendee or viewer not booked: email after 2 days.
    3. Booked call marked no-show: message after 15 minutes.
    4. Proposal with no answer: email after 48 hours, then a call a day after it.
    5. Keep the missed-call email under 80 words.
    6. Check that an empty follow-up never sends, and that anyone who books or pays gets none.

    Done When Four chase clocks are set, each one stops on a booking or payment, and each email is approved.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Chases stop on book or pay.

    Common Mistakes

    • A chase that keeps going after payment.

    9.13 Prepare the Call-Stage Assets

    Owner Claude drafts, the operator approvesTime Half a daySystem Booking page, GHL, documentsSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    The call decides the sale, and everything around it is prepared in advance. Booking questions that double as call prep save the first ten minutes. Reminders with a reschedule link turn a miss into a move. Scripts and battlecards make the call repeatable, and a four-email sequence closes the loop afterwards.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Drafts the booking questions, scripts, battlecards and the four emails from the offer and the objections heard most.
    What the Operator Does
    • The operator edits and approves each. The operator decides the proposal template.

    Every Step

    1. Booking page: 3 to 6 qualification questions, one per line. Ask what helps prepare: where they are now, the goal and the timeline. Each answer should change how the call runs.
    2. Confirmation plus reminders at 48 hours, 24 hours and 1 hour before. Put a reschedule link in every reminder. A moved call beats a no-show.
    3. Scripts: discovery, walkthrough, close.
    4. Battlecards for the two objections heard most: the objection in the buyer's words, the answer, one piece of proof.
    5. Proposal template and a pricing calculator, so a proposal takes ten minutes.
    6. After the call, four emails: the recap with the next step, the recording with a rebooking link, the plan, one final follow-up. Then stop.
    7. If the sale happens in one call, skip the proposal stage. If several people must say yes, give the contact something to forward.

    Done When Every asset exists, has been read aloud once, and has been tested on a fake booking.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Every reminder carries a reschedule link.

    Common Mistakes

    • Booking questions that collect data but do not help prepare the call.

    9.14 Build Task and Alert Workflows That Never Message the Contact

    Owner Claude designs, operations buildsTime 2 hoursSystem GHLSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    Every email and WhatsApp message in this funnel is already sent by WebinarGeek, GHL's templates or the sequences set up for the event. A GHL workflow that also sends an email or text would reach the person twice. So these workflows only assign tasks and alert the team. They send nothing to the contact.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Writes the spec for each workflow and reads them back to name any that are missing or still drafts.
    What the Operator Does
    • Build each workflow in GHL with the exact name, save it as a draft, test on one contact and publish after a go.

    Every Step

    1. Build a workflow for each row of the table, named with the FC prefix.
    2. Use the tag as the trigger, a wait where shown, an if-else check for a booking, and then only a task or an internal alert.
    3. Never add a send email or send text step to these workflows. Alerts go to team members.
    4. Walk one test contact from registration to proposal and check each task and alert appears.
    5. Publish. Leave any older draft email workflow unpublished.

    Done When Seven workflows exist, none sends a message to the contact, and a test contact produced every task.

    WorkflowTriggerWhat it does

    Common Mistakes

    • Adding a send step. It reaches the person twice.

    9.15 Get Every Call Into GHL and See Where It Is

    Owner Operator, operationsTime Setup half a day, then automaticSystem GHL Calendars, GHL pipeline, the dashboardSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    Every call must end up on the contact in GHL, whichever door the person came through and whichever booking option it used: Calendly, which is already connected to GHL, or a GHL calendar. That keeps the contact, the appointment, the pipeline stage and the reminders in one place. A call that never reaches the contact is invisible to the reminders and to the no-show recovery.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Writes the booking questions and the test plan, and reads a test booking back: the contact, the appointment, the stage and the tags.
    • Reads the contact's record after a booking and says which of the places below holds it.
    What the Operator Does
    • Build the calendar, the team and the booking page in GHL from the steps below.
    • Switch each link only after its test passes, and cancel the old booking tool last.

    Every Step

    1. For a GHL calendar: in GHL open Calendars and create one calendar for the call: its length, the buffer, the working hours in the audience's time zone and the team members. Add them as a round robin so a booking lands on whoever is free.
    2. Write the booking questions so they double as call preparation (9.13): current board status, what they want from the call, anything the setter should know. Map each answer to a contact field.
    3. Set the confirmation: an immediate email and the calendar invite, from a template that carries the reschedule link.
    4. Set what a booking does: create or update the contact by email, add a call-booked tag, and move the contact to Call Booked in the Sales Pipeline (25.6).
    5. Replace or keep the booking link at every door in the table below, one door at a time. A link may point at Calendly or at the GHL calendar. Test each with a test address and read the result.
    6. Mark call bookings that come from the webinar with the webinar tag, so the dashboard can credit the right event.
    7. Retire an option only after a week with no booking problems, and only if the team decides to use one option (9.5).

    Done When A test booking from each door creates the contact, the appointment on the right team member's calendar, the call-booked tag and the Call Booked stage, and the confirmation arrives.

    The offer minute and the call-to-action slidesThe link on the slide and in the chat (8.5).Same booking page, with the source tag on the link.As above, plus the tag showing it came from the webinar
    A poll answer in the live sessionFour yes answers trigger a personal booking message within the hour (8.5).The message carries the same booking link.As above
    The thank-you page and the replay pageA skip-the-wait door where it is tested (13.2).Same booking page.As above
    Chase emailsEnquiry, attendee and proposal chases carry the rebook link (9.12).Same booking page; the chase stops on a booking.As above

    Where a Booked Call Can Be Seen

    PlaceWhat it showsWho uses it
    GHL CalendarsEvery appointment by day, week and team member, with its statusSetter and closer, every morning
    The contact recordThe appointment, the answers to the booking questions, the messages and the tagsAnyone preparing for the call
    The Sales PipelineEach person as a card in Call Booked, Call Reminder Sent, Call Completed, No Show, Follow-Up Sent or WonThe operator, in the weekly review

    Two Facts About GHL Calendars

    The 1:1 call bookings sit in a specific GHL calendar that the standard calendar list does not show, so look for it by name. The access token the connection uses does not yet cover calendar events; adding that permission would let the dashboard count calls from the calendar itself.

    What Good Looks Like

    • One calendar, one booking page, many links.
    • Every link carries a source tag, so the dashboard knows which door produced the call.

    Common Mistakes

    • Leaving an old booking link in a sent email or a slide.
    • Booking questions that are never read before the call.

    9.16 Run the Post-Webinar Sales Call Workflow: Reminders and No-Show

    Owner Claude designs, operations buildsTime Half a day, then automaticSystem GHL workflows, Sales Pipeline, email templatesSafety Send now

    Why It Matters

    A booked call that nobody attends is the most expensive miss in the funnel. The call workflow does four jobs: confirm the booking, remind before the call, record what happened, and follow up after it. It is the one place where a GHL workflow does message the contact, because no other tool sends call reminders. It still sends nothing that another tool already sends (9.14).

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Writes the spec for each step and the message copy for approval.
    • Reads the workflow list and says whether it is a draft or published, and reads a test contact's messages and tags.
    What the Operator Does
    • Build the workflow in GHL from the table, save it as a draft and test it on one contact.
    • Say send now before publishing, because it will message people.

    Every Step

    1. Start from the existing draft named Sales Pipeline: Call Reminders (read its status first; it is a draft until published). Use the Sales Call Emails templates for the 24 hour and 1 hour reminders.
    2. Trigger: an appointment is booked on the call calendar. First condition: the contact has an email address; if a phone number is present, the reminders can also go by text or WhatsApp where consent allows.
    3. Send the confirmation immediately, with the date and time in the person's time zone and the reschedule link.
    4. Wait until 24 hours before the appointment, then send the first reminder and move the contact to Call Reminder Sent.
    5. Wait until 1 hour before, then send the second reminder. Skip any reminder whose time has already passed.
    6. After the appointment time, the team sets the outcome in GHL: Call Completed or No Show. Do not guess an outcome automatically.
    7. On Call Completed: start the four-email follow-up from 9.13 and move the contact to Follow-Up Sent. On a proposal with no answer: the chase in 9.12.
    8. On No Show: start the recovery run in 9.11 and tag the miss with its own tag, never the webinar no-show tag.
    9. On payment confirmed: stop every reminder and chase, move the contact to Won and start the client journey in 9.17.
    10. Test with a contact booked 65 minutes ahead, check both reminders and both stops (booked again, paid), then publish after send now.

    Done When A test contact booked 65 minutes ahead receives the confirmation and both reminders, an outcome moves them through the stages, a no-show starts the recovery run, and a payment stops everything.

    Reminder 1Appointment bookedUntil 24 hours beforeAppointment still bookedFirst reminder, the booking questions as call preparationCancelled or rebookedGHL workflow, Sales Call Emails template
    Reminder 2Reminder 1 sentUntil 1 hour beforeNot already pastShort reminder with the join detailsThe appointment startsGHL workflow, Sales Call Emails template

    The rule in 9.14 says a GHL workflow must not send what WebinarGeek or another tool already sends. Call confirmations and call reminders are sent by no other tool, so this workflow is the single sender for them. Publishing the six February starter drafts, or any of the webinar email drafts, would still double-send.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Reminders are anchored to the appointment time, not to the booking time.
    • The outcome is set by a person, so the stage is true.
    • Every message stops on a payment.

    Common Mistakes

    • Publishing the draft without a test.
    • Setting Call Completed automatically for every appointment.
    • Sharing one tag between a webinar no-show and a missed call.

    9.17 From Applicant to Client: The Journey in GHL

    Owner Operator, operationsTime Read in 15 minutesSystem GHL contacts, pipeline, paymentsSafety Read

    Why It Matters

    A person becomes a client in a fixed order: registered, applied, accepted, call booked, call held, paid. Every step leaves a mark in GHL, so that at any moment the record says where the person is, who owns the next move and what will be sent. This card is the map. The cards 9.4 to 9.16 are the steps.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Reads a contact and says which step they are on, from the tags, the fields, the appointment and the payments.
    What the Operator Does
    • Own the decision at each gate: the acceptance, the call outcome and the offer.

    Every Step

    1. Registered: the registration creates the contact and the webinar tags (7.4).
    2. Applied: the application form writes a row to the Programme Applicants tab and the contact record (9.4).
    3. Accepted or rejected: the operator sets Approval and the matching email goes out. Accepted carries the booking link (9.4).
    4. Call booked: the booking creates the appointment and moves the contact to Call Booked (9.15).
    5. Call held: the team sets Call Completed, and the follow-up starts (9.16).
    6. Paid: the payment system confirms the payment to GHL. Nobody marks a payment by hand (9.6).
    7. Client: the contact moves to Won, every chase stops and the onboarding in 9.18 starts.

    Done When For any contact, the team can name the stage, the next event and who owns it from the record alone.

    StageWhat GHL holdsWhere to read it
    Registered, attendedThe webinar tags and the broadcast date fieldThe contact record, Tags
    Applied, acceptedThe application answers, the decision and its email statusThe applicant sheet and the contact record
    Call booked, heldThe appointment, the answers to the booking questions, the pipeline stageGHL Calendars, the contact record, the Sales Pipeline
    PaidThe transaction, with its amount in GBPPayments, Transactions
    ClientThe customer tag and the pricing tier Potential, the course access, the welcome emailThe contact record and Courses

    What Good Looks Like

    • One event per stage.
    • The stage is read from the record, not remembered.

    Common Mistakes

    • Moving a stage by hand to make a report look right.
    • Counting orders as clients.

    9.18 After Someone Becomes a Client: Onboarding in GHL

    Owner Operations, ClaudeTime 15 minutes per client, then automaticSystem GHL payments, workflows, courses, email templatesSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    The sale is the start of a second funnel. Once the payment succeeds, a short list of things must happen the same day: the person is welcomed, given access and told what comes next, and every sales message stops. A client who has paid and still receives chase emails is the fastest way to lose trust.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Reads the new client's record and checks each item in the table: the payment, the tag, the welcome email, the course access and the stopped chases.
    • Drafts the welcome message and the check-in for approval.
    What the Operator Does
    • Approve the welcome copy and the check-in.
    • Check the first client of each cohort by hand.

    Every Step

    1. Payment succeeds. The payment system confirms it to GHL and the transaction appears under Payments. Count the person once (9.6).
    2. The contact moves to Won in the Sales Pipeline and every call reminder and chase stops.
    3. Add the customer tag and record the pricing tier on the contact. The tier field exists, but it is blank on current payers, so fill it for each new client Potential.
    4. The payment-success page sends the welcome email, the joining link and the cohort WhatsApp group, from the Courses welcome template.
    5. The course access workflow gives the contact access to the course. A separate workflow does the same for the lecturer cohort. Read the workflow status first; its trigger cannot be read by the tool connection, so test it on one new client.
    6. Remove the client from every cold and webinar sequence, so they receive invites only if the team decides to invite them.
    7. Send the first check-in before the cohort starts, and a review request after the first module Potential. GHL ships a stock review-request workflow, still a draft, that can be adapted.
    8. Update the dashboard figures: the new client counts once, credited to the last webinar whose list held them before they paid.

    Done When A new client has one recorded payment, the Won stage, a welcome email, course access, no further sales messages and a tag and tier that make a clean list of clients.

    ItemDone byCheck
    Payment recorded onceThe payment system and GHLOne transaction, GBP, one person
    Stage Won, chases stoppedA GHL workflowNo reminder or chase after payment
    Customer tag and tierOperations, then a workflow PotentialThe tag is on the contact and the tier field is filled
    Welcome and joining linkThe payment-success page and the Courses welcome templateThe email arrived, the group link works
    Course accessThe Grant Course Access workflow (published)The client can open the course
    Out of cold and webinar sequencesA suppression ruleNo invite in the next batch
    Check-in and review requestA GHL workflow PotentialSent before the start and after module one
    What Is Not Built Yet

    The customer tag, the tier on every payer, the check-in and the review request are proposals. Today most payers share one tier tag and the tier field is blank. Build them as drafts in GHL, test on one contact, then publish after a go.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Every item in the table can be read from the record.
    • The first client of each cohort is checked by hand.

    Common Mistakes

    • Marking a client paid before the payment system confirms it.
    • Leaving the client in the cold sequences.
    • Never recording the tier, so revenue cannot be read by tier.

    The Lessons in This Section

    • The first three days decide most of the revenue. Schedule the sequences before the event.
    • A no-show list comes from WebinarGeek, never from a GHL tag.
    • The only manual decision in the application step is the operator's. The email and the log are automatic.

    Tools and Systems

    What every tool is, what it does in this funnel, what else it can do, and how the tools connect as one system.

    Master Playbook

    The Tools at a Glance

    Ten tools carry the funnel today. Everything else in this part is either a detail of one of them or an option beside them.

    The Tools as One System

    This part answers one question: if I change something here, what else is affected? The map shows the whole chain, from where leads come from to the dashboard. Below it, every tool has the same profile, so any tool can be understood without reading the rest of the playbook.

    Read each profile as three layers: what the tool is, what it is used for now and what else it can do. The last two are marked Current Available. Each profile also says how Claude reaches the tool, what it reads, what it writes and what needs a person's approval.

    The Tools as One System

    Pick a Tool. See What Moves.

    Select a tool. Its stages light up, the tools that feed it show above it in blue, the tools it feeds show in green, and what travels along each connection is listed here.

    How to Use the Map

    Each column is a stage of the journey. A tool that appears in more than one column does work in more than one stage. Selecting a tool lights its stages, draws the connections it has with its neighbours, and lists what travels along each. A change to a tool can affect every tool in blue (what feeds it) or green (what it feeds).

    How Data Moves

    Two animations. The first follows a wave from decision to review and shows who touches it. The second follows one registration.

    How Claude Reaches Each Tool

    Claude never has one master key. Each tool is reached in one of four ways, and the way sets what Claude may do without asking.

    Tool Profiles

    Open any tool. Every profile has two groups. The permanent profile says what the tool is, why FINTECH uses it, what it owns, what it connects to, what can go wrong and how to verify it; it stays true when a campaign ends. The current state says how the tool is configured today and carries its read date.

    Evidence words in the current-state group. Verified: read live on 20 October 2026. Tool present: a connector tool for it is visible in the 20 October session but was not called. Documented: recorded in the project sources, not re-read. Unverified: no source read. AI potential is what Claude could do, not a verified integration. Automation potential is not the same as what is implemented today.

    ApolloSupplies new leads that match the persona, with companies already owned excluded so they are not paid for twice.Current Official connector A person in the tool's own screen
    Permanent profile RULE
    What it is
    A people and company database. Searches by industry, seniority and country and exports contact details.
    How Claude reaches it
    Official connector A person in the tool's own screen

    Search and counts through the official Apollo connector. Buying and exporting are done by a person in Apollo's own screen.

    What Claude reads
    Search results, counts and headroom by industry, geography and title.
    What Claude writes
    Nothing. Claude never buys or exports.
    What needs approval
    Any purchase or export, and the spend behind it (Go).
    What it is used for
    Supplies new leads that match the persona, with companies already owned excluded so they are not paid for twice.
    Where it sits
    Lead
    Inputs
    Search criteria (industries, geographies, titles) and the exclusion lists.
    Outputs
    A raw lead list for cleaning.
    How it is used
    1. Read the headroom and touch counts on the dashboard (3.1).
    2. Decide whether to buy at all (3.2).
    3. Write the search order: industries, geographies, titles, owned companies excluded.
    4. Operations buys and exports. Searching is free to read; buying spends money.
    5. Hand the file to cleaning (3.3).
    What it connects to
    Before: audience analysis from past webinar results. After: lead cleaning.
    What else it can do
    Enrichment, saved lists, sequences and enrolment. The connector can search and count; buying and bulk export stay with a person. Available
    Automation potential
    Searching and counting headroom. Building the search order from the dashboard.
    AI potential
    Turning a persona into a search order; reading headroom against owned counts; flagging off-persona results.
    Human responsibility
    Deciding to spend, approving the list in writing, running the purchase.
    Risks and common mistakes
    • A raw list can be mostly off-persona: the 110k list was 70 percent non-financial.
    • Bought lists can carry other clients' contacts and swapped first and last names.
    • Buying spends money and cannot be undone.
    Failure modes
    • Credits spent on a list that is mostly off-persona.
    • A duplicate purchase of companies already owned.
    • Swapped first and last names in the export.
    How to verify it works
    Compare the export count with the search count before paying, and run the cleaning pass on a sample of 50 rows.
    Safety
    Any purchase or export, and the spend behind it (Go).
    System of record
    Not a system of record. The owned pool is held in the cleaned files and the outreach sheet.
    Alternatives
    ZoomInfo, Clay, LinkedIn Sales Navigator (not in use)

    What it is
    A set of rules that Claude applies to the shared list files, turning raw lists into one clean pool.

    Claude on shared files

    Claude applies the rules to the list files the team shares with it and reports back. No outside tool is needed.

    What Claude reads
    The raw lists and the exclusion sources.
    What Claude writes
    A cleaned list file and a short report of what was removed and why.
    What needs approval
    The cleaned list, before it is loaded anywhere (Go).
    What it is used for
    Makes sure nobody is contacted who should not be, and nobody twice.
    Where it sits
    Lead
    Inputs
    Raw lists, the exclusion sources (webinar attendees, RSVP responders, applicants, paid customers, opt-outs).
    Outputs
    A deduplicated, industry-filtered, exclusion-checked pool with LinkedIn links re-attached.
    How it is used
    1. Collate every source and deduplicate by lowercased email. Never by phone.
    2. Keep only the nine financial industries.
    3. Remove everyone engaged before: attendees, RSVPs, applicants, paid.
    4. Remove other clients' contacts.
    5. Re-attach LinkedIn links by email.
    6. Normalise countries; split UK from other European where needed.
    What it connects to
    Before: Apollo and earlier lists. After: the Outreach Sheet.
    What else it can do
    Any additional exclusion source can be added as another file. Segment exports in any column order. Available

    All of it, once the exclusion files are current. Claude reads the list and reports before anything is run.
    AI potential
    Applying the rules, counting what each rule removed, and reporting before any file is written.
    Human responsibility
    Approving the result and confirming the exclusion sources are current.
    Risks and common mistakes
    • Cleaning against a stale exclusion file re-contacts people who already attended.
    • Phone-based deduplication merges unrelated people on shared switchboards.
    Failure modes
    • A stale exclusion file re-contacts attendees.
    • Phone matching merges unrelated people.
    • Another client's source rows slip in.
    How to verify it works
    Report the count removed by each rule and sample ten removed rows.
    Safety
    The cleaned list, before it is loaded anywhere (Go).
    System of record
    The cleaned pool is the record of who is eligible.

    A database query on the same rules

    A set of connector tools that select, send, verify and stamp one outreach wave.
    How Claude reaches it
    Connector tool

    The connector's wave tools: preview, send, status and cancel. Claude shows the preview as the plan card.

    What Claude reads
    Unsent rows, the broadcast date, past contact history and sender capacity.
    What Claude writes
    Calendar campaigns and the stamps that record them.
    What needs approval
    Every send (Send now). The preview is Read.
    What it is used for
    Applies every safety rule in one place, so no wave depends on someone remembering them.
    Where it sits
    Traffic
    Inputs
    Unsent leads, the webinar date and broadcast, the invitation text and variation.
    Outputs
    Calendar campaigns and a send record.
    How it is used
    1. Select and filter the leads.
    2. Preview: Claude shows the plan card through the connector.
    3. On an explicit send now, create the campaigns. Creating one is sending.
    4. Wait, verify each reached ready, then stamp only those.
    5. Read the RSVPs; bridge Yes and Maybe replies into the webinar.
    What it connects to
    Before: the outreach sheet. After: Tantra.
    What else it can do
    Native staggered timing with a schedule per chunk. Cancelling a wave through the connector. Available
    Automation potential
    Everything after the send now.
    AI potential
    Selecting the pool, filtering, and checking the date, the balance and the contacted history before the plan card.
    Human responsibility
    Choosing the size and the mix, and typing send now.
    Risks and common mistakes
    • The wave tools have no daily-limit guard of their own. Keep to the real ceiling (16.15).
    • Two campaigns are stuck active and cannot be recovered. Do not retry a failed create without reading what exists.
    Failure modes
    • A campaign created with the wrong date.
    • Auto-register off, so RSVPs are never registered.
    • A stuck campaign that cannot be paused.
    How to verify it works
    Verify the campaign reached ready, then compare invites with the sending mailboxes' calendars.
    Safety
    Every send (Send now). The preview is Read.
    System of record
    Not a record. The calendar campaigns and the RSVP pull are.
    Alternatives
    Instantly email only
    Related sections
    4.1, 4.2, 4.5, 16.15

    What it is
    An outreach tool that adds the webinar to a lead's Google Calendar from a pool of sender mailboxes.
    How Claude reaches it
    Connector tool API

    The connector's tools read RSVP counts and senders. Campaigns are created through the wave tools, which call Tantra's API.

    What Claude reads
    Sender mailboxes, RSVP counts for each list, campaign status.
    What Claude writes
    Calendar campaigns, only through an approved wave.
    What needs approval
    Every campaign (Send now).
    What it is used for
    The largest invitation channel. The lead answers Yes, Maybe or No inside their own calendar.
    Where it sits
    Traffic
    Inputs
    Leads, invitation text, sender mailboxes, an event time in the audience's time zone.
    Outputs
    Calendar invitations and RSVP answers.
    How it is used
    1. Plan the wave (4.1).
    2. Send through the wave tools only (4.2).
    3. Read RSVPs from the list counts, never the sent counter.
    4. Bridge Yes and Maybe replies into the webinar.
    What it connects to
    Before: the wave sender. After: the sender mailboxes, then the landing page and WebinarGeek.
    What else it can do
    Other channels on the account (LinkedIn, WhatsApp, personalised messages) are reported as available and expected to be usable on the current plan. Available
    Automation potential
    Sending, scheduling and RSVP collection.
    AI potential
    Reading RSVP counts and reporting acceptance by wave and segment.
    Human responsibility
    Writing the invite, approving each wave.
    Risks and common mistakes
    • Creating a campaign is sending: no draft, and pause fails.
    • The campaign list under-reports sends because deleted campaigns vanish.
    • The sent counter is always zero for calendar campaigns.
    • Auto-register cannot be added after creation.
    Failure modes
    • The campaign list under-reports sends.
    • sentCount shows zero for calendar campaigns.
    • Contacts are duplicated per list.
    How to verify it works
    Read RSVP counts from the list endpoint; never derive pending.
    Safety
    Every campaign (Send now).
    System of record
    The calendar RSVP pull is the record of who answered. The contact history is the record of who was invited.
    Alternatives
    Instantly, A calendar invite sent from the CRM

    What it is
    A cold-email platform: campaigns, sending mailboxes, warm-up and analytics.
    How Claude reaches it
    Connector tool

    The connector's Instantly tools: campaigns, analytics, duplicate, preview leads, add leads, update, activate and pause.

    What Claude reads
    Campaign settings, sent and bounced counts, lead previews.
    What Claude writes
    A duplicate campaign, added leads, an updated date, a pause or an activation.
    What needs approval
    Duplicate, add leads and update need a go. Activate is Send now. Pause is always allowed.
    What it is used for
    Runs a three-step email sequence for each webinar from separate sending domains.
    Where it sits
    Traffic
    Inputs
    A lead list, the sequence copy, sending mailboxes.
    Outputs
    Sent, bounced and reply counts.
    How it is used
    1. Duplicate the last campaign and update the date (4.3).
    2. Add leads from the sheet.
    3. Read the status again before and after activation: a campaign can go live without a start call.
    4. Read replies and run the suppression sweep.
    What it connects to
    Before: the outreach sheet. After: the landing page.
    What else it can do
    Separate sequences by segment, A/B copy testing, more mailboxes and domains. Available
    Automation potential
    Duplicating, adding leads, pausing; activation after send now.
    AI potential
    Drafting copy variants, reading replies and reporting reply, bounce and sent counts.
    Human responsibility
    Approving the copy and the activation.
    Risks and common mistakes
    • Reply analytics under-report badly, and opens are not tracked.
    • High bounce on older lists damages the domains (11.6).
    Failure modes
    • A campaign goes active without a start call.
    • Reply counts under-report and open counts are zero.
    • Campaign ids change for every webinar.
    How to verify it works
    List the campaigns live before saying anything about status; read replies, not counters.
    Safety
    Duplicate, add leads and update need a go. Activate is Send now. Pause is always allowed.
    System of record
    Send and bounce counts. Not a reliable record of replies.
    Alternatives
    Another cold email platform
