    Part 16

    The Build Method: Stand Up, Extend and Protect the Estate

    The phases that built the sending estate, and the plain steps for extending, repairing and handing it over.

    Master Playbook

    16 task cards2 sectionsReviewed by Technical owner

    The Phases and the Rule That Keeps Them Reusable

    This part is the method that built the sending estate and that extends or repairs it. It is client-agnostic: the same phases apply to any funnel, and each client's own values live in its own settings and notes, never baked into a shared tool. For FINTECH Circle the estate already exists, so this part matters in three situations: adding capacity (a new domain, mailbox or channel), replacing something that has worn out, and handing the system to someone new.

    Two tracks run at once. The infrastructure track is the long pole, because warm-up takes two to three weeks, so it starts on day one. The data track (persona, ICP, list, cleaning) runs in parallel. Campaigns need both tracks finished: a validated list with cold mailboxes cannot send, and warm mailboxes with no approved ICP have nothing to send to.

    The Rule That Keeps It Reusable

    Sheet ids, access, geographies and industries live in each client's own settings and key store, never baked into a shared tool. One method, any client, zero risk of pointing at the wrong account. The client's own workspace is the boundary: Claude working on one client cannot reach another's data. Anything phrased 'remember to' is a latent bug, so enforce it in the tool and let the document point at the tool.

    16.1 Provision in the Right Order

    Owner OperationsTime Plan 1 day, build 2 to 3 weeksSystem All toolsSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    The order matters because some tools need another to exist first. The sequencer account must exist before the mailbox vendor's intake form, because the form asks for its credentials. A mailbox clock starts when warm-up starts, not when the form is sent. Doing these out of order costs weeks.

    Every Step

    1. Infrastructure track, day 1: the CRM sub-account (early, so scaffolding can happen in parallel); the Instantly account, sized for the capacity needed; domains (shortlist, then decide who buys); the mailbox vendor intake; the Google Cloud project and service account for the calendar channel; the Tantra account with connectors and senders; LinkedIn seats if a LinkedIn channel is added.
    2. Data track, day 1: the questionnaire, then the buyer-persona call, the persona document and written approval; the ICP to the data vendor; cleaning, segregation and validation; the master outreach sheet.
    3. When both have landed: WebinarGeek and the remaining setup, then the booking calendar connected in the CRM before the first campaign sends, then content, campaigns and running.
    4. Keys: every key goes in the client's own key store, never in a document or the shared files. Non-secret settings (sheet ids, geographies, daily limits, landing pages) go in the client's settings.

    Done When Both tracks finished, with the booking calendar connected and every key in its own place.

    What Good Looks Like

    • The infrastructure track is never left waiting on the data track.

    Common Mistakes

    • Sending the intake form before the Instantly account exists.

    16.2 Fill the Ownership Register

    Owner Operator, operationsTime 2 hoursSystem One documentSafety Person

    Why It Matters

    Domains, DNS, mailboxes and accounts can each be held by a different party. That decides what survives if a relationship ends. On a vendor path it is normal to end up holding neither the registrar nor the DNS for any sending domain, which puts both outbound channels on one vendor's infrastructure. That can be a legitimate trade, but it must be a decision, not a discovery.

    Every Step

    1. For each asset, write who holds it: the cold-email root domains' registrar; the calendar root domains' registrar; the Cloudflare DNS zones; the Google Workspace inboxes (inbox reputation is the real asset and does not transfer cleanly); the Instantly account; the Tantra account and the Google Cloud service account; the LinkedIn sender accounts; the CRM sub-account.
    2. Write the risk if the relationship ended, row by row.
    3. Mitigate in order of value: move the registrar accounts into the client's or GrowthClub's name even if DNS stays with a vendor; keep the internal Workspace path (below) a real capability; document, per domain, who holds it.
    4. Share the register and keep it current.

    Done When Every row answered in writing, and shared.

    AssetShould be held byRisk if the relationship ends
    Domain registrar, cold-email rootsDecide per clientDomains leave with whoever holds them
    Domain registrar, calendar rootsDecide per clientAs above
    Cloudflare DNS zonesDecide per clientAuthentication and mail routing leave with the holder
    Google Workspace inboxesDecide per clientInbox reputation does not transfer cleanly
    Instantly accountGrowthClub
    Tantra account and Google Cloud service accountGrowthClub
    LinkedIn sender accountsThe client
    CRM sub-accountThe client

    What Good Looks Like

    • A transition becomes an admin task, not an excavation.

    Common Mistakes

    • Discovering months in that nobody holds the registrar.

    16.3 Keep a Cost Register

    Owner OperationsTime 1 hour a quarterSystem Work Tracker cost tabSafety Person

    Why It Matters

    The dashboard's tool cost is a floor, because Tantra, Apollo and hosting are not costed. A cost that is not recorded cannot be compared to what it buys, and a subscription that quietly changes tier is not noticed.

    Every Step

    1. Record every recurring line: its plan tier and what it buys. Instantly (mailbox capacity), the mailbox vendor (inbox count), WebinarGeek, the CRM, Metricool, Tantra, Apollo and hosting.
    2. Record data vendor lists per list, not per month: vendor, ICP, row count and amount.
    3. Reconcile each invoice against the plan tier at every renewal.
    4. Agree in writing whether each subscription is in the client's name or GrowthClub's. That decides what survives if the engagement ends.
    5. Complete the tracker's cost breakdown tab.

    Done When Every line has a cost, a tier and an owner of the account.

    What Good Looks Like

    • The register shows what a customer costs when the dashboard's tool cost is no longer a floor (14.7).

    Common Mistakes

    • An invoice that matches no published tier, and nobody checks what it actually buys.

    16.4 Choose Domains and Authenticate Them

    Owner OperationsTime 1 day plus propagationSystem Registrar, Cloudflare, WorkspaceSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    Inbox reputation is the asset. Authentication, warm-up, pacing and list hygiene all exist to protect it. Domains are chosen for what they signal and are never the brand's main domain. Authentication means three public records that prove a message really came from the domain.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Does the read-only check on every name (11.1) and shows what exists.
    What the Operator Does
    • Choose names and who buys them. Add records exactly as the tool shows.

    Every Step

    1. Split the pool by purpose. A few branded domains close to the company identity, used for follow-ups and warm communication. More anonymised domains for genuinely cold outreach and calendar campaigns: no company name, but related to the problem space (the pattern is topic plus format). Keep every name simple, readable and neutral. Never send cold from the main domain.
    2. Generate the shortlist from the company's own pages: services, positioning, industry terms, recurring phrases. Turn them into naming ideas. Confirm with the client before purchase.
    3. MX for Google Workspace: remove any pre-existing MX records so only Google's remain. SPF (who may send): one TXT record, v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com ~all. Exactly one per domain: two break authentication silently.
    4. DKIM (a signature on each message): in the Workspace admin, Gmail, Authenticate email, pick the domain, generate with selector google, add the TXT record at google._domainkey, then return and click Start Authentication. Repeat per domain.
    5. DMARC (what to do if the checks fail): a TXT record at _dmarc, v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=.... Starting at none is deliberate: it monitors without rejecting, so authentication can be confirmed healthy before tightening (11.5).
    6. Validate every domain before sending, in Google Admin Toolbox, MXToolbox and DNS Checker: SPF present, DKIM valid and active, DMARC detected, MX pointing at Google, no duplicate or conflicting records. A stale SPF or MX left in place is the most frequent silent cause of authentication failure.

    Done When Every domain passes in all three checkers with no duplicate records.

    What Good Looks Like

    • The tracking domain in Instantly is active. Without it, open and click measurement is blind.

    Common Mistakes

    • Two SPF records.
    • Sending cold email from the main brand domain or its subdomains.

    16.5 Warm Up and Set the Limits

    Owner OperationsTime 2 to 3 weeksSystem Instantly, TantraSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    Warm-up is not optional and not a formality. A cold mailbox sending hundreds on day one is how domains get burned, and the damage is slow to appear and slow to repair.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Reads the sender list through the connector and confirms the expected count is connected, with the right warm status and daily maximum.

    Every Step

    1. Confirm warm-up is running and that a gradual increase is configured, not a jump to full volume. Instantly ramps a new mailbox over roughly two to three weeks.
    2. Keep warm-up enabled even after campaigns go live. Continuous warm-up beside live sending maintains reputation.
    3. Do not move an account into a live campaign until its warm-up signals are clean.
    4. Set limits per client. They are policy: calendar per warmed sender, calendar per cold sender, calendar estate-wide, cold email per mailbox, cold email estate-wide, and LinkedIn connection requests. The worked numbers are in 11.7.
    5. In Instantly, the campaign's own daily limit is the binding cap, not the sum of the mailbox limits. A campaign capped below its mailboxes' total leaves paid capacity idle with nothing flagging it.
    6. Make the limit enforceable. The method's campaign-creation tools should refuse a create that would push the day's calendar invites over the configured daily limit. The FINTECH wave tools do not yet carry that guard, so the daily cap is checked by hand on the plan card until it is added.
    7. Verify: the sender list in Tantra shows the expected count connected on this client's service account, with the right warm status and daily maximum.

    Done When Warm-up is running, limits are set, and the connected sender count matches expectation.

    What Good Looks Like

    • To send more, add mailboxes. Never raise a per-account cap.

    Common Mistakes

    • Reading the mailbox limits as the cap when the campaign's own limit is lower.

    16.6 Approve the Persona and ICP in Writing

    Owner Operator, operationsTime 1 daySystem Persona document, data vendorSafety Person

    Why It Matters

    A data vendor scrapes against an ICP (ideal customer profile) the client has approved. That ICP is a commercial commitment, not a working note: an unapproved or sloppy one buys the wrong list at the client's expense, and the invoice is per list, so a rebuilt list is a second invoice.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Drafts the persona document and the filter slice from the call, and reads the vendor's reported total against the send plan.
    What the Operator Does
    • Complete the questionnaire, join the persona call and give written approval.

    Every Step

    1. The questionnaire: what the company sells and to whom, the problem the buyer already knows they have, target industries, titles and seniority, geographies, company size, named accounts to include, accounts and competitors to exclude, and existing customer and lead lists to suppress. Exclusions are the field most often left blank and the most expensive to miss.
    2. The persona call: pressure-test three things. Does the title list exist in the tools, or is it a real job and a near-empty filter? Is the geography the buying geography or the headquarters geography? Is the seniority the buyer or the signer? Measure per client which converts.
    3. Write the persona document and the machine-readable slice (target industries, geographies, seniority, headcount) so every tool filters the same way.
    4. Get written approval. Record the date, who approved and the exact ICP text. When a list comes back wrong, the first question is always which ICP it was built from.
    5. Send the ICP to the vendor. They check the available total in Apollo or ZoomInfo and report it before scraping. Read that number against the send plan: working days to the webinar times daily sending capacity is how many contacts the build can use. A total far below it means the ICP is too narrow, so widen it before paying. A total far above it means buy in tranches.
    6. Record per list: vendor, date, the ICP it was built from, row count, source tool and the invoice amount.

    Done When A written, dated approval on file for every list, and a record of what each list cost and where it came from.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Geography is re-derived from the data, never read off the settings. A stale settings line misleads for months.

    Common Mistakes

    • Sending the ICP to the vendor before the written approval.

    16.7 Clean, Validate and Apply the Exclusion Stack

    Owner OperationsTime 1 to 2 days per listSystem Cleaning pipelineSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    No list enters a campaign unvalidated. One bad list spikes the bounce rate and can damage several sending accounts at once. Nothing in the tooling forces this, so the operator is the gate.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Does the cleaning and shows the counts at each step on a plan card: rows in, rows removed and why.
    What the Operator Does
    • Decide the filters. Check the counts. Say 'go' before the list is loaded.

    Every Step

    1. Keep the vendor file untouched as the receipt for what was paid for. Never edit it in place.
    2. Dedupe by lowercased email across every pool the client has, not only the new one. The overlap between vendor deliveries is routinely large.
    3. Drop rows with no email or no first name, because personalisation fails loudly on them. Segregate into the slices campaigns will use, by geography (check the email domain, not only the country column), persona tier and channel eligibility.
    4. Reconcile the row count against the invoice. A short delivery is a conversation with the vendor that must happen before use.
    5. Validate in four layers, cheapest first: syntax, metadata (free provider, disposable, role account), DNS (does the domain publish MX), then a mailbox check. A syntax or disposable failure stops. The result is reachable yes (the only positive confirmation), reachable no (remove it) or reachable unknown (the check could not find out: not the same as bad). A yes is a point in time, so re-verify before a large send. Validate the pool about to be sent to, not the slice that was easy to validate.
    6. Apply the exclusion stack in this order: the do-not-contact list (unconditional); everyone already in Tantra, from a freshly read snapshot; webinar registrants and attendees; RSVP responders from prior calendar sends; bounces and unsubscribes; region and persona filters.
    7. Refresh the contacted snapshot immediately before every build. A snapshot taken before the last lists existed re-offers the leads just invited. This is the most repeated mistake.
    8. Name every data file with its row count. If the count changes, rename the file. A count that lies is worse than none.

    Done When A list that is deduped, validated, excluded against a fresh snapshot, and reconciled to the invoice.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Zero overlap between batches, checked by joining on email and not by trusting the builder.

    Common Mistakes

    • Sizing a pool from the contacts total. It counts list memberships, not unique people.
    • A channel that predates the current tooling is invisible to the snapshot. Any such channel is a hole in the exclusion stack.
    • Suppressing an address in one system and assuming it is suppressed everywhere. Tantra's unsubscribe works only on contacts already imported. Exclude by email at build time.
    • Trying to remove someone from a Tantra list. Membership cannot be edited. Build a new list. The original must never be attached to a campaign.

    16.8 Write the Copy Under the Rules

    Owner Operations, ClaudeTime 1 daySystem Instantly, Tantra, Consolidated DocumentSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    Each copy rule below was learned from something that went wrong. They are checked on the live campaign, not by reading the draft.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Drafts to the rules, then reads the live campaign back through the connector and compares it with the approved text.
    What the Operator Does
    • Approve the copy and read a real test send in a real inbox.

    Every Step

    1. Zero long dashes, verified by counting characters in the live campaign.
    2. Only the merge tokens that actually resolve. Token syntax does not transfer between platforms. Send a test to a team mailbox and confirm.
    3. Fallbacks drop the name mid-sentence, never substitute a placeholder.
    4. An unsubscribe line in every cold email, verified on every step, not just step one.
    5. Every link tagged for tracking. Zero untagged links is a verification criterion.
    6. Follow-up steps carry no subject, so they thread as replies to step one.
    7. A/B tests need matched audiences or they prove nothing: same title, same event, same list construction, zero overlap, sent on consecutive days. Compare registrations by send date, not by total. Rotate copy across waves and choose on evidence.
    8. Verify the copy went out as written. Every calendar campaign is checked against the template live: character count, link count and dash count. A campaign cloned from another does not necessarily carry the same description. Compare it first.

    Done When The live campaign matches the template, with tokens resolving and every link tagged.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Sequence shapes in use: cold email in several steps a few days apart with an A/B subject only on step one; a single calendar invite where the description is the whole message; a LinkedIn sequence with delays measured from the accept.

    Common Mistakes

    • Trusting the draft that was sent and not the live campaign.
    • A cloned campaign carrying an older description.

    16.9 Pass the Pre-Launch Gate

    Owner OperationsTime 30 minSystem All channelsSafety Send now

    Why It Matters

    Creating a Tantra campaign sends, with no draft. Instantly and LinkedIn campaigns are drafts that need an explicit start. Three platforms, two different send semantics. Know which one is in use, and block the launch if any of the checks below fails.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Builds the plan card (the preview) and reads the whole of it with the person: contact count, event time, description length, sender count and the headroom line.
    • Reads each campaign back after it is created.
    What the Operator Does
    • Open the test links. Say 'send now' only for the exact preview.

    Every Step

    1. Plan the volume first. Count working days to the webinar, divide the audience by them for the daily volume, distribute across accounts within their limits, and record date, owner and leads used for every batch. If the arithmetic does not fit the limits (11.7), the answer is more inboxes or an earlier start, never a higher per-account cap.
    2. Preview first, always, and read the whole plan card, including the headroom line, which catches a mailbox whose remaining quota is being used by something else.
    3. Pin senders explicitly. A clone of an older campaign lists that campaign's senders, which may have been disconnected since. Rotate sender sets between days.
    4. After a create, verify every time: the campaign reads ready, not paused; it runs on one day unless a multi-day spread is intended; and events times guests equals the list size.
    5. Dispatch has taken up to 13 minutes to start, and RSVPs read zero the whole time. Do not conclude a send has failed at five minutes, and do not create a replacement: that is how duplicates happen.
    6. A scheduled campaign can show an event error in Tantra's screen despite a clean status. Re-check after the scheduled time passes.
    7. The gate: every sending account passed warm-up and every domain passes authentication; the list is validated, deduped and excluded; zero overlap with any other list in flight; copy verified live; limits respected; senders pinned and re-read immediately before start; the row map ready to mark; a test send received and read in a real inbox; every link in the sequence opened in a real browser, including the booking link, which must load and show bookable slots.

    Done When Every item passes. If any fails, the launch is blocked.

    What Good Looks Like

    • The booking link is tested by booking a test slot. A dead booking link makes the funnel end in nothing.

    Common Mistakes

    • Creating a campaign to see what happens. Preview first, always.

    16.10 Run the Daily Loop

    Owner OperationsTime 20 min a daySystem Dashboard, sheet, toolsSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    Deliverability is maintained continuously, not periodically. An account that underperforms despite warm-up and clean lists drags down the accounts around it, and a campaign that keeps sending while deliverability degrades burns the inboxes needed for the next one.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Reads the live state through the connector and the dashboard each day, and names anything failing.
    What the Operator Does
    • Say 'go' or 'send now' for the day's batch.

    Every Step

    1. Read live state. Never answer a question about a campaign from prose in a file.
    2. Read the dashboard and check the generated time.
    3. Check account health across every channel: bounces, failures, disconnections.
    4. Send the day's batch through the tools (Part 4).
    5. Mark the sheet after dispatch is confirmed, never before. A row marked for a campaign that never sent falsely claims those people were contacted, and every future build will skip them. The next plan refuses to run while any batch is unmarked.
    6. Pace and rotate. Respect the caps, rest a sender set for about two days between uses, and scale in steps, never in jumps. A sudden volume spike is the clearest signal to a spam filter.
    7. Keep the lists clean. Remove bounced and invalid addresses promptly: bounce rate is the fastest way to damage a reputation. Every unsubscribe, bounce and do-not-contact request goes into the do-not-contact file and is suppressed in each live system.
    8. If deliverability slips, pause or adjust. Do not push through. Replace what is failing.

    Done When State read, health checked, the day's batch sent and marked, and any failing account dealt with.

    What Good Looks Like

    • A silently stale dashboard is the worst failure mode: it looks current and is believed. Alert on failure by email. If the pipeline can fail without anyone hearing, assume it already has.

    Common Mistakes

    • A dashboard that refreshes on a laptop that is asleep.
    • A vendor starting to block a fetch because it does not identify itself.

    16.11 Use the Reporting Language Rules

    Owner EveryoneTime Standing ruleSystem ReportsSafety Read

    Why It Matters

    Two rules about words, because the wrong word produces the wrong decision.

    Every Step

    1. RSVPs are never registrations. Report WebinarGeek subscribers. A registrant is someone who filled in a form. A calendar Yes or Maybe bridged into the broadcast counts as interest, and the funnel equation shows auto-registrants separately for that reason. Do not quote an RSVP-to-registration rate.
    2. Vendor counters are not delivery. Confirm outcomes at the system that did the work. Tantra reports a sent count of zero on campaigns that provably sent, so calendar invites are verified by reading the sending mailboxes' calendars.
    3. Quote the generated or read time with every figure.
    4. A zero is a measured zero. A blank or a dash means not available.

    Done When Reports use these words, and name which of three customer counts is meant.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Every figure is attributed to the system that produced it.

    Common Mistakes

    • Presenting a bridged RSVP as a registration.

    16.12 Audit the CRM Before Anyone Reports From It

    Owner OperationsTime 1 hourSystem GHLSafety Read

    Why It Matters

    Three defects are common in any CRM scaffold. Assume they exist until checked, because reporting from a CRM that has them gives confident wrong numbers.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Reads contacts and tags through the connector and compares them with WebinarGeek attendance.

    Every Step

    1. Attendance tags under-count. Some attendees keep a registrant tag despite having watched, or a tag from the previous webinar. Filtering by tag misses people. The custom fields from WebinarGeek are the reliable signal, and tags are not.
    2. Two writers can use different formats for the same field. A timestamp or a yes value in two formats means anything that parses it must handle both.
    3. The lifecycle field is never populated. A status field that is empty for every attendee, a pipeline with no opportunities, and a source field that is blank on most records means the scaffold is not a CRM until someone fills it.
    4. There is no reliable revenue in the opportunity pipeline. Revenue is read from payment transactions (9.6).
    5. Do not 'correct' GHL watch links from the WebinarGeek screen. Close the cycle: add the next webinar's tab, rebuild the pool and start again.

    Done When The three defects are checked and any found are recorded.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Webinar engagement fields keep a consistent suffix so they stay filterable as a group.

    Common Mistakes

    • Building a re-invite audience from the watched flag. It is not the no-show list.

    16.13 Add a LinkedIn Outreach Channel (If Wanted)

    Owner Operator, operationsTime 1 to 2 weeksSystem LinkedIn, outreach toolSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    FINTECH uses LinkedIn for content, an event page, forms and ads today, not for automated outreach. This channel is Available. The call mentioned LinkedIn connection requests and messages as a later option inside Tantra. If it is added, these structural facts apply, and each one cost someone a rebuild.

    Every Step

    1. Use the sender's own account, connected by them. The operator writes the connection steps and never holds the credentials.
    2. One campaign per sender voice. A campaign cannot have per-sender copy, and its lead list cannot be changed after creation. A second voice means a second campaign and a second list. Plan the voice split before building lists.
    3. Token syntax is specific to the tool. Prove it with a seed test, not by reading documentation.
    4. The delay after a not-accepted branch is the acceptance deadline. A short wait means a lead who accepts later never gets the sequence. Set it in days. The effective window is also capped by the request's auto-withdrawal.
    5. A campaign's sender list can drift. Re-read it immediately before starting.
    6. The daily connection-request ceiling observed is about 20, not 25. Plan to it. Sending hours are an account-level setting, not controlled by the copy.
    7. The lead list is append-only, so get it right before creation. Build as a draft and start only on a typed word.

    Done When A tested, draft LinkedIn campaign with a recorded sender and voice, started only on 'send now'.

    What Good Looks Like

    • LinkedIn already drives registrations through content. Outreach should not harm the account that carries the content.

    Common Mistakes

    • Retrofitting a second voice into an existing campaign.

    16.14 Point Every Sending Domain at a Real Page and Check Its Reputation

    Owner OperationsTime 1 hour per batch of domainsSystem Cloudflare, Google Postmaster ToolsSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    A person who receives a cold message often types the sender's domain into a browser. A parked or error page looks like spam, and some filters check. Sending domains are separate from the main brand by design, so each one needs somewhere sensible to land. This card also holds the reputation checks that come before any scale-up.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Does the read-only check on a name, lists the existing records and writes the redirect plan card.
    • Reads the weekly deliverability report and flags a domain whose authentication or blacklist status changed.
    What the Operator Does
    • Approve the plan card. Add the domains to Google Postmaster Tools, which needs a person with access to the domain.

    Every Step

    1. Use separate sending-brand domains, never the main brand, each with a few mailbox subdomains such as team., events. and info..
    2. Redirect each domain. Add a 301 redirect rule in Cloudflare for the apex, www and the subdomains to the real webinar page.
    3. Do not leave the registrar's parking address as the origin. Point the record at a placeholder address that cannot answer (192.0.2.1, proxied) so the redirect fires at Cloudflare's edge and the parking page is never reached.
    4. Check authentication on every mailbox: SPF includes the sender, DKIM exists for each mailbox subdomain, and DMARC exists at the domain root. A subdomain with no record of its own inherits the root's policy (11.5).
    5. If DMARC reports flood an inbox, either remove the report address tags (enforcement stays, the mail stops) or point them at a free aggregator dashboard. Do not remove them if the reports are needed to raise enforcement safely.
    6. Check blacklists before scaling: Spamhaus DBL, SURBL and URIBL should be clean.
    7. Sending through Google Workspace uses Google's shared pool of addresses. There is no dedicated address to list, and the pool is not controllable per domain.
    8. Add each domain to Google Postmaster Tools to watch real domain reputation and spam rate.
    9. Keep the weekly audit running (11.6) with a notification on failure.

    Done When Every sending domain lands on the real page, authenticates, is blacklist-clean and is watched.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Typing a sending domain into a browser shows the webinar page.

    Common Mistakes

    • Leaving the registrar's parking page live.
    • Removing the report tags and then raising DMARC enforcement blind.

    16.15 Pace the Send Under the Real Ceiling and Judge at Day 3 to 4

    Owner OperationsTime Each waveSystem Tantra, Instantly, Google CalendarSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    Most sending mistakes are pacing mistakes. Mailboxes that share one Google service account share one Calendar quota, so the real daily limit is far below mailboxes times the per-mailbox cap. A rule of thumb from this estate is roughly 750 to 1,500 invites a day through one service account, whatever the tool's headline capacity says. The other costly mistake is judging a wave on its first day.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Plans each wave against the service-account ceiling and the audience's local time, and flags a wave that exceeds it (the wave tools have no daily-limit guard, 16.5).
    • Reads results at day 3 to 4 from the calendars, not the vendor counter.
    What the Operator Does
    • Decide how many days to spread a large send over. Approve the plan card. Say 'send now'.

    Every Step

    1. Respect the ceiling. Do not schedule more per day than one service account can deliver. Spread across more days, or add service accounts in separate cloud projects (about one per thousand a day) if volume must rise.
    2. Use balanced distribution. Fill-first maxes the first accounts, so the next same-day campaign finds them full and sends nothing.
    3. Set the event time in the audience's time zone (Europe/London), never the operator's.
    4. Send three to seven days before the event. The reference method says 8 to 12 days; FINTECH's own evidence supports 3 to 7, so keep that.
    5. Choose slots in the recipient's local time. Tuesday to Thursday are best. Avoid Monday morning and Friday afternoon. Useful slots are 07:30 to 08:30, 11:00 to 12:00, 13:30 to 14:30 and 16:00 to 17:00.
    6. Test copy by splitting the list into equal random samples, one per campaign, with several titles and one constant description. Rotate the titles across time slots in a Latin-square pattern so no title is stuck in a good or bad slot. Equal volume per title gives a clean read.
    7. Keep personalisation out of the invite unless asked. It avoids merge errors.
    8. Test-render one invite and one email to a team mailbox. The vendor preview can flatten line breaks that the delivered invite shows correctly, so only a real test settles it.
    9. After launch, watch for a large Not Sent count. It means the ceiling was hit and the invites never went out, which silently kills response. Pause and re-pace.
    10. Do not judge on day 1. RSVPs and replies accrue all week. Re-judge at day 3 to 4, and log the result in the campaign log for that run.

    Done When The wave was paced under the ceiling, tested to the sender, read at day 3 to 4 and logged.

    What Good Looks Like

    • A wave log shows the date, volume, title, slot and the day 3 to 4 read.

    Common Mistakes

    • Reading the Tantra sent counter as delivery. It is always zero for calendar campaigns (10.1).
    • Calling a title a loser after one day.

    16.16 Use the Cold-Outreach Benchmarks Only as a Starting Line

    Owner OperationsTime 15 minutesSystem DashboardSafety Read

    Why It Matters

    Before a funnel has its own history, a rough benchmark shows whether a number is in the right region. Once it has history, its own numbers replace the benchmark. These are method defaults, not FINTECH results, except the bounce bars, which are FINTECH's own dated figures.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Puts FINTECH's own rate beside the benchmark on every report and names which is which.

    Every Step

    1. Calendar outreach to senior executives: acceptance of about 0.2 to 0.3 percent, and total response (Yes, Maybe and No) of about 2 to 3 percent at maturity. Volume, not just rate, drives the absolute numbers.
    2. Webinar funnel conversions when there is no history: invites to page visits about 20 percent, visits to registrants about 40 percent, registrants to attendees about 50 percent, attendees to calls about 25 percent, calls to customers about 20 percent.
    3. The weekly gate for cold email (reference starting points): scale when click-through is at least 3 percent, conversion at least 1.5 percent and bounce at most 2 percent. Stop an inbox today at bounce over 5 percent or open under 15 percent. Click-through under 1 percent means the message needs rewriting, not the inbox.
    4. Replace each benchmark with the funnel's own rate from the dashboard as soon as it has two or three events, and read it with the funnel equation in Part 1.
    5. The growth cadence. Run the live event with roles assigned, hold the sync call, hold the improvement call to analyse where people leaked, choose one hypothesis for one lever, log it in the tracker and repeat.

    Done When Each number has a benchmark or its own history beside it, and the source is named.

    What Good Looks Like

    • The first webinar is judged against a benchmark and the sixth against its own past.

    Common Mistakes

    • Treating a benchmark as a target.
    • Comparing an early FINTECH number to a benchmark from a different audience.

    The Risk Register

    #RiskHow to check
    1The operator holds neither registrar nor DNS for the sending domains, so both channels sit on one vendor's infrastructureThe ownership register, filled in and signed off
    2Credentials shared with a vendor were never rotatedA rotation date on record
    3An API key is hardcoded in landing-page client-side code, readable by view-sourceView source on every live page
    4A landing-page fallback id points at an ended webinar, so a backend failure silently registers people to the wrong eventRead the fallback id every cycle
    5The dashboard refreshes on one machine, so asleep means silently staleIs there an alert on failure?
    6Validation is a convention, not an enforced gateCan an unvalidated list physically reach a campaign?
    7The acceptance window is shorter than configured on a LinkedIn channelThe auto-withdrawal setting against the branch delay
    8No cross-channel contacted ledger, so one person is touched on two channelsIs the master sheet the ledger for every channel?
    9Vendor billing matches no published plan tierReconcile at renewal
    10No analytics tag on the landing pagesView source
    11A list was scraped against an unapproved or stale ICPA written approval on file, dated, per list
    12A delivered list is short of what was invoicedRow count reconciled before use
    13The booking link is dead or has no slotsOpen it and book a test slot
    14A client touchpoint silently blocks the work: billing, ICP approval, LinkedIn connectionTrack each by name and date

    The roadmap, in value order: make validation a hard gate; rotate vendor-shared credentials on a schedule and after every setup; automated account-health alerting so a degrading inbox is pulled before it harms its neighbours; one cross-channel contacted ledger; per-domain ownership documented; a pre-launch gate that blocks a campaign when any account failed warm-up or any domain fails authentication.

    The Lessons in This Section

    • Inbox reputation is the asset. Everything in this part protects it.
    • Every gate exists because skipping it once cost something real.
    • Ownership is decided in writing before the build, not discovered after.
    • Read the whole plan card first, verify after, and never replace a send that merely looks slow.
    Part 12

    Operating the System Safely

    How a request becomes an action, the rules the chat answers by, one version of every document, the move to a shared home, and security and backups.

    Master Playbook

    4 task cards1 sectionReviewed by Operator as runner

    Requests, Plan Cards and Safety

    This part covers how the system is run safely: how a request becomes an action, how the team stays on one version of every document, and how it is protected.

    How a Request Runs

    1. A person types the request in the chat.
    2. Claude reads the knowledge files (the rules and traps) and calls the connector tools for live data.
    3. Claude shows a plan card: what was found now and when, what it will create, what it will change (before to after), what it will not touch, risks, rollback, how it will verify.
    4. The person replies 'go' (change) or 'send now' (reaches people).
    5. Claude reports each figure from its own source, in the turn it read it.

    A plan card is needed for infrastructure, anything that reaches people, editing something already live, bulk writes of more than 25 records or tags that can fire GHL workflows, and anything that costs money. It is not needed for reads, analysis, reports, drafts or previews. If the thing already exists, Claude says so and stops: it never recreates or overwrites it.

    12.1 Keep One Version of Every Document

    Owner EveryoneTime Standing ruleSystem Work Tracker, Consolidated DocumentSafety Person

    Why It Matters

    Standalone files are how work gets duplicated and lost. A team member creates a separate sheet that nobody else knows exists, and in six months nobody can find which is current. One home per kind of file removes the problem, and a status line removes the next one.

    Every Step

    1. A spreadsheet goes in the Work Tracker, as a tab. Webinar queues live in the Master Outreach Sheet, one tab per webinar.
    2. A document goes in the Consolidated Document, as a tab.
    3. A dashboard figure comes from the dashboard and its data sheet and is never typed into a document.
    4. Automation and rules go in the shared, owned home described in 12.2.
    5. Every dated document carries a status line on its first lines: STATUS: SENT | DRAFT | SUPERSEDED BY <file> AS OF: YYYY-MM-DD. When the status changes, the line is corrected and the filename is renamed too. Filenames are what get skimmed.
    6. A routine check compares each filename with its status line and flags any contradiction.

    Done When Everything has one home and a status line.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Older tabs and documents may be out of date. That is acceptable. The purpose of consolidation is that everything is in one place and access is never lost.

    Common Mistakes

    • A filename that says NOT_SENT about something that sent nearly caused a duplicate 3,000-invite send.

    12.2 Move the Automation to a Shared Home and Add Claude Code

    Owner The operator decides, operations buildsTime 1 to 2 daysSystem GitHub, Claude CodeSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    Chat acts only when someone types. It cannot run on a timer or change the files behind the landing page. For everything to be automated properly, the work must live in a shared, versioned home (a repository: a folder that remembers every change) where Claude Code can work on it, and where a change can be reviewed and undone.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Claude Code unlocks: landing page edits with preview and rollback; scheduled jobs (the daily dashboard, the weekly deliverability report, a reply sweep before each wave); building the lead tools in 17.3; the unsubscribe sync between GHL and Instantly; reading calendar-invite replies; version-controlled templates; reviewed, reversible changes.
    What the Operator Does
    • Decide the owner, the access levels and the repository for the landing page.

    Every Step

    1. Create the home. One FINTECH-owned GitHub account or organisation, with at least two owners (so access is never lost with one person), two-factor authentication on, and team members added by role.
    2. Create a private repository, one client per repository so data can never mix.
    3. Add the work in a clear layout: the method and playbook, the lead and wave tools, the connector behind the chat tools, the Tantra tool server, the Claude Project files, the monitoring reports, and a rules file that Claude Code reads first.
    4. Keep these OUT of the repository, enforced by an ignore list and an automatic secret check before anything is saved: passwords and API keys, service-account files, raw and processed lead lists, engaged-people and suppression exports, generated state files and anything with personal data.
    5. Keep related repositories separate. The landing page and the technology ecosystem page already have their own private repositories and stay there.
    6. Add Claude Code with the same rules file and knowledge layer. Give it only the access it needs. Secrets are supplied at run time, never stored.
    7. Work through branches. Every change goes on a branch (a private copy), is reviewed, then merged. Nothing goes live from an unreviewed branch.
    8. Add the scheduled jobs and checks, with failures reported to the team. Hand over a short README: how to ask for a change, how it is reviewed, how to roll back.

    Done When The work is in a private, owned repository, with a review flow and a README.

    Decision neededWhy
    GitHub account or organisation, and who owns itSo access is never lost with one person
    Who gets access, and at what levelLeast privilege
    Which repository holds the landing pageToday it is the GrowthClub repository
    Whether the lead pool is stored in the cloud for chat searchA data-protection decision: store only the fields the search needs

    What Good Looks Like

    • Anything live (campaigns, sends, GHL) still waits for a plan card and a typed word, even from Claude Code.

    Common Mistakes

    • One person owning the only copy.
    • Committing a key. A secret check runs before every save for this reason.

    12.3 Security and Backups

    Owner OperationsTime StandingSystem GitHub, Cloudflare, GHLSafety Person

    Why It Matters

    The most valuable thing built is the system itself. The question is what the realistic risks are and what protects it. The main risk when AI builds software is a leaked key, usually saved into a public repository.

    Every Step

    1. Keys stay in each system's own secret store, or a local file that is never saved to the repository. They are never printed, pasted in chat or put in a document.
    2. An automatic secret check and an ignore list block keys, service-account files, lead lists and personal data.
    3. Backups: the funnel pages, tools and rules live in a local copy and the private repository. A page is saved before it goes live. The landing page has its own repository and rollback is promoting the previous version. The ecosystem page has its own private repository.
    4. Contact data of people entering the funnel is held in GoHighLevel, which is the source of truth. Keeping the account secure and backed up protects the most important data.
    5. Public pages: the dashboard is public by decision, on a domain the team owns. It is not indexed by search engines. Adding Cloudflare Access in front of the hostname is an open decision.
    6. Worst realistic outcome: a few days of lost promotion, or some API credit used. Moving to a tool without AI for pages would remove the risk, but is not recommended because a broken page is visible and can be fixed.

    Done When Keys, backups and public exposure are each accounted for.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Each client has its own Cloudflare, Google and service-account setup, and nothing is shared across clients.

    Common Mistakes

    • Pasting a key in chat. Rotate anything pasted in chat.

    12.4 Know the Rules the Chat Answers By

    Owner OperationsTime 20 minutes to read, 5 to re-check each monthSystem Claude Project instructions (knowledge file 00)Safety Read

    Why It Matters

    The Claude Project behaves the way its instructions say, so anyone who runs the funnel from chat should know them. They explain why the chat quotes a figure with a time, refuses to guess whether a campaign is sending, and stops to show a plan card. When the chat does something unexpected, the answer is almost always in these rules, and when a rule is wrong the fix is to change the instruction, not to argue with the chat.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Follows the source order below on every question.
    • Names the file, tab or connector behind each answer and says when an answer comes from past chats or memory.
    • Refuses to state a status it has not just read, and shows a plan card before anything that changes something.
    What the Operator Does
    • Check the Project instructions against this card each month and after any new knowledge file.
    • Type 'go' or 'send now' only after reading a plan card.
    • Update the instructions, not the chat, when a rule needs to change.

    Every Step

    1. Source order. The knowledge files come first. If two files disagree, the one with the later AS OF date wins, and new facts arrive as new numbered files. Then the live Drive files (the Work Tracker, Consolidated Document, Master Outreach Sheet, Dashboard Data). Then the live dashboard for any current figure. Then other live connectors. Past chats and memory come last and are named as such.
    2. Current figures are fetched, never recalled. Revenue, customers, registrations, RSVPs, outreach and bounce rates come from the live dashboard or the Dashboard Data sheet, quoted with the dashboard's Generated time. If the dashboard shows a Partial refresh banner, the chat names what it says failed. If the page cannot be fetched, the chat falls back to the files and says so.
    3. Customers are people, not orders, and the chat says which of the three valid counts it means: total, webinar-attributed or outreach-sourced. Old figures such as 41 paid customers or 34 customers are never quoted as current. Community reach and newsletter subscribers are audience, not customers.
    4. Live beats written. If a connector can read a thing, the chat reads it. Otherwise it quotes the file figure with its AS OF date and says it may have moved.
    5. Read the file before quoting a number, and check the known-traps file before any metric. Vendor counters are wrong in known ways, and quoting one unchecked is the most common error.
    6. Say what is missing. If the answer is in neither the files nor a connector, the chat states what would be needed. It never answers 'I can't find details' without naming the file, tab or connector that should hold them.
    7. Never guess a status. Whether something is sending, paused or finished is true only at the moment it is read, so it is read again before it is stated.
    8. Changes follow the change protocol. Drafts are free, with tool approval. Live reversible changes need a stated plan and 'go'. Anything that reaches people needs the exact preview and 'send now'. Calendar campaigns are created only through the connector's preview and send tools. Deleting data, edits to existing DNS records, DMARC policy, payments and GDPR erasure stay with the operations team. Every change is logged.
    9. Check first, then confirm. For domains, DNS, mailboxes, Workers, anything that reaches people, changes to live assets, bulk writes and anything that costs money, the chat reads what already exists and shows a plan card: found now, will create, will change, will not touch, risks, rollback, verify. If the thing already exists it says so and stops. New things go beside existing ones.
    10. Know where things are before changing them. If a connector the task needs is not enabled, the chat names it and stops. It does not substitute another system.
    11. How-to questions are walked, not performed. For a task that only a person can do in a tool's own screen, or an infrastructure how-to, the chat checks which account holds the thing, then guides the person step by step.
    12. Style. UK English, clear and senior, no hype or exclamation marks, no emoji in client-facing copy. Numbers state their denominators and exclusions. Recommendations are framed as decisions with trade-offs. The brand is written FINTECH Circle.
    13. Content. A content request uses one of the ten approved formats, follows brief, draft, checklist, sign-off, and reads the operator's LinkedIn content brief first because it overrides general style. Nothing invented: no statistics, client names or testimonials. Example carousels from other work are used for layout only.
    14. Credentials and data. A password is given only in a direct chat when the operator asks for a tool's login or is being walked through a task in a tool's own screen. It never goes into a document, post, email, summary or anything shared, and nobody is asked to paste a key into the chat. Lead emails and names stay in the source systems. A removal or deletion request is flagged to the operations team the same day.

    Done When The rules are read, and the Project instructions match them.

    What Good Looks Like

    • A figure arrives with its source and time.
    • A refusal names the missing connector or file.
    • A plan card appears before any change.

    Common Mistakes

    • Quoting a figure from memory because it was seen earlier in the chat.
    • Treating the chat's last stated status as current.
    • Adding a new fact to an old knowledge file instead of a new numbered file with its own AS OF date.

    The Lessons in This Section

    • A plan card comes before anything that reaches people, goes live, or costs money.
    • One home per kind of file, and a status line on every dated one.
    • Keys never enter a repository, a chat or a document.

    Claude and People

    Where Claude fits, who decides, what executes, and who releases.

    Master Playbook

    The Loop

    In every process that matters the same four steps repeat. A person is at both ends.

    1 Humandecides and approves
    2 Claudeplans, analyses, drafts, checks
    3 Toolexecutes
    4 Humanapproves or releases

    Who Does What

    ProcessHuman decidesClaude doesTool executesRelease
    Choose the audienceSegments and spendReads results, ranks segmentsApollo searchGo
    Clean a listApproves the resultReads and reports; writes the briefCleaning rulesGo
    Send a waveSize, mix, send nowBuilds the preview plan cardWave tools and TantraSend now
    Write invites and emailApproves wordingDrafts within the rulesTantra, InstantlySend now
    Post on LinkedInThe operator approves every postDrafts and runs the media craft loopMetricool, CanvaSend now
    Change the landing pageApproves the previewDrafts the change and checks itLanding page project and CloudflareGo
    Build a CRM workflowApproves the specificationWrites the specificationA person builds it in the CRMGo
    Run the live sessionThe operator hostsPrepares polls and promptsWebinarGeekGo
    Decide applicationsAccepted or RejectedPrepares a summaryApplication sheet and GmailSend now
    Review resultsChooses what changesReads the dashboard, names the weakest linkDashboardRead
    Change a broadcast dateThe new dateLists every copy of the old dateA person, in WebinarGeek's screenGo
    Test a registrationUses their own addressTags it and checks the countsLanding page, CRMGo
    Run a Meta ads testBudget and the switch-onDrafts two ads and reads resultsA person, in Meta Ads ManagerSend now
    Recover a missed callWording and consentWrites the specificationA person builds it in the CRMGo
    Rebalance spendWhere money movesTotals spend and buyers by channelCost register, CRMGo

    What Claude Cannot Do

    Claude does not act on its own. It cannot send an email on its own authority, create or edit a CRM workflow, edit or cancel a webinar broadcast, change an existing DNS record, or release anything to people without a typed send now. The list is in 17.3 and the connector settings are in 25.7.

    The Prompt Library

    The central library. Copy a prompt, fill the angle brackets and paste it to Claude. Every prompt asks for a plan card or a read; none sends anything. The exact prompts for each task also sit inside the task. The setup prompts are in 17.4.

    Read and report3 prompts
    The weekly read
    Read the live state through the FINTECH connector: the webinar broadcast and its date, the cold-email campaign status, the calendar RSVP counts, WebinarGeek registrations and attendance, and the CRM revenue figures. State when each figure was read. Name the weakest step in the funnel and the number behind it. Do not change anything.
    The day 3 to 4 outreach read
    For the latest wave, read the RSVP counts from the calendar tool's list view, not its sent counter. Compare Yes, Maybe, No and Pending with the previous three waves. Say which segments are consistent winners and which are consistent losers. Do not draw a conclusion from one webinar alone.
    The weekly scale, hold or fix gate
    For each cold-email campaign and mailbox, read sent, bounced and clicked for the week. Apply these reference lines: scale at click-through 3 percent or more, conversion 1.5 percent or more and bounce 2 percent or less; fix today if bounce is over 5 percent; rewrite the offer if click-through is under 1 percent. Say which rules cannot be applied because the data is not tracked. Give one decision per campaign.
    Plan before acting4 prompts
    The wave plan card
    Prepare the plan card for the next wave. Show the live check and its time, the number of leads, the mix by segment, the webinar date and broadcast, the invitation text and variation, what will be created, what will not be touched, the risks, how to undo it, and what to verify afterwards. Do not send. Wait for send now.
    The date change checklist
    The webinar date is changing from <old> to <new>. List every place that carries the old date: the landing page, each reminder email, the cold-email sequence, the invitation text, the WhatsApp workflow and the deck. Show a plan card. Remind me that the broadcast date and the reminder times must be changed by a person in WebinarGeek. Draft a short correction note for people who already have the old time.
    The new mailbox pre-flight
    I want to add a sending mailbox <name> on <domain>. Check, read-only, whether the name or domain already exists in Workspace, the cold-email tool, the calendar tool and DNS. If it exists, stop and say so. Otherwise show a plan card with what will be created, what will not be touched, the warm-up plan and how to undo it.
    The Meta test plan
    Prepare a plan card for a small Meta ads test. Use the funnel's own show rate and close rate to set a target cost per registration, and show the arithmetic. Draft two ads that differ only in angle, with tagged links. State the daily budget I must approve, the tracking checks needed before spending, and the rule for scaling, holding or pausing. Do not build or switch on anything.
    Check and test3 prompts
    The test contact walk-through
    I have registered my own address <address> as a test. Find the contact and, after a plan card, add the tag "test". Then check that the confirmation and reminders arrive, and that the dashboard and the outreach sheet do not count this contact. Tell me plainly if they do.
    Trace a missing registration
    <Name> says they never received the join link. Look up their address in WebinarGeek, the Work Tracker and the CRM. Report which record exists and which is the first one missing. Do not register or message anyone until I approve.
    What else is affected
    I am about to change <tool>. Using the tool profiles and the chains in the tools part, list the tools it feeds and the tools that feed it, what travels between them, and what could break. Rank the risks.
    Draft2 prompts
    Open a content batch
    Open this week's content batch. Read the context bucket and the used-content list. Research sources from the last 30 days. Propose ideas for the formats in use. Wait for the operator's picks before drafting, then draft in the operator's voice, run the media craft loop and prepare the approval view. Do not schedule anything.
    The no-show recovery specification
    Write the specification for a missed-call recovery workflow: the trigger tag, a rebook link within the hour, the follow-ups on the first day, the mixed touches across seven days, the rule that stops it on booking or payment, and what happens to someone silent at day seven. Keep it separate from the webinar no-show tag. Describe it so a person can build it in the CRM.
    Decide2 prompts
    The monthly cost-per-buyer rebalance
    Total last month's spend for each channel from the cost register. Count buyers for each channel by the source on their registration. Say clearly where the source is missing. Calculate cost per buyer, rank the channels, and propose moving budget from the dearest toward the cheapest, keeping total spend the same and a small test budget on each. Show the arithmetic.
    Which funnel shape fits
    Using the funnel shapes in the options part and the current numbers, name the weakest link in the funnel, then suggest at most two shapes or channels that could fix it. For each, give the first test, the number to judge it by and what must be true for it to be worth doing. Do not recommend anything that does not address the named weak link.
