    Part 10

    Review and Learn

    The dashboard, the post-event review, and the next wave mix.

    Master Playbook

    7 task cards1 sectionReviewed by Operator as runner

    Where the Numbers Come From

    A funnel improves only if someone reads the numbers, decides what to change, and checks the next webinar to see if it worked. The dashboard does the reading every day. The review is where a person turns it into a decision.

    The live dashboard: dashboard.fintechcirclepro.com. It is rebuilt every day from Instantly, WebinarGeek, Tantra, GHL, the 20 sender calendars and Google Sheets, and shows outreach, webinars, attendance, revenue, lead availability and deliverability. Every number carries a badge: live, operator, derived or awaiting input.

    Is It Current?

    To check whether the dashboard refreshed, ask Claude for the last run status: status, duration, whether the live page deployed, and which stages failed. When a run was not clean, the page shows a "Partial refresh" banner naming what failed. The page itself is public with no login, so anyone with the link sees revenue. Putting access control in front of it is an open decision.

    10.1 Read the Dashboard

    Owner Operator, operationsTime 20 min per weekSystem DashboardSafety Read

    Why It Matters

    The dashboard exists so no one has to open eight tools to know how the funnel is doing. But a dashboard can look healthy while a stage is broken, and some inputs are blank by design. Reading it well is a skill.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Reads the same data from the sheet behind the dashboard and quotes figures with the time they were generated.
    What the Operator Does
    • Open the dashboard, check the refresh time, read the funnel panel, then the deliverability panel.

    Every Step

    1. Open the dashboard address. Read the generated time.
    2. Look for a Partial refresh banner. If present, treat the numbers it names as missing.
    3. Read the current webinar's panel: invited, RSVPs, registered, viewers.
    4. Read per-webinar stats for the past webinars.
    5. Read the Deliverability and List Hygiene panel. The SMTP-vendor domains show a Google SPF warning that is expected for them.

    Done When The team knows what is current, what is missing, and what is a known artefact.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Three customer counts are all correct at once: total, webinar-attributed and outreach-sourced. Always say which one is meant.
    • The tool cost on the dashboard is a floor: Tantra, Apollo and hosting are not costed.

    Common Mistakes

    • Treating a blank tile as zero. A blank means not available.

    10.2 Run the Post-Event Review

    Owner Operations, OperatorTime 45 minSystem Claude ProjectSafety Read

    Why It Matters

    The review is what turns a webinar into the next one. The same seven questions are asked every time, so the answers can be compared and the equation's weakest link is named, not argued about.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Reads each figure from its source, applies the consistency rule to every segment, and names the weakest link and one experiment.
    What the Operator Does
    • Read the answer, challenge anything that looks too good or too bad, and choose the one change for the next event.

    Every Step

    1. Wait until day 3 to 4 for outreach, and until the manual numbers are entered (9.3) for the rest.
    2. Paste the review prompt below.
    3. Read the answer. Check it names where each figure came from.
    4. Record the one experiment in the change log for the next webinar.

    Done When One named weakest link and one experiment for next time.

    Post-Event Review Prompt
    Review the webinar that has just finished. Read every figure live, quote the time it was
read, and say which system each figure came from. Never use Tantra's sentCount or Instantly's
reply count and open count.

1. FUNNEL. Invited, calendar yes and maybe, registered, attended, call-to-action clicks,
   applications, calls booked, customers. Use calendar RSVPs for invites and WebinarGeek for
   registration and attendance. Flag anything still "awaiting input".
2. COMPARE to the last three webinars at the same distance from the event. Which stage moved
   most?
3. SEGMENTS. Yes rate by country, seniority and invite title. Apply the rule: a segment must
   win consistently across webinars. Show wins out of total, not only the pooled rate.
4. FATIGUE. Yield per invite compared to earlier webinars, and the share of the pool that was
   a second or third touch.
5. DELIVERABILITY. Bounce rate by campaign and domain, in rates not counts.
6. THE WEAKEST LINK. Using the funnel equation, name the single stage to fix first and the
   one experiment to run next webinar.
7. NEXT WAVE MIX. Propose the split by country, title and invite title, with reasons.

Do not change anything. This is a read.

    What Good Looks Like

    • The answer shows wins out of total for segments, not only pooled rates.

    Common Mistakes

    • Running it on day 1.

    10.3 Choose the Next Wave Mix

    Owner Operator, operationsTime 30 minSystem Dashboard, Master Outreach SheetSafety Read

    Why It Matters

    Outreach has a limited budget of people. Putting volume where it converts is the cheapest improvement in the funnel. The analysis of webinars 1 to 9 estimated about 14% more yes (about 186 more) from moving volume away from six consistent losers to the UK rate, with no extra sends.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Proposes the mix by country, title and invite title, with the evidence and the number of webinars each segment has won.
    What the Operator Does
    • Accept, change or reject. Record the decision.

    Every Step

    1. Ask for the proposal from the review.
    2. Check each moved segment has won consistently, not just pooled.
    3. Weight the invite titles toward V2 unless a new test is planned.
    4. Carry the mix into the next wave plan (4.1).

    Done When A recorded mix, with reasons.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Germany stays excluded until it wins webinar by webinar.

    Common Mistakes

    • Moving volume on a pooled number.

    10.4 Know the Daily Run and the Manual Tasks

    Owner OperationsTime 20 min to learnSystem Dashboard pipelineSafety Read

    Why It Matters

    The dashboard is only as current as its last clean run, and some numbers can never be automated. Knowing which stage feeds which tile is how a missing or odd number is traced to its cause in minutes, not hours.

    Every Step

    1. Where it is served: the desk view at the dashboard hostname is the page to share, rebuilt and redeployed by the daily run. An older design is kept as a fallback. The earlier Claude artifact is retired and must never be shared: its link is version-pinned, so viewers see an old build forever.
    2. The schedule: a full rebuild at noon India time (about 07:30 UK in summer), ending in the deploys, and a retry guard at 13:15 that re-runs the whole pipeline if the day has no successful run. A scheduled job that exists but was never loaded fires nothing, and a sleeping Mac runs a missed job once on wake, sometimes hours late and without announcing it.
    3. Did it run? Ask Claude for the last run status first. It shows the status, the duration, whether the live page deployed and which stages failed. The page also shows a Partial refresh banner naming what failed, only when today's run was not clean. Judge freshness from the status, never from the clock.
    4. The stages, in order: the backend build (the gate, retried three times); the next-webinar detector; the WebinarGeek export (must come before the stages that read it); calls; the webinar funnel; payments; capacity; the work tracker; outreach; registrant enrichment; the calendar override; webinar RSVPs; segments; deliverability; the daily snapshot; the render; the conversion table; the outreach-set check; the status write; and the Worker deploy. Only the first is gated on the backend succeeding, because a Sheets timeout must not skip unrelated work. The render exits with an error rather than publish a zeroed page.
    5. Manual tasks, and what under-reports if skipped: the outreach-set build the day after a webinar airs (the conversion table under-reports that webinar); call-to-action clicks, applications and calls typed in after each webinar (those tiles show a dash); the participation master after new outreach data (firmographics and attribution degrade); notes after each webinar; and the tools, costs and lead-purchases files when an invoice arrives (cost figures stay estimates). Call-to-action clicks can never be automated, because WebinarGeek has no endpoint for them.
    6. Before trusting the page, reconcile five things: funnel totals match GHL customers and revenue; the 21-day ramp totals match the webinar panel; the windowed subscriber count matches the broadcast's own count; no aired webinar shows 0, 0, 0; and the live URL serves the same generated stamp as the local file.

    Done When Any dashboard number can be traced to the stage that produced it, and the team can say whether the last run was clean.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Each number carries a badge: live, operator, derived or awaiting input.

    Common Mistakes

    • Judging freshness from the clock.
    • Sharing the retired artifact link.

    10.5 Read the Weekly Metric Tree

    Owner Operations, OperatorTime 15 minSystem DashboardSafety Read

    Why It Matters

    One number tells nothing. The funnel is a chain of rates multiplied together, so a single weak link caps everything after it. Reading the chain from the top down shows which rate moved and which only followed. The tree below uses the stages the dashboard already shows.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Reads each rate from its source and fills the tree with live values and the time they were read.
    What the Operator Does
    • Open each branch and ask which rate moved since the last webinar.

    Every Step

    1. Start at customers and open the branch.
    2. For each step read the rate and the number behind it, and the source.
    3. Compare with the same step in the last three webinars.
    4. Mark the step that moved most, and the one that is lowest.

    Done When Each rate in the chain has a value, a source and a comparison.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Every number has its source named.

    Common Mistakes

    • Reading one rate alone.

    10.6 Find the Worst Step and Fix That One

    Owner OperationsTime 15 minSystem DashboardSafety Read

    Why It Matters

    The quickest gain in a funnel is almost never the part that is already working. Fixing the step with the biggest gap to its own history moves everything after it. Two fixes at once means nobody knows which one worked.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Ranks every step by its gap to the last three webinars and names the lowest.
    What the Operator Does
    • Challenge the ranking. Choose the one step to fix.

    Every Step

    1. List each step's rate for this webinar and the last three.
    2. Compute the gap for each step.
    3. Rank the gaps. The largest negative gap is the candidate.
    4. Check the cause is real and not a missing input, such as a blank manual number.
    5. Write the one step in the change log.

    Done When One named step, with the evidence.

    What Good Looks Like

    • The weakest step is named before any fix is chosen.

    Common Mistakes

    • Fixing the step that is easiest rather than the one that is weakest.

    10.7 Run One Experiment at a Time

    Owner OperationsTime 10 min per webinarSystem Change logSafety Read

    Why It Matters

    Learning needs a clean comparison. If the invite title, the segment mix and the offer all change in one webinar, a better result cannot be traced to any of them. One change, one metric, one webinar.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Writes the experiment as a short sentence with the metric and the comparison, and reads the result at the next review.
    What the Operator Does
    • Approve the change and record it before the event.

    Every Step

    1. Write the hypothesis: changing this step should move this rate.
    2. Pick the one metric that proves it.
    3. Record the change in the log with the date, before the webinar.
    4. Run the webinar. Change nothing else on purpose.
    5. Read the metric at the review. Keep, drop or repeat.

    Done When One logged experiment with a metric and a result at the next review.

    What Good Looks Like

    • The change log has a date and a result for every entry.

    Common Mistakes

    • Changing three things and calling the result a test.

    The Lessons in This Section

    • The dashboard reads. A person decides.
    • Ask the same seven questions every webinar so results can be compared.
    • Name the weakest link, run one experiment, and read the result next time.
    Part 5

    The Content Engine

    The system that turns the operator's experience into a week of reviewed LinkedIn posts, with a matched sample behind every post, two human moments and a loop that compounds.

    Master Playbook

    21 task cards2 sectionsReviewed by Operator as owner

    The Engine at a Glance

    STATUS: OITI LOADED WITH CONTEXT, NOT YET USED FOR A POST   AS OF: 2026-10-14

    Here is the problem this fixes. Good content takes a researcher, a writer, a designer and an editor, and it still comes out uneven. Content produced so far was about 80% good: not perfect enough to post. And the audience is the most discerning one the brand can reach, a board-level reader who spots two things instantly: anything that reads as AI slop, and any statement so generic that anyone could have written it. Either one costs credibility.

    The engine below separates the one-time setup from a weekly loop. The context bucket is built once and grows every week. The operator stays the editor and the face: the operator picks which ideas to build and signs off every post. The production work moves to Claude, OITI and the team's tools.

    Claude reaches each tool in the way the tool allows: it reads and writes the Claude Project and the Consolidated Document directly, builds designs through the Canva connector where it is connected, and reads post analytics from Metricool where the paid plan allows it. Nothing is posted by Claude on its own. A person schedules, and the operator approves.

    9files in the context bucket, built once
    200creator samples, one matched to every post
    2human moments: the pick and the sign-off
    1post a day for the operator, one for FINTECH Circle
    The Audience Bar

    Every post does three jobs: it builds authority, it positions the Board Programme, and it moves readers toward the webinar. A post that could be about leadership in general has failed. The operator reviews every post until quality is proven, and only then is more of the process automated.

    ToolJobStatus
    OITIDrafts general board-governance posts at scale from a knowledge base of 50+ thought-leadership papersLoaded with context. First week of posts not yet produced.
    Claude (a Claude Project for LinkedIn posts)Personal posts from event notes; checks drafts; outreach copyIn use. Works well for event-based posts, but is not scalable for generic governance topics.
    MetricoolScheduling and analytics, with an API that can feed the dashboardIn use for scheduling. Detailed analytics and API need the paid plan.
    CanvaBanners, deck, carousel designsIn use. Moving gradually toward designs built with Claude.

    The Lessons in This Section

    • The setup is built once and grows every week. A weekly batch is cheap because the setup is rich.
    • The operator is the editor. The operator picks the ideas and signs off the posts. Everything else is production.
    • Craft is enforced by a checklist and a matched sample, not hoped for.

    5.1 Build the Context Bucket

    Owner Operations, OperatorTime Half a day to startSystem Consolidated Document, OITI, Claude ProjectSafety Person

    Why It Matters

    The context bucket is the whole reason this works. It is nine plain documents that hold everything the writer needs to think like the operator's best editor: what is sold, to whom, how the operator talks, what is true, and what proof exists. The richer it gets, the less the writer has to guess, and the less it invents.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Reads the Consolidated Document tabs and the Claude Project knowledge files, and writes a first draft of each file.
    • Interviews for gaps: asks focused questions, a few at a time, and writes the answers down. Never writes anything as fact that has no source.
    What the Operator Does
    • Answer the interview questions in the operator's own words. Numbers beat adjectives.
    • Mark anything that cannot be supported as UNVERIFIED so it is never used.

    Every Step

    1. Company and offer. What FINTECH Circle sells, the Board Programme, its modules (the count is an open decision, D1 in 28.4), the three tiers, and the lines never to cross.
    2. Positioning and pillars. The five to six themes every post ladders up to: board-readiness, SMCR accountability, AI governance, headhunter shortlists, portfolio careers, the hidden board market. Plus the one call to action this season.
    3. Voice and rules. the operator's questionnaire answers and the hard rules (the next card lists them). Held in: Consolidated Document tabs "The operator's LI Content Project Instructions" and "Tone of Voice Questionnaire".
    4. Verified facts and sources. Every claim with its source link, in one dated file. A number that has no source is marked UNVERIFIED and never used.
    5. Brand kit. Ocean #0060de, navy #1d293d, dusk #6f46b7, sky #2bc7cb, sun #fea152, an off-white paper background, the identity chip and the footer logo. Measured from the live site.
    6. The webinar deck and the call to action. The next webinar's date, time and registration link, so posts never promote a past event.
    7. Cleared case studies and testimonials. Only those with confirmed permission. The Consolidated Document holds the testimonials.
    8. The used-content registry. A running list of every angle posted, so nothing repeats. Start empty. Source for the history: tab "The operator LinkedIn Posts".
    9. The creator taxonomy. The 200 sample posts that set the craft bar, and the ten approved formats they map to (5.10).

    Done When Nine files exist, every claim has a source, and the registry starts as a list of everything already posted.

    Where It Lives

    Documents in the Consolidated Document, as tabs, not new files. The same text is loaded into OITI's knowledge base and the Claude Project. The three copies must say the same thing, so one is edited and the others refreshed.

    What Good Looks Like

    • The facts file is the only place a number may come from.
    • Anything weak is marked UNVERIFIED and left out, even if it sounds right.

    Common Mistakes

    • Putting statistics in a post that came from memory. Invented research, clients or quotes are the fastest way to lose a board-level reader.
    • Skipping the registry. Without it the writer repeats the strongest angle every week.

    5.2 The operator's Voice and the Hard Rules

    Owner OperatorTime 30 min to reviewSystem Consolidated DocumentSafety Person

    Why It Matters

    The voice is what stops the content sounding generated. The rules below came from the operator's own answers and the operator's own corrections. They are the standing brief every draft is checked against.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Writes in the first person, as the operator, with authority lived and never claimed: "I joined my first board in 2016."
    • Applies every rule below and checks the draft against the approval checklist before it goes anywhere.
    What the Operator Does
    • Review this list once. Add or remove rules. After that it is the standing brief.

    Every Step

    1. Tone: friendly, knowledgeable, positive. Never rude, insulting or critical of others. Nothing negative or controversial. British English.
    2. The operator's bet: fintech keeps growing, and AI plays a key role across every financial-services sector and most company functions.
    3. Structure: a hook in one or two lines, a reframe or tension, three crisp numbered points, the stakes, one call to action, and end on it. One idea per line, short sentences, white space.
    4. Hooks that work: the striking stat, the insider confession, the contrarian two-liner, the named failure (real cases only). Never sensationalist.
    5. Calls to action: for the webinar, put the registration link in the first comment and end the post with "Link in the first comment." For a follow: "I share my thoughts here on fintech and board governance. Follow along if it is useful." One call to action per post. Most posts end on the webinar, some on a light follow, so the feed never reads as an advert.
    6. Never: hype words, "comment X and I'll DM you", manufactured urgency, fake vulnerability, a closing question to the reader, talking down to a senior reader, emoji decoration, more than minimal hashtags, anything market-sensitive, confidential to a board, or investment advice, invented statistics or research, and the long dash (use a short hyphen).
    7. The listed bank: the operator sits on the board of a London-listed bank. Never name it in a post. Say "a listed bank I sit on."

    Done When The list is reviewed and is now the standing brief for every draft.

    What Good Looks Like

    • A post makes the reader feel seen. A senior financial-services reader should recognise themselves in the hook.
    • Calibrate against the gold-standard rewrite in the instructions tab, not against the earlier drafts.

    Common Mistakes

    • A closing question to boost comments. The rule exists because the audience reads it as engagement bait.
    • Naming the listed bank.

    5.3 Match Each Post to a Sample and a Format

    Owner Claude proposes, the operator confirmsTime 30 minSystem Work Tracker, CanvaSafety Person

    Why It Matters

    A format name says nothing about craft. A real post from a creator with millions of impressions shows everything: the hierarchy, the density, the restraint. So every post is matched to one unused sample from the creator taxonomy (5.10), and the format follows from that sample. Ten approved formats keep the output looking like one brand and make every draft easy to brief. They were approved on 25 September and come from the same library of 200 posts by four creators.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Lists the samples no earlier batch has used and picks one per planned post, spread across formats and across the two profiles.
    • Reads the sample's format and layout, maps it to the closest approved format, and writes a slide by slide design brief for the named template with the fill-in fields.
    What the Operator Does
    • Confirm the match when the ideas come back. Supply any real photo or book cover needed. The template files are not yet linked in the tracker; until they are, the design is finished in the named template by hand.

    Every Step

    1. Before any idea is written, Claude picks the craft targets: one unused sample per post. Nothing is reused while unused samples remain.
    2. Read the sample's format and map it to the closest house format in the table below. Image: I1 to I4. Carousel: C1 to C6. Videos are out of scope for now.
    3. Study the matched sample's media and copy, and write down what is borrowed from it: the hierarchy, the density, the layout idea. Borrow structure, never words, numbers, names or branding.
    4. Check the example file. The examples are finished carousels from another GrowthClub client and are a visual and structural reference only.
    5. After the operator's pick, check each kept idea still fits its sample. A six-step method fits a numbered carousel; one striking number fits a quote card or an infographic. If it does not fit, swap to a better unused sample and say why.
    6. Note: no example exists yet for C5 Book or Resource, or I3 Quotes. Follow the anatomy in the table.

    Done When Each idea has a recorded sample, a house format and a named template.

    Decision for this playbook

    Matching to an unused sample wins. The setup and weekly prompts below have been rewritten so they pick the sample first and read the format from it. The ten house formats stay as the catalogue of what can be built and as the fill-in fields. The brand furniture policy is a separate open decision (5.11).

    #FormatWhat it isFill-in fields
    I1ExperientialA real moment from the operator's work turned into a lessonPhoto, story hook, the moment, the lesson, soft call to action
    I2Thought LeadershipOne sharp point of view on boards, governance or fintechHeadline, payoff phrase, 3 to 5 points, source line
    I3QuotesOne quotable line from the operator, or a cited public figureQuote, key phrase, attribution, optional photo
    I4CheatsheetA dense, save-worthy reference sheet in a gridTopic, layout, item list, footer or source
    C1Framework DeckA step by step method, such as the six-step path to board-readyTopic, hook, steps, cover idea. 8 to 12 slides
    C2Comparison DeckOld and new thinking, such as executive thinking against NED thinkingTopic, labels, 5 to 8 pairs
    C3Checklist DeckA practical list, such as due diligence before accepting a board seatTopic, context, 7 to 12 items
    C4Illustrated StoryA short narrative in one visual worldConcept, character, slide statements. 6 to 10 slides
    C5Book or ResourceRecommendations with real covers, anchored on the seven FINTECH booksHeadline, books, blurbs, real covers
    C6Case StudyA real, permissioned outcome told as the steps behind itRole, result, steps. Real cases only

    The Craft Laws

    Eleven design rules distilled from the taxonomy (they live in the Design DNA tab). For this senior audience favour 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8; use 10 and 11 sparingly; no memes and no cartoon mascots.

    1. Concept first: one ownable visual idea per post.
    2. A real information structure: a correct diagram for the idea.
    3. Text on objects, not floating over them.
    4. A real type system: a bold display for hooks, clean sans for body.
    5. Colour means something: green good, red stop; one disciplined accent.
    6. Brand furniture on every slide: identity chip, page numbers, footer logo (open decision, see 5.11).
    7. Imagery is proof: real photos, real covers, logos only with permission.
    8. Dense but disciplined: numbering rhythm, strict grids.
    9. Layout variety across slides.
    10. Rawness is a valid mode: a real photo can beat a polished graphic.
    11. Texture over flat fills: avoid pure white and pure black.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Carousels run 6 to 12 slides: a strong cover, calm interiors, a poster-style closing slide.
    • Real photos and real book covers only. Imagery is proof, never filler.

    Common Mistakes

    • Using another client's words or numbers because the example looked good.
    • Picking a format first and a sample afterwards. That brings back the sameness the samples are there to prevent.

    5.4 Run the Setup Prompt and the First OITI Week

    Owner Operations, OperatorTime Half a daySystem Claude Project, OITISafety Person

    Why It Matters

    The first week of OITI output is the blocker on the whole content workstream. OITI has been loaded with the board-governance knowledge base, but no post has been produced and reviewed with it. Until that happens, nobody knows whether its quality clears the bar. One prompt sets everything up and produces the first test posts so the judgement can be made on real output.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Reads the sources, writes the nine files and the rules, sets up the render checks, connects and tests each tool, loads the taxonomy, then drafts three test posts in three formats, each matched to an unused sample and checked against the approval checklist.
    • Stops whenever it needs a key, a decision or a file, and says exactly what to do.
    What the Operator Does
    • Paste the prompt into the Claude Project, or into OITI, with the inputs filled in.
    • Review the three test posts as the operator would: does it read as AI slop, is it generic, would the operator post it?
    • Decide: use OITI for general governance topics, Claude for event-based posts, or both.

    Every Step

    1. Copy the prompt below and fill in the inputs. About twenty are listed; leave a field blank if unsure, and it will interview the operator.
    2. Paste it into a fresh session in the Claude Project or OITI.
    3. Answer the questions as they come, a few at a time.
    4. Read the three test posts and the checklist results.
    5. Record the decision on which tool does which job, and note it in the Consolidated Document.

    Done When Three reviewed test posts, a decision on OITI's role, and a first context bucket.

    Setup Prompt: Content Engine
    You are setting up the LinkedIn content engine for the operator, Chair and Founder
of FINTECH Circle, in this Claude Project (or in OITI). Work autonomously. Whenever you need a
key, an access grant, a file or a decision I have not given you, STOP and ask me in one short
block: the exact place to go, what to paste or click, and what happens next. Then continue.
Never invent a fact, a number, a client, a quote or a credential.

=============================== INPUTS ===============================
# Fill what you know. Leave a field blank and interview me for it.
COMPANY:            FINTECH Circle, fintechcircle.com
WHAT_YOU_SELL:      Free live webinar, then the Board Programme (Digital, Flagship, Elite)
ICP:                UK Portfolio Finance Leader (15 to 30+ years, banking, insurance,
                    asset management, fintech, consulting or audit; NED or board-minded)
POSITIONING:        (how FINTECH Circle wants to be seen; what must NEVER be said or attacked)
CONTENT_PILLARS:    board-readiness, SMCR accountability, AI governance, headhunter
                    shortlists, portfolio careers, the hidden board market
PRIMARY_CTA:        the next webinar (date, time, registration link in the FIRST COMMENT)
VOICE_SOURCES:      Consolidated Document tabs "The operator's LI Content Project
                    Instructions", "Tone of Voice Questionnaire", "The operator LinkedIn Posts"
PROOF_POINTS:       each with a source link; mark guesses UNVERIFIED
CLEARED_CASE_STUDIES: only those with confirmed written permission
PROFILES:           one line each: name | role | time zone | voice in 5 words | real photo y/n
                    Operator | Chair and Founder | Europe/London | (from VOICE_SOURCES) | y
                    FINTECH Circle company page | company | Europe/London | (to confirm) | n/a
BRAND:              ocean #0060de, navy #1d293d, dusk #6f46b7, sky #2bc7cb, sun #fea152
TAXONOMY_SHEET:     Work Tracker, tabs "LinkedIn Creator Taxonomy" and "Design DNA"
FORMATS:            I1 to I4 and C1 to C6, mapped from the sample formats (see the mapping table)
FURNITURE_POLICY:   identity chip, page numbers and footer logo on every slide (open decision)
POSTS_PER_WEEK:     (to confirm)  # target: 1 personal and 1 company post a day
REVIEWERS:          the operator signs off every post; name a second approval role if wanted
IMAGE_SERVICE:      (an image service for non-person illustration, or "none"; ask privately for any key)
REVIEW_PAGE:        (a shared review page with phone previews, or "none" for now)
SCHEDULER:          Metricool
USE_DASHBOARD:      yes, add a content view (see the dashboard card)
======================================================================

DO THIS, IN ORDER
0. SCAFFOLD. Set up the project space: a folder for the context bucket, one for brand, one
   for batches and one for ideas, a private place for keys and photos, and a rules file that
   will hold the binding rules. Never print or store a key anywhere shared.
1. CONTEXT BUCKET. READ the sources named above. Do not rely on memory. WRITE the nine files:
   company and offer, positioning and pillars, voice and rules (one section per profile),
   verified facts (every claim with its source; UNVERIFIED items kept apart), brand kit,
   webinar deck and call to action, cleared case studies, the used-content registry (start
   from the posts already published), and the pointer to the creator taxonomy.
   Where an input is blank, INTERVIEW me a few questions at a time and write the answers down.
2. RULES. WRITE the rules file: no invented statistics, clients or quotes; one call to action
   per post and end on it; the registration link goes in the first comment; no closing
   question; no hype words; nothing market-sensitive, confidential or investment advice;
   never name the listed bank; British English; no long dashes (use a short hyphen);
   nothing negative or critical of others; introduce every person on first mention; the
   furniture policy above; and a definition of done with nine checks.
3. RENDER CHECKS. Set up how every design is checked: render at twice the final size, check
   marked elements for overflow, convert straight quotes to curly ones, FAIL on any long dash,
   export a lossless PDF for every carousel, and make a contact sheet of every folder.
4. REVIEW PAGE. If REVIEW_PAGE is not "none", set up a shared page that shows each post as
   the LinkedIn phone app shows it: header, copy with the "...more" clamp, a swipeable
   carousel or a poll, the action row and the first comment. Each card has an approval box
   for each reviewer role, a shared feedback box, a full-quality download with its size,
   Copy post copy and Copy first comment buttons, and a panel showing the matched sample, the
   template and the sources. Otherwise record this as a decision and use the Content
   Calendar tab for approvals.
5. SHARED REVIEW STORE. Approvals and feedback must be shared and never lost: one row per
   approval or comment, never deleted. To undo an approval, add a retract row. Walk me
   through creating it.
6. TOOLS. Connect and PROVE each one with a test: the Claude Project (it answers "what is true
   about X" from the files), Canva (open one named template), Metricool (a test post appears
   in the planner; note whether analytics need the paid plan), the dashboard (loads this
   week's numbers), and the image service if used (one test image and its cost).
7. TAXONOMY. Read the creator taxonomy and confirm the count (200 samples, 4 creators, 10
   formats). Read the Design DNA tab. Map every sample format to the closest house format.
8. VERIFY AND HAND OVER. PROVE IT: draft three test posts in three different formats, each
   matched to an unused sample. For each show the post, the first comment, the slide text,
   the design brief and a pass or fail against the approval checklist. Write a setup record of
   every decision, key location and access grant. Then give me: anything still needed from
   me, and the exact weekly prompt to use next. STOP and wait for my feedback.
At every step, if something needs me, do everything around it first, then hand it over in one
short block with the full link and the exact action. Do not argue a step that only I can do.

    What Good Looks Like

    • The test is judged by the operator on the audience bar, not by whether the post looks polished.
    • The prompt ends with a hand-over, including the exact weekly prompt.

    Common Mistakes

    • Judging OITI before it has been used. It has been loaded but not tested.
    • Skipping the test posts and going straight to a calendar.

    5.5 Run the Weekly Batch

    Owner Operations, ClaudeTime 1 to 2 hours plus the operator's picksSystem Claude Project, OITISafety Read

    Why It Matters

    Once the setup exists, a week of content is four steps with exactly one pause. The operator spends their attention where it is worth most: choosing which ideas are worth building. The target is one post a day from the operator's personal account and one a day from FINTECH Circle, a week at a time. The order matters. The craft targets come first, so every idea is born already matched to a sample. The ideas come second, then the operator's one confirmation, then copy, media and the review link.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Boots, reads the rules and the bucket, resumes from the build-state file if the batch is half built, and computes every post's publish date.
    • Picks one unused sample per post, then produces exactly as many ideas as asked and stops.
    • After the operator's picks, writes each post, builds the media, runs the craft loop, verifies the batch against the definition of done with evidence, and updates the registry.
    What the Operator Does
    • Paste the weekly prompt with this week's number, the next webinar, the minimum share of webinar posts, must-cover topics and any event notes.
    • Read the idea list, strike what does not fit, keep what does, and say go.
    • Review the drafts and hand them to the scheduling step.

    Every Step

    1. Open the dashboard and read last week's numbers (5.8).
    2. Paste the weekly prompt below and fill in the thirteen inputs. Most default sensibly; the usual ones to set are the number, the webinar and the must-cover topics.
    3. Read the idea list. Strike, keep, and reply with the picks.
    4. Review each draft, its first comment and its design brief on a phone.
    5. Pass the approved drafts to the scheduling step (5.7) and record them in the tracker's Content Calendar tab.

    Done When A week of drafted, checked posts waiting for the operator's sign-off, with a pass or fail and its evidence for every row of the definition of done.

    Weekly Batch Prompt
    You are building the next batch of LinkedIn content for the operator and FINTECH
Circle, end to end, at the quality of the matched creator samples. Work autonomously until the
definition of done is met.
Process: 1 choose one unused creator sample per post, 2 write one idea per sample from the
context bucket plus fresh research, 3 STOP and wait for me to confirm which ideas to build,
4 write the copy, 5 build the media, 6 assemble and publish for review, 7 verify and hand over.

=============================== INPUTS ===============================
BATCH_NUMBER:       (the next number)
TOTAL_POSTS:        (e.g. 14: one personal and one company post a day for a week)
SPLIT:              auto            # auto = spread evenly across the two profiles
START_DATES:        auto            # the day after each profile's last scheduled post
CTA_SHARE:          40%             # the minimum share of posts that carry the CTA below
CTA:                (the next webinar: title, date, time in Europe/London, registration link)
FALLBACK_CTA:       "I share my thoughts here on fintech and board governance. Follow along if it is useful."
IDEA_APPROVAL:      yes             # yes = show me the idea list and wait (the standard)
MUST_COVER:         (topics, news, events or stories that must appear this week)
IDEATION_INPUTS:    (links, documents, transcripts, the operator's event notes, questions from members)
EXTRA_CONTEXT:      (new positioning, new proof points, things to avoid, new people)
FORMAT_WISHES:      (optional, e.g. "two carousels", "one quote card")
PROFILE_CHANGES:    (optional: add or remove a profile, change a time zone or a headline)
======================================================================

0. BOOT AND RESUME. Read the rules file, then the context bucket in this order: voice, used-
   content registry, verified facts, the newest research file, brand kit, every batch so far,
   and the previous batch's build-state file. If a build-state file for this batch exists,
   RESUME from it and never redo finished work; otherwise create it with the inputs, the
   computed split and the schedule. Check what you need is present (the taxonomy, photos,
   fonts) and, if something is missing, say in one line what and continue with everything
   that does not need it. Compute every post's date and time FIRST, one per profile per day,
   in UK time. Nothing may promote an event that has already passed: after the CTA date use
   FALLBACK_CTA.
1. CRAFT TARGETS. List the creator samples no earlier batch has used. Pick one per planned
   post, spread across formats and across the two profiles. Nothing is reused while unused
   samples remain. Study each pick's media and copy and write down what is borrowed.
2. IDEAS. Produce exactly TOTAL_POSTS ideas, one per sample. Priority: MUST_COVER first, then
   IDEATION_INPUTS and EXTRA_CONTEXT, then fresh research from the last 30 days. Read social
   or gated sources only through a safe reader, never by scraping. Verify every fact at its
   primary source and save it with its link; mark weak facts UNVERIFIED and do not use them.
   Each idea carries: the profile, the hook as it will read, one or two lines of what is
   inside, the matched sample and house format (I1 to I4, C1 to C6), CTA yes or no, and its
   sources. No repeated angle: check the registry AND every idea in every past batch. At
   least CTA_SHARE of posts carry the CTA, ordered as a countdown to the event. Save the list.
   If IDEA_APPROVAL is yes, SHOW IT TO ME AND WAIT. This is the only pause.
3. AFTER MY CONFIRMATION, check each kept idea still fits its sample. If not, swap to a
   better unused sample and say why. Build exactly what I confirmed, nothing else.
4. COPY. Write each post with the matching copy structure in the operator's voice. Apply every rule:
   no long dashes; the hard rules per profile; the cold-reader rule (introduce every person,
   no insider names, no relative dates that will be wrong on the publish day); list every
   number for sign-off. CTA posts get a first comment with a personalised line and the link
   on its own line, and the post ends "Link in the first comment." Links stay out of the body.
5. MEDIA (the most important milestone). Build each asset to the brand, matched to its
   sample's sophistication. Real photos for people; an image service only for non-person
   illustration. No filler, logo in place, a source line only where a number is cited. Render
   at twice the size, run the render checks, critique each asset at phone size against its
   sample and fix until it reaches that level. Then get an independent second-model critique
   that has not seen your first one, and fix every real issue.
6. ASSEMBLE AND PUBLISH FOR REVIEW. Add the batch to the queue and publish it for review one
   profile at a time. After each profile open the review link as a reviewer (the batch list, the
   posts render, no broken images, no long dashes, the sync badge shows saved) and send me the
   link with a one-line status.
7. VERIFY, THEN HAND OVER. Run the definition of done item by item and report each pass or
   fail WITH EVIDENCE. Add this batch's angles to the used-content registry, finish the build-
   state file, and give me: the review link, the posts per profile and the CTA count, any
   numbers awaiting sign-off, any UNVERIFIED items dropped, and the exact steps to schedule
   the approved posts in Metricool. Do not mark anything approved. Only the operator approves.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Raw material comes from the operator's own events and notes, which is the strongest content and the hardest to fake.
    • Research is fresh: the last 30 days, read through a safe reader, every fact saved with its link and weak ones dropped.
    • A half-built batch resumes where it stopped and never redoes finished work.

    Common Mistakes

    • Asking for ideas without the next webinar. A post dated after the event cannot promote it.
    • Brainstorming ideas first and designing later. That is how a great idea gets a lazy design.

    5.6 The operator's Approval Gate

    Owner OperatorTime 10 min per daySystem Work Tracker Content CalendarSafety Person

    Why It Matters

    One person approves every post, and it is the operator. It is the single control that protects the brand with a discerning audience, and it stays in place until quality is proven. After that, more of the process can be automated, but the gate is relaxed only by the operator, in writing. A second approval role per post is possible (5.12); whether to add one is the operator's decision.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Runs the checklist below on every draft and reports each pass or fail with evidence.
    • Lists every number and claim for confirmation.
    What the Operator Does
    • Approve, edit or reject each post.
    • Record the approval in the Content Calendar tab.

    Every Step

    1. Read the post as the target reader would, on a phone. Does it make them feel seen?
    2. Check the list below. Any failed item sends it back.
    3. Record the approval: date, post, version, decision.
    4. Only then does the post go to scheduling. To take an approval back, add a retract entry; never delete the row.

    Done When Every post that is scheduled has a recorded approval from the operator.

    The Approval Checklist

    • Hook in the first one or two lines; one idea per line; short sentences.
    • Every statistic, case and citation is real and verifiable. No invented research, clients or quotes.
    • Testimonials and case studies used only with permission.
    • British English; no hype; no emoji decoration; minimal or no hashtags; no long dashes.
    • Positive: nothing negative, critical or controversial.
    • The listed bank is not named; nothing market-sensitive or confidential; no investment advice.
    • Exactly one call to action and the post ends on it: webinar (with "Link in the first comment.") or follow. No closing question.
    • FINTECH Circle spelled correctly; the operator's title correct.
    • No other client's content, names or claims.

    What Good Looks Like

    • The first read is on a phone. The audience reads on a phone.
    • Anything market-sensitive or confidential to a board is removed, not softened.

    Common Mistakes

    • Scheduling a post before the approval is recorded.
    • Deleting a row to undo an approval. A copy that is still open somewhere can send it again.

    5.7 Design, Schedule and Boost

    Owner OperationsTime 1 hour per weekSystem Canva, Metricool, LinkedInSafety Person

    Why It Matters

    Approved posts become finished designs and queued posts. Then the second half of the strategy begins: after a couple of weeks of results, the posts that performed are promoted with LinkedIn ads. A post published from a personal profile can now be boosted through the company page, which was not possible before.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Writes the design brief, the first comment text and the schedule date and time. Can build or edit designs through the Canva connector where it is connected.
    What the Operator Does
    • Finish the design in the named template. Schedule in Metricool, or LinkedIn directly. Attach the first comment. Check any company tag stays a tag, not a link.

    Every Step

    1. Build the design in the named template. Every slide currently carries the identity chip, page numbers and the footer logo (open decision, 5.11).
    2. Schedule at the planned date and time, in UK time. One post per profile per day.
    3. Paste the first comment with the registration link, so the link is not in the post body, which cuts reach.
    4. A carousel or a poll is uploaded by hand; text and single-image posts can be sent through Metricool where the paid plan allows it.
    5. After two weeks, read the results (5.8) and pick the top posts.
    6. Boost the winners from the company page. Start small, read the result, then scale. The posts are the ad creative.

    Done When Posts queued with first comments, and a short list of winners chosen for boosting.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Scheduling stays with a person, so a human sees what goes live.
    • The free Metricool plan covers scheduling. Analytics and the API that feeds the dashboard need the paid plan, which is an open decision (28.4).

    Common Mistakes

    • Putting the registration link in the post body. Keep it in the first comment.
    • Boosting a post before it has proven itself organically.

    5.8 Read the Content Results

    Owner Operations, OperatorTime 20 min per weekSystem Metricool, dashboardSafety Read

    Why It Matters

    The feedback loop is what makes the engine compound. The dashboard does not yet carry content metrics, so today results are read in Metricool. Once connected, the dashboard should show per post the format, topic, call to action, reach, engagement and registrations attributed to it.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Reads post analytics and lists the top and bottom posts by reach and engagement.
    • Proposes what to repeat, what to retire, and what to add to the used-content registry.
    What the Operator Does
    • Decide what changes next week: topics, formats, calls to action.

    Every Step

    1. Open Metricool analytics (or the dashboard when the content section exists).
    2. Ask: "Which posts last week performed best, by format and topic?"
    3. Add the angles used to the registry.
    4. Take the winners to the boost step (5.7). Carry the lessons into next week's prompt.

    Done When A short list of what worked, what did not, and what changes.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Registrations attributed to a post need tagged links. Until then, results are about reach and engagement.

    Common Mistakes

    • Judging a post by likes alone.

    5.9 Run the Media Craft Loop Before Anything Reaches the operator

    Owner OperationsTime Part of each batchSystem Canva or HTML render, ClaudeSafety Read

    Why It Matters

    The operator sees a post only after it has already reached the craft of the sample it was matched to. A loop of build, check at phone size and second opinion catches weak design before the approval gate (5.6), so their ten minutes go on judgement and not on spotting avoidable flaws.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Builds the media, renders it at twice the final size and compares it with the matched sample at phone size.
    • Asks for an independent second critique, from a separate model or a second pass with a different brief, and fixes what it finds.
    What the Operator Does
    • Open the finished batch the way the audience will see it, on a phone, before it goes to the operator.

    Every Step

    1. Build the asset in the named template, matched to one unused sample (5.3).
    2. Render at 2x so small text and edges can be inspected, and run the render checks (5.11).
    3. Self-check at phone size against the sample: hierarchy, spacing, contrast, text that is cut off, brand furniture present.
    4. Get an independent second critique that has not seen the first. Fix what it raises.
    5. Re-render and repeat until the asset reaches the sample's level.
    6. Preview each post as the feed shows it, with the copy, first comment and image together, before sending it for approval.
    7. Record any recurring flaw in the used-content registry notes, so the next batch avoids it.

    Done When Every asset has passed a phone-size check and a second critique before it is sent for approval.

    What Good Looks Like

    • The operator's edits are about meaning and tone, not alignment or clipped text.

    Common Mistakes

    • Checking only on a desktop screen.
    • Using the same pass for the critique that built the asset. It repeats its own blind spots.

    5.10 The Creator Taxonomy: 200 Samples to Match

    Owner Operations, ClaudeTime 1 hour to load and mapSystem Work Tracker, Design DNASafety Read

    Why It Matters

    This is what keeps the output from looking generated. Rather than invent a layout, every post is matched to one real post from a world-class creator and has to reach that post's craft level. The taxonomy is the library of those posts: 200 samples by four creators, torn down into the dimensions that make them work. A format name such as carousel says nothing about craft. A sample shows the hierarchy, the density and the restraint.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Reads the library, lists the samples no batch has used, and picks one per planned post.
    • Reads the matched sample's eight design dimensions and the Design DNA craft laws, and builds to that level, then tries to beat it.
    What the Operator Does
    • Confirm where the library lives and who may open it. Decide the open mappings in the table: text-only posts and the event graphic.

    Every Step

    1. Where it lives. In the Work Tracker workbook, in the tab "LinkedIn Creator Taxonomy" (the 200 samples) and the tab "Design DNA" (the 11 craft laws, the layout archetype library and a house system per creator). The workbook has other tabs with logins and keys, so only the two tabs are ever shared, copied into a standalone sheet.
    2. What a row holds. 29 columns: who made it, where it ran, the content format, the copy structure, the media family, a link to the original, the full copy, and the eight design dimensions below.
    3. Match. Each planned post gets one unused sample, chosen on format, layout and copy structure. Each sample also carries a copy-format group (promotion, tactical education, prompt and engagement, proof and case study, narrative lesson, point of view) and a media family (image, carousel, text-only, animated, video).
    4. Map to the set in use. Read the format from the sample and map it with the table below to I1 to I4 or C1 to C6.
    5. Keep it fresh. A used sample is recorded on the post. Nothing is reused while unused samples remain, and the library grows as more teardowns are added.

    Done When The library is loaded, the count reads 200 samples, 4 creators and 10 formats, and every format has a house mapping or a recorded open decision.

    Matching every idea to one unused sample, then building to beat it, is how volume stays world-class instead of drifting into template sameness. The mapping above is a closest-fit list for the operator to confirm.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Every post records its matched sample, so craft can be audited.
    • The Design DNA sets the bar the engine must clear, and then beat.

    Common Mistakes

    • Sharing the whole workbook into a shared project. Only the two tabs are copied.
    • Treating the sample as something to copy. Borrow structure and craft, never words, numbers or branding.

    5.11 Renderer Checks and the Furniture Decision

    Owner Operations, OperatorTime 30 min to decideSystem Canva or HTML renderSafety Person

    Why It Matters

    Two things decide whether a design looks expensive or sloppy: whether basic faults can slip through, and what repeats on every slide. The first is solved by checks that fail the asset. The second is a policy that needs a person to choose.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Runs every check on every asset and reports a pass or a fail with the asset named.
    • Applies the furniture policy that the operator chooses.
    What the Operator Does
    • Decide the furniture policy below. Until then, the current rule stands.

    Every Step

    1. Every asset is rendered at twice the final size and checked for overflow, straight quotes and long dashes.
    2. A carousel also exports a lossless PDF, and every folder gets a contact sheet.
    3. Read the contact sheet once per batch to see the whole set at a glance.
    4. Furniture, open decision. The reference playbook bans slide numbers, swipe or save footers and kickers. FINTECH's current rule requires the identity chip, page numbers and the footer logo on every slide. This playbook keeps FINTECH's rule for now and flags it for the operator: keep page numbers, or follow the reference and remove them.
    5. Record the decision in the Consolidated Document and in the rules file, so every batch follows it.

    Done When Every asset passes the checks, and the furniture policy is written down.

    What Good Looks Like

    • A long dash is a hard fail, not a note.
    • Whatever is chosen, it is the same on every slide and every post.

    Common Mistakes

    • Treating the furniture rule as settled because it is written down. It conflicts with the reference.
    • Fixing a dash by hand in one place and leaving it in another.

    5.12 The Review Experience: Phone Preview and Two Approvals

    Owner Operations, OperatorTime Setup once, then part of each batchSystem Review page, shared sheetSafety Person

    Why It Matters

    A document cannot show what a reader sees. A phone can. A review page that shows every post exactly as LinkedIn will, and lets each reviewer approve it in their own role, removes the surprise of a hook cut off by the more clamp or an image cropped through a face. Potential Today the operator reviews in the Work Tracker Content Calendar; this card describes the better version.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Builds the review page from the finished batch and posts the link.
    • Reads every approval and note back from the shared sheet, fixes each post with a note, and republishes.
    What the Operator Does
    • Open the link on a phone. Approve in the reviewer's own role, or leave a note.
    • Decide whether a second approval role is wanted, and who holds it.

    Every Step

    1. Preview. Each post is shown in a phone frame: the header, the copy with the more clamp, a single image or a swipeable carousel or a poll, the action row and the first comment.
    2. Two approver roles. Each reviewer role approves independently. A post counts as approved only when every role has ticked it, and a count shows per profile and per batch. For FINTECH, the operator is one role; the second is open.
    3. Saved feedback. Notes save to a shared sheet and read back with a saved badge. A browser that was offline re-sends anything pending.
    4. Copy and download. One click copies the post copy and another copies the first comment. A download gives the full-quality image or the carousel PDF, with its file size.
    5. Matched sample panel. An expandable panel shows the matched sample, the template and the sources, with the numbers to sign off.
    6. Where the review link lives. The batch sits in one code repository (the rules, the creator library and every batch). A free static host serves the review site as a public link, and the deploy step rebuilds it and republishes in about a minute. Proof: the review link loads over https and shows the newest batch.
    7. The shared review store. A Google Sheet holds approvals and notes, with a small web app as the endpoint the review page reads and writes. It is append-only and deduplicated, runs with access for anyone who has the link, and needs no reviewer login. Proof: an approval on the page shows a "saved to shared sheet" badge and the row appears in the sheet.
    8. Retract, never delete. To take back an approval, Claude adds a retract entry that hides the old one and keeps the record. A deleted row can be sent again by a browser that still holds it.

    Done When Every post in the batch shows as the feed shows it, and each role's approval is saved and counted.

    What Good Looks Like

    • A team of three can review at once and nobody loses a comment.
    • The first read is on a phone.

    Common Mistakes

    • Deleting a row to undo an approval.
    • Approving from a desktop preview that hides how the post is cut on a phone.

    5.13 Connect the Content Tools and Prove Each One

    Owner OperationsTime Half a daySystem Claude Project, Canva, Metricool, dashboardSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    An unproven connection is a guess. Each tool below is connected once and then proved with a small test. Only the steps that need a person are done by a person: signing in, pasting a key, or granting access. The rest is done by Claude.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Walks through each connection and asks for exactly what it needs, one clear block at a time.
    • Runs the proof test for each tool and reports what came back.
    What the Operator Does
    • Sign in, paste a key or grant access when asked. Nothing else.
    • Compare each proof with what the tool itself shows.

    Every Step

    1. Connect the Claude Project and load the nine files. Proof: it answers a question from the files and names the file.
    2. Connect Canva through the connector and name the templates. Proof: Claude opens one named template.
    3. Connect each LinkedIn profile to Metricool. Proof: a test post appears in the planner.
    4. Decide on the paid Metricool plan for analytics and the API (28.4).
    5. Point the dashboard at the posts. Proof: the content view loads this week's numbers.
    6. Record each result: tool, test, answer, match or mismatch.

    Done When Each tool has a recorded proof that matched what the tool shows.
