    • Ticking a tool as connected because a key exists, before the proof matched.

    5.14 Add a Content View to the Dashboard

    Owner OperationsTime A few hours to addSystem Dashboard, Metricool, funnelSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    A month of posting can pass with the likes climbing and still no sign of whether a single post filled a seat. A content view beside the funnel fixes that. Potential It is not built yet: today the dashboard carries no content metrics.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Reads each post's reach, engagement and clicks from Metricool, and the sign-ups from the funnel, joined by the tag on each post's link.
    • Shows a number it cannot read as blank with the reason, never as zero.
    What the Operator Does
    • Decide who sees the view. Read the last two cards first: reach says a post was seen; registrations and booked calls say it worked.

    Every Step

    1. Five cards, this week against last: reach, engagement rate, clicks, registrations from content and booked calls from content.
    2. Top posts, by pillar, by format: reach, engagement and clicks next to the registrations and calls each brought.
    3. By profile and network: followers and followers gained, from Metricool.
    4. Newsletter and WhatsApp: sends, clicks and replies per week once those channels run (Part 14).
    5. The one tag. Write every post link with a label made of pillar, format and post number. Untagged, a post still shows reach, but its registrations stay blank.
    6. A source that is not connected stays blank, with the card that connects it.

    Done When Five cards load beside the funnel, and a test link shows its sign-up under its post.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Registrations first, then clicks, then reach. Likes come last.
    • A blank is information. It is never filled with a guess.

    Common Mistakes

    • Posting a link without its own tag, so the post's registrations stay blank.
    • Reading reach alone.

    5.15 The Weekly Feedback Loop

    Owner Operator, operationsTime 90 min a weekSystem Dashboard, Metricool, bucketSafety Person

    Why It Matters

    Content compounds only when last week's numbers shape next week's ideas. One fixed slot a week keeps the engine running. Without it the engine keeps making the format nobody clicks, and keeps the post with the most likes while the one that filled the event is dropped.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Rolls the numbers up by format, pillar and profile and writes keep, change and repeat the mechanism at the top of next week's ideas.
    • Writes back the batch's results, each post's result beside its registry line, and every rule a reviewer gave in a note.
    • Says so when a winner rests on a handful of clicks.
    What the Operator Does
    • Block 90 minutes on the same weekday every week.
    • Read last week's numbers before running the batch, then say what to do more of and what to drop.

    Every Step

    1. Read last week, post by post: registrations and clicks first, then reach.
    2. Write three lines. Keep: the formats and pillars with the most registrations per post. Change: the weakest, and what to try (a new hook, a new format, the call to action moved higher). Repeat the mechanism, never the angle: what made the best post work, carried into a new angle.
    3. Read the review flags. Any post a reviewer flagged, and why, is a lesson. A repeated flag becomes a standing rule.
    4. Run the batch with the three lines at the top.
    5. Write back. Add results to the registry, and reviewer rules to the voice or brand file with the date and their words.
    6. How much data is enough. A few posts a week is a weak signal. Keep the pillar mix balanced until a pattern holds for three batches.

    Done When The slot is in the calendar, the three lines are written before every batch, and every batch writes back.

    What Good Looks Like

    • A post with half the reach and four registrations beats it.
    • Early in the week leaves time to review and schedule before the posts start.

    Common Mistakes

    • Reading reach alone.
    • Calling a winner on a handful of clicks.
    • Skipping a week. The registry and the samples only stay fresh when every batch writes back.

    5.16 Add a Blog: One Pillar Post a Month

    Owner Operations, OperatorTime 2 to 3 hours a monthSystem Claude, funnel site, Google AnalyticsSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    Available FINTECH does not run a blog today. A blog is an extra source of traffic that keeps earning: one pillar post a month that answers a question the buyer already asks, with an invitation to the next webinar at the end. It is also the raw material for the social batch.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Drafts the post from the buyer persona, offer and method, using only facts in those notes.
    • Tags the registration link and reads the click-through each week.
    What the Operator Does
    • Pick the pain point and approve the draft.
    • Change the call to action when the weekly read says so.

    Every Step

    1. Pick one named buyer pain. Give the post a title that makes a promise and has a number in it.
    2. Claude drafts it: the promise, the problem in the buyer's words, three to five sections with one idea each, one worked example and the invitation. Anything it cannot source is marked and dropped.
    3. The operator approves it as the operator approves any post.
    4. Publish it on the funnel's own site. Check the date, that the link opens the registration page with its tag intact, and that no placeholder is left. Read it on a phone like a stranger.
    5. Tag the link with source blog, medium organic and the event as the campaign.
    6. Each week divide the clicks that reached the registration page by the post's views. Read the verdict below.
    7. Hand the post on: cut it into the social batch (5.17) and use it as the month's newsletter issue.

    Done When The post is live, its link is tagged, and a test click shows as blog traffic.

    What Good Looks Like

    • The post is dated content: refresh the webinar date and link before each new cycle.
    • Read by source and medium, not by channel group, or the blog has no row of its own.

    Common Mistakes

    • Judging the post by engagement instead of clicks to the registration page.
    • An untagged link, so the channel cannot be judged.

    5.17 Add Social Repurposing: One Pillar Cut Into a Batch

    Owner OperationsTime 1 sitting per pillarSystem Claude, Canva, MetricoolSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    Available A week of posts does not need seven separate ideas. Take one pillar, such as the month's blog post or a recorded session, and cut it into clips, short versions, quote cards, a poll and a carousel. The posts are approved as one batch and scheduled together.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Drafts twelve posts from the pillar, one per clip, version or quote, and tags each link.
    • Schedules them once approved, a person confirming each.
    What the Operator Does
    • Pick the five best moments. Read each post, swap any that does not sound like the operator, and approve the batch.

    Every Step

    1. Cut the pillar into five pieces: from a recording, pick five moments of 2 to 4 minutes each that answer a real objection or show the method working. From a blog post, make five quote cards and one carousel instead.
    2. Make 60-second versions: trim each clip, set it to portrait and add captions so it works with the sound off.
    3. Pull quotes and graphics: lift lines word for word into one named quote card template. Turn one into a poll if it splits opinion.
    4. Approve the batch: twelve posts, one per clip, version or quote. Keep an event post every 3 days.
    5. Tag every link with its source and its post number, so a registration can be traced to one post.
    6. Read clicks, not likes. Make 60-second versions of the winning clips and cut the next pillar around those topics.

    Done When Twelve approved posts are scheduled before the week starts, with an event post every 3 days and every link tagged.

    What Good Looks Like

    • At least 40% of a batch promotes the event unless another share is set, and those posts run as a countdown.
    • Posting one at a time on the day is how the channel quietly stops, so the whole batch is planned at once.

    Common Mistakes

    • Writing every post from scratch instead of cutting from one pillar.
    • A post link without its own tag.

    5.18 The Content Owner: Who Decides What

    Owner Susanne, content ownerTime About 2 hours a weekSystem Claude Project, review page, Content CalendarSafety Person

    Why It Matters

    The engine does the production. A person still decides what is worth saying and what is safe to publish. Susanne is the content owner: the one person who picks the ideas, supplies the proof and signs off every post. Naming one owner stops a batch from stalling while two people each assume the other approved it.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Prepares the ideas, the copy, the designs and the review page, and reports each rule as a pass or a fail.
    • Reads the results every week and brings the three posts to repeat and the three to drop.
    What the Operator Does
    • Pick which ideas to build. This is the one pause in the week.
    • Approve every post, or leave a note on it.
    • Supply real photos, real examples and written permission for any named client.

    Every Step

    1. Monday, the pick (15 minutes). Read the ideas Claude returns, strike what does not fit, keep what does and reply go.
    2. Midweek, the sign-off (30 to 45 minutes). Open the review link on a phone. Approve each post in the reviewer's own role, or leave a note and read the fix.
    3. Proof supply (as needed). Add each new case study, number or quote to the context bucket with its source. A claim with no source is dropped, not rewritten.
    4. Permission. Confirm in writing before any client, firm or individual is named. Without it, the post stays anonymous.
    5. Profile sign-in (once). Connect each LinkedIn profile to the scheduler. This one step stays with the profile owner, because LinkedIn posting runs through an approved profile.
    6. Friday, the read (15 minutes). Open the content view and read the last week against the one before (5.15). Decide what the next batch repeats.

    Done When One named person has picked, approved and read results for a full week, and the batch went out without waiting on anyone else.

    Still Open

    Posts per week is not yet set. The batch prompt takes the number each week, so it can start at a small number and grow. Whether a second approval role is wanted is also open (5.12).

    What Good Looks Like

    • The pick takes minutes because the ideas arrive already sourced.
    • Every post carries the content owner's approval in the record.

    Common Mistakes

    • Approving on a desktop preview that hides how the post is cut on a phone.
    • Naming a client from memory, without the written permission on file.
    • Letting a second approver exist informally. If a second role is wanted, it is added to the review page (5.12).

    5.19 Create Posts with Claude in the Claude Project

    Owner Susanne, content ownerTime One working session a weekSystem Claude ProjectSafety Read

    Why It Matters

    The Claude Project is a chat that already knows the business. The nine knowledge files are loaded once, so every conversation starts from the same facts, voice and rules instead of from a blank page. Because the files hold the proof, the posts come back sourced, and because the rules are in the project instructions, they are checked before the content owner sees anything.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Reads the knowledge files, proposes ideas that are not in the registry, drafts the copy and the first comment, and checks every rule.
    • Marks anything it cannot source as [check] instead of guessing.
    What the Operator Does
    • Ask for the ideas in one sentence, pick the ones to build, and say what to change.
    • Answer each [check] with a source, or tell Claude to drop the claim.

    Every Step

    1. Set up the project once. Create a Claude Project named for the LinkedIn posts, paste the project instructions below, and upload the nine knowledge files: offer, voice, verified facts, brand, audience, case studies, registry of past posts, creator samples and the rules. Proof: ask "what is the webinar title and date?" and check the answer names its file.
    2. Ask for ideas. One sentence is enough, for example: "Give me 10 ideas for next week, two for each pillar, and say which past post each is least like."
    3. Pick. Reply with the numbers to build and any change of angle. Nothing is written until this reply.
    4. Read the drafts. For each pick Claude returns the post, the first comment, the design brief, and a one-line rule check. Anything marked [check] needs an answer before it can ship.
    5. Revise with a note. Say what is wrong in plain words: "the hook is a claim, make it a scene", "cut the second paragraph", "this number is not from our files, remove it". Claude rewrites that post only.
    6. Run the second read. Ask: "Check this batch against every rule and the registry, and list anything a sceptical reader would challenge." Fix what it finds.
    7. Hand over. Ask for the batch as a table (date, profile, post, first comment, tag, design brief) so the designs can be built in Canva and the posts queued in the scheduler.
    8. Close out. Ask Claude to add the new posts to the registry and the new proof to the files, so the next batch starts richer.

    Done When A batch of approved posts, each sourced and rule-checked, with the registry updated.

    Claude Project Instructions: LinkedIn Posts
    You are the LinkedIn content writer for FINTECH Circle. You write only from the knowledge files in
this project. They are the single source of truth for the offer, the voice, the facts, the brand and
the registry of past posts.

RULES (every post, no exceptions)
1. Truth: every number, fact and date comes from the verified-facts file. If a claim is not in the
   files, mark it [check: source needed]. Never invent a figure, a client, a quote or a result.
2. Punctuation: no long dashes anywhere. Use a short hyphen, full stop, comma, colon or the word "to".
3. Clarity: write for a cold reader. Introduce every person on first mention. No relative dates
   such as "tomorrow" or "last week". Use the date.
4. Freshness: before proposing an idea, check the registry of past posts. A fact may return only with
   a new hook, a new argument and a new takeaway.
5. Reach: keep the link out of the post body. Put it in the first comment. Tag company pages, do not
   link them.
6. One call to action per post, at the end. Never promote an event that has passed.
7. Tone: positive, measured, specific. No hype words, no manufactured urgency, no closing question to
   the reader, nothing negative or market-sensitive, no client named without written permission.

WORKFLOW
Ideas first. When asked for N ideas, return exactly N, each as: pillar, hook, the argument in two
sentences, the proof it rests on (with the file it comes from), the matched format. Then STOP and wait.
Only after the content owner confirms which to build, write the copy, the first comment and a design
brief for each.

HOW TO ANSWER
Show the post exactly as it would appear. After each post, list in one line: sources used, rules
checked, anything marked [check]. If the files do not hold the answer, say so and ask for it.
    To getSay
    IdeasGive me 10 ideas for next week, two for each pillar, none that repeat the registry.
    A post from an ideaWrite idea 4 as a post with the first comment and a design brief. Match the voice file.
    A tighter versionCut this to 120 words. Keep the hook and the proof. Do not add anything.
    A different angleSame proof, a different hook. Give me three, each in a different style.
    A countdown runWrite three posts for the webinar on [date]: three days out, the day before, and the morning of. One call to action each.
    A pollTurn the point in idea 6 into a poll with four answers that are all reasonable.
    A rule checkCheck this batch against every rule and tell me what fails.
    Proof requestList every [check] in this batch and what source would settle each.

    What Good Looks Like

    • The first answer already cites the file it used.
    • Revisions are small notes, not rewrites from scratch.
    • The registry grows every week, so repeats are caught.

    Common Mistakes

    • Pasting facts into the chat instead of adding them to the files, so the next conversation does not know them.
    • Asking for finished posts before picking ideas. The pick is the part that needs a person.
    • Accepting a number that has no source.

    5.20 Example Posts for FINTECH Circle

    Owner Susanne, content ownerTime Read onceSystem Claude ProjectSafety Read

    Why It Matters

    These are shapes to start from, not finished posts. Every bracket is a gap the Claude Project fills from the knowledge files, and a [check] marks a claim that must carry a source before it can ship. No figure, name or result below is real until the files supply it.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Fills each bracket from the knowledge files and marks what it cannot source.
    • Matches one unused creator sample to each shape for the design.
    What the Operator Does
    • Read the shapes to decide which fit the voice.
    • Supply the proof and the permission for the case-study shape.

    Every Step

    1. Use the board-readiness shape for a pillar post, with a hook that is a scene.
    2. Use the countdown shape three days out, the day before and the morning of the webinar.
    3. Use the poll shape when a point splits opinion; share the result later as a new post.
    4. Use the proof shape only when the case study file holds the outcome and a written permission.
    5. In every shape the link is in the first comment, never the post body.

    Done When The content owner has picked the shapes to start with and told Claude which pillar each belongs to.

    Shape 1: Board Readiness (Pillar Post)
    Two board candidates. Equal experience. One gets the seat.

The difference is rarely the CV. It is whether the nominating committee can picture the candidate in the room on a hard day.

Three things make that easy to picture:

1. A clear view on one risk the board is carrying right now.
2. One example of a decision made with incomplete information.
3. A reason to be trusted that does not depend on a title.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Each post makes one point and ends on one call to action.
    • The hook is a specific scene or claim, not a question to the reader.

    Common Mistakes

    • Publishing a shape with the brackets still in it.
    • Writing a result that is not in the case-study file.

    5.21 What Sits Behind the Review Link: Hosting, Store and Alternatives

    Owner OperationsTime Half a day, onceSystem Code host, shared sheet, image serviceSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    The review link is the one thing the content owner sees, so it should open fast and never lose a note. Behind it are three small pieces. Each has a free option and a simple alternative, so the build does not depend on one vendor.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Builds the review site from the finished batch and publishes it.
    • Reads approvals and notes back from the shared sheet and applies them.
    What the Operator Does
    • Create or confirm the accounts: the code host, the sheet and the image service.
    • Check that the link opens on a phone.

    Every Step

    1. Pick the host. Any code host with free static pages works. Alternatives: a Cloudflare Worker, or the existing Cloudflare account already used for the dashboard and landing page.
    2. Pick the store. A Google Sheet with a small web app as the endpoint. Alternative: the CRM, if notes should sit beside the contact.
    3. Pick the image service. One service that creates illustrations and avatars for people who are not photographed. The avatar for each person is made once and reused, and requests are cached so repeats cost nothing. Real photos are always used for named people.
    4. Keep keys private. The image key lives in a private file that is never committed. Nothing in the repository or the review page holds a key.
    5. Prove each piece. Link loads over https, an approval shows saved, a test prompt returns an image with its cost.

    Done When The review link, the shared sheet and the image service each have a recorded proof.

    The Non-Negotiable Rules and the Definition of Done

    RuleWhat it means
    TruthNo claim without a source. Every number, fact and date traces to the verified-facts file. Unverifiable claims are dropped.
    PunctuationNo long dashes anywhere. A short hyphen, full stop, comma, colon or the word "to" for ranges. The renderer fails on one.
    ClarityWrite for a cold reader. Introduce every person on first mention. No insider names, and no relative dates that will be wrong on the publish day.
    FreshnessNo duplicate angles. Check the used-content registry and every past idea. A fact may return only with a new hook, argument and takeaway.
    DesignMatch one unused creator sample. Brand furniture on every slide as currently required (open decision, 5.11). No filler.
    PeopleReal photos. Clients named only with written permission.
    ReachKeep the link out of the post body. Put it in the first comment. Tag company pages instead of linking them.
    Call to actionOne per post, end on it. Webinar or follow. Meet the minimum webinar share and run those posts as a countdown. Never promote an event that has passed.
    HumilityPositive and measured. Nothing negative, critical or controversial. Nothing market-sensitive or confidential.

    Definition of Done for a Batch

    A batch is done when every row is true. Claude reports each row as a pass or a fail, with the evidence, before it says the batch is finished.

    CheckWhat good looks like
    Count and splitThe number asked for, spread across the two profiles
    Dates and timesOne per profile per day, consecutive, UK time, nothing after a past event
    Call to actionAt least the set share carry the webinar call to action, each with a first comment and the link, ordered as a countdown; the rest use the follow line
    SamplesEvery post matched to a sample no earlier batch has used, and the sample recorded on the post
    SourcesEvery claim sourced; numbers listed for the operator; no registry duplicates
    CraftEvery asset rendered with no overflow, passed its own phone-size critique and an independent second-model critique
    RulesZero long dashes, no hype words, no closing question, the listed bank unnamed, furniture as decided
    ApprovalEvery post approved by the operator, recorded in the Content Calendar
    Closed outRegistry updated, build-state complete, results read, scheduling steps handed over, next week's prompt ready
    The One Test That Matters

    Open the schedule on a phone. If every post looks like it belongs to a brand that knows exactly what it is doing, and the operator would be happy to see it in their own feed, the week is done. If one post makes the operator wince, it is not.

    The Four Jobs of Any Funnel

    FINTECH Circle runs one funnel shape today: the webinar. It is the right first shape, because one live session shows which message lands. But it is not the only shape, and a funnel that has a clear weakest link may be better fixed by changing the shape than by tuning it. This part explains the shapes that exist, and which are worth testing next. It is the "what else could be run" part of the playbook.

    The four jobs of any funnel. Whatever the shape, a funnel does the same four jobs. What changes is the moment and the format in which the sale is asked for.

    1. Convert a completely cold audience. Named people who have never heard of FINTECH Circle are reached directly and given a reason to look. This is the calendar invite and cold email.
    2. Generate traffic from many sources. Outreach, content, ads and partners all point at one place, so no single platform can starve the funnel.
    3. Give value first. A live session, a video or a workshop day gives real value before anyone asks for money. For this audience, an insider view of how board searches really run is the value.
    4. Keep delivering value for the whole journey. Reminders, follow-ups, a newsletter and a community keep the relationship warm long after the first touch.

    And there is a door at every stage: a person ready to apply, book a call or buy can do so at the stage they are in, not only at the end.

    STATUS: SUGGESTIONS, A JUDGEMENT TO TEST, NOT DATA   AS OF: 2026-10-17

    How to Read the Fit Ratings

    The shapes below are general funnel models. The fit column is a judgement about FINTECH Circle's audience, offer and assets. It is a starting hypothesis to test small, never a decision. Nothing here changes a live system.

    Why Six Stages

    Capture sounds like one thing until a landing page and a show-up sequence turn out to be different assets with different failure modes. A great page with no nurture still loses registrants before the event starts. Six stages give every failure its own place to be found and fixed. This is also why the funnel equation in Part 1 has one metric per stage.

    Which Shape Fits the Buyer

    Choose by how the buyer can be reached, not by what looks interesting. The same question appears in the reference playbook as a three-part test: a live session fits when the buyer is list-addressable, a reverse squeeze page fits when the buyer is content-reachable, and a series fits when the buyer can show up several days running.

    Build hours and weekly run hours are starting points from the reference playbook, not FINTECH figures. Every one of these runs on the same six stages as the webinar. What changes is what happens inside each stage and which stage carries the weight. Pick by the weakest link in the equation, not by what looks interesting.

    13.1 Choose the Next Funnel

    Owner Operator, operationsTime 1 hourSystem Dashboard, funnel equationSafety Read

    Why It Matters

    The temptation is to add a new funnel because it looks good. The better reason is that the equation names a weak link the webinar shape cannot fix. A new funnel adds a build, a set of pages, and an operating load. It must earn that.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Reads the last several webinars, names the weakest link with the funnel equation, and lists which funnel shapes address that link.
    • States the build effort and the stage each would change.
    What the Operator Does
    • Choose one funnel to test, never two at once.
    • Decide the number that will decide whether it worked.

    Every Step

    1. Run the post-event review (10.2) and name the weakest link.
    2. Match the link to a shape using the chain below.
    3. Pick one from the High fit list and write what it changes in each of the six stages.
    4. Write the smallest possible test (this card and the cards after it), the deciding number and the date it will be read.
    5. Show a plan card. Anything that reaches people needs "send now".

    Done When One funnel, one test, one deciding number, one date.

    What Good Looks Like

    • The funnel chosen addresses a named weak link.
    • The test is small enough that being wrong is cheap.

    Common Mistakes

    • Starting two new funnels in one quarter. Neither can be read.

    13.2 Test a Skip-the-Wait Door on the Thank-You Page

    Owner OperationsTime Half a daySystem Landing page, Calendly, GHLSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    Most webinar funnels make the most motivated people wait days for an offer they would accept today. A registrant who is already a Flagship or Elite prospect may want a call now, not after a webinar. The thank-you page already asks for one action: the WhatsApp join link. A second door costs little.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Writes the second-door copy and the change request, and checks the result of a test registration.
    What the Operator Does
    • Add a clearly separate option: "Prefer to talk first? Book a 15-minute call." Keep the WhatsApp ask as the main action, because it is load-bearing for reminders.

    Every Step

    1. Write the second-door text. It must not weaken the WhatsApp ask.
    2. Follow the landing page change flow: pull, edit, preview, test registration, plan card, promote (6.3).
    3. Tag the link ?utm_source=thankyou so its bookings can be counted.
    4. Run it for one webinar. Read calls booked from the thank-you page against the previous webinar.
    5. Keep it only if show-up rate did not fall.

    Done When One webinar run with the second door, and a read on bookings and show-up.

    What Good Looks Like

    • The test changes one thing on one page.

    Common Mistakes

    • Replacing the WhatsApp ask. Registrants without the join-link message get no WhatsApp reminders.

    13.3 Run the Downsell to Declined Applicants

    Owner Operations, ClaudeTime 1 daySystem GHL, WebinarGeekSafety Send now

    Why It Matters

    A declined applicant has told the funnel they are interested, qualified enough to apply, and not right for the tier they applied for. A lower-priced option turns a decline into a customer, and a customer into a candidate for the next tier. A draft for this already exists in two versions.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Builds the audience: declined applicants, minus anyone suppressed or already a customer.
    • Prepares the two draft versions for review and a plan card.
    What the Operator Does
    • Choose which version to send first and approve the wording.
    • Reply "send now" for the exact preview.

    Every Step

    1. Ask for the audience: "Build the declined-applicant list, excluding customers and opt-outs."
    2. Review Version A and Version B of the Digital-tier invitation.
    3. Send Version A to half and Version B to the other half, each with its own tag.
    4. Read payments and replies after a full week, not after a day.
    5. Keep the better version and log the result.

    Done When Both versions sent, split evenly, and the result logged.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Quote the Digital tier at the price in Part 1, from the confirmed price list. Never the older prices.

    Common Mistakes

    • Sending without checking the price in the copy.
    • Reading the result after one day.

    13.4 Turn a FINTECH Book Into a Lead Door

    Owner Operator, operationsTime 2 to 3 daysSystem Landing page, Claude, GHLSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    A published book is a trust anchor that a cold email cannot match. The operator co-edits seven FINTECH books. A board-readiness bonus inside a book, such as a checklist, gives a reader a reason to leave their email, and the next step is the webinar.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Drafts the bonus (a checklist or a short guide) in the operator's voice, using the Book or Resource format (5.3).
    • Drafts the three-email teaching sequence that follows the sign-up.
    What the Operator Does
    • Choose which book and which bonus. Approve the copy. Add the bonus link to the book's pages.

    Every Step

    1. Pick the book and the single most useful piece of board-readiness help it can offer.
    2. Build a short sign-up page. Tag it ?utm_source=book.
    3. Write a three-email sequence: the bonus, one insider insight, an invitation to the next webinar.
    4. Run it for a month and count sign-ups and webinar registrations from it.

    Done When A tagged sign-up page and a three-email sequence, running for a month.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Every email ends on one call to action.
    • The bonus is genuinely useful. A thin bonus damages the book's authority.

    Common Mistakes

    • Using real book covers without checking permission for the use.

    13.5 Extend the Partner Funnel

    Owner Operator, operationsTime 1 weekSystem Partner form, GHL, CalendlySafety Go

    Why It Matters

    A partner funnel with CISI already runs, kept apart so it never touches the main pipeline: its own form, its own sheet, its own tag, its own decision emails. The pattern can be repeated for other partners with an audience of board-minded executives.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Writes the partner brief: audience, offer, revenue split, form wording, tags, and what stays separate from the main pipeline.
    What the Operator Does
    • Approach the partner. Agree the split in writing. Sign off the form and the emails.

    Every Step

    1. Choose one partner whose audience overlaps with the persona.
    2. Copy the CISI pattern: a branded form, a separate sheet tab, a separate GHL tag and workflow, separate decision emails.
    3. Keep the partner's contacts out of the main cold-email and calendar pools.
    4. Agree what each side promotes and when, and how results are shared.
    5. Start with a single promotion and read the result.

    Done When One new partner funnel live, separate, with a written agreement.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Each partner's data stays in its own place.

    Common Mistakes

    • Mixing partner contacts into the main lists, which breaks the opt-out guard and the attribution.

    13.6 Pilot a Three-Day Board-Readiness Challenge

    Owner Operator, operationsTime 2 weeks to buildSystem WebinarGeek or Zoom, GHLSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    The webinar's weak link is often show-up and commitment. A short cohort where people do the work, such as a board CV, a target list of companies and a positioning statement, builds commitment day by day, and the offer lands on someone who has already done the work. It is a bigger build and a bigger ask of the audience, so it is a pilot, not a replacement. Potential The teaching content for running a series is outside this playbook. This card only sets up the test.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Drafts the three-day outline, the daily deliverables, the reminders and the offer day, using the modules as the source.
    What the Operator Does
    • Decide whether the audience can give three days of attention. Host each day. Decide the offer on day three.

    Every Step

    1. Write what a participant produces each day, small enough to finish in an hour.
    2. Pick the platform. A multi-day event needs one registration and the same join link each day.
    3. Build reminders for each day and a replay of each day.
    4. Hold the offer for the last day, only to people who completed the work.
    5. Pilot with a small invited group first. Read completion, then applications.

    Done When A small pilot run with completion and application counts read.

    The weak link this shape bets on is show-up and commitment, so day-one show-up and the series stick rate are the numbers to watch. No FINTECH history exists for them yet. Set the deciding number before the pilot: for example, that applications among those who stay beat the webinar's application rate per attendee. If they do not, the shape stays a pilot.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Each day ends with something finished.

    Common Mistakes

    • Making the daily tasks too large. People drop out on day two.

    13.7 Build a Reverse Squeeze Page From the Best Replay

    Owner OperationsTime 3 to 4 daysSystem Landing page, WebinarGeek replay, GHLSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    Potential The replay page gates a recording on name, email and company. That is already close to a reverse squeeze: value first, then the ask. Removing the wall for part of the video, adding two or three permissioned case studies, and ending on the offer turns the best replay into an always-on page that works between webinars. In this shape how far someone gets decides what happens next, never the calendar.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Writes the page structure, picks the cut points from the recording's polls and calls to action, and drafts the case-study blocks.
    • Lays out the depth stages, tags and score bands in the CRM for a person to approve.
    What the Operator Does
    • Confirm permission for every testimonial or case study. Approve the page. Preview and test registration as in 6.3.
    • Choose the depth threshold. The reference starts it at three-quarters through Part 1.

    Every Step

    1. Pick the replay with the highest watch time and split it into Part 1 (open, no form) and Part 2 (after the bridge).
    2. Add the depth stages: VSL Started, then tag depth-25, depth-50 and depth-75 as people watch. A message at 24 hours follows the band: under 25 percent, 25 to 74 percent, or 75 and over without Part 2.
    3. Make the bridge form the registration. It stays hidden until the threshold is passed, tags webinar registrant, and delivers Part 2 at once on a page and by a backup email.
    4. Score each application and route it: top to a booked call and the shared chain, middle to a lower-ticket checkout, bottom to the 52-week list. Write the band rule down before building.
    5. Switch off the timed reminder engine for this pipeline. Nurture fires per person, on depth, and reminders still apply to booked calls on the top band.
    6. Add two or three case studies with written permission. Tag the page ?utm_source=vsl.
    7. Send a small amount of traffic between webinars and read applications.

    Done When A tagged video page with permissioned proof and depth tags landing on a test contact, and a read on applications.

    The equation below is a teaching model in the reference form. Compare half-watchers and the bridge opt-in with the webinar's visit-to-registration rate. The page earns its place only if it produces more applications per thousand visitors than the registration page does, at a lower or equal cost. The starting figures come from the replay's own watch data, not from another funnel.

    What Good Looks Like

    • The page gives real value before it asks.
    • Each contact carries the depth tag the page sets, and each band reaches its next stage in a test.

    Common Mistakes

    • Using a testimonial without confirming permission.
    • Leaving the clock-driven reminders on, so people get a countdown to an event that does not exist.

    13.8 Place the Summit, the Angel Network and the Book Series in the Funnel

    Owner OperatorTime 1 hour to decideSystem Landing page, GHL, WebinarGeekSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    FINTECH Circle has offers beyond the Board Programme: a Summit, an angel network and a book series. Each can be a door into the funnel, a reward at the end of it, or a separate product. Leaving the placement open means each is sold ad hoc, the tags that mark them (such as a Summit attendee tag, in Part 15) trigger nothing consistent, and attribution blurs. This card sets a default placement so that the build can proceed. It is a proposal until the operator confirms or changes it.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Writes the placement spec for the chosen option, the tags, the follow-up and the dashboard line for each offer, from the table below.
    What the Operator Does
    • Decide, for each offer, whether it is a door in, a rung up or a separate product. Confirm who owns each offer's list.

    Every Step

    1. Proposed default. The book series is a door in (see 13.4): it feeds the same registration page. The Summit is a rung beside the programme: attendees are tagged and invited to the next webinar, and attendance is never counted as a webinar attendee. The angel network is a rung up: it is offered only to completed Board Programme members, never to cold traffic.
    2. For each offer, write one sentence: who it is for, what the first action is, and which number proves it works.
    3. Give each a tag and a source value, so contacts from it are counted separately (see Part 15).
    4. Choose where each is shown: the thank-you page, a follow-up email, or nowhere until the person is a member.
    5. Add one line to the dashboard brief for each offer, using only fields that already exist, and leave a blank where no data exists yet.
    6. Review after two events, and keep, move or drop each placement.

    Done When Each offer has a placement, a tag, a first action and a deciding number, confirmed by the operator.

    What Good Looks Like

    • A person is offered the next rung only after the previous one.
    • Counts for each offer are separate from webinar counts.

    Common Mistakes

    • Offering the angel network to cold traffic.
    • Counting a Summit attendee as a webinar registrant.

    13.9 Decide Whether to Add Text Messages and an AI Voice Call

    Owner The operator decides, operations buildsTime 1 hour to decideSystem Reminder tools, GHLSafety Read

    Why It Matters

    Potential Roughly half of the people who register never turn up, and a reminder that works costs almost nothing. Email and WhatsApp carry the reminders today. A text and a short AI voice call at go-live are two more rails, and they only reach people who ticked a consent box for them. Neither is running. This card is the decision. The consent rules and the build are in 4.21 and 15.8.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Lists what each rail needs and how long the outside waits are, before anything is built.
    • Drafts the text and the 30-second call script for approval.
    What the Operator Does
    • Decide whether the audience would welcome a text or a call.
    • Check the consent rules for the countries involved before anything is built.

    Every Step

    1. Name the moments that would get a text: a new cohort opening, a deadline, a live session starting today. Every other week gets none.
    2. Check what must exist first: a verified sender, an unticked consent box for text, an unticked box for the call, and a way for STOP to work from the first message.
    3. Read show-up for people on the new rails against people without, in a small test, before widening.
    4. Rules for UK sending are to be confirmed before any build.

    Done When A written yes or no for each rail, with the test that would settle it.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Text is the rare rail and never doubles a reminder that already went out.
    • Only people who ticked the box are texted or called.

    Common Mistakes

    • Ticking the consent box by default.
    • Texting every week.

    13.10 Decide Whether to Test Meta Paid Ads

    Owner The operator decides, operations buildsTime 1 hour to decideSystem Meta Ads Manager, Google AnalyticsSafety Read

    Why It Matters

    Available Paid traffic burns budget faster than any other channel. Meta can reach people beyond the contact list and the professional network, but LinkedIn ads on top posts are the nearer option for this audience. Neither paid route is running. This card is the decision. The test itself, with its tracking, tagged links and weekly read, is in 4.15.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Checks what already fires on the registration page, so nothing is added twice.
    • Proposes a target cost per registration from the numbers that exist.
    What the Operator Does
    • Decide whether the aim is to widen the audience, or only to reach the same people again.
    • Approve any spend. Switching a campaign on needs "send now".

    Every Step

    1. Name the reason: more reach, a new audience, or a cheaper cost per registration than the current channels.
    2. Write the target cost per registration before any ad runs. If the number cannot be estimated, the answer is not yet.
    3. Choose the nearer paid route first, and test one paid channel at a time.
    4. Read the result weekly by cost per registration, never by clicks.

    Done When One paid channel chosen or declined, with a written target.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Cost per registration against a written target is the only number that decides.

    Common Mistakes

    • Starting two paid channels at once.
    • Launching before a test registration is counted once in the analytics.

    13.11 Decide Whether to Sync LinkedIn Lead Forms Into Registration

    Owner OperationsTime 30 minutes to decideSystem LinkedIn Campaign Manager, WebinarGeekSafety Read

    Why It Matters

    Available A LinkedIn Lead Gen Form lets someone register without leaving LinkedIn. Without a link to the webinar, that sign-up stays inside Campaign Manager and nobody confirms or reminds the person. A small sync can register each one within minutes. First read how form sign-ups reach WebinarGeek today. If that is already handled, there is nothing to add. The set-up is in 4.16.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Reads how form sign-ups reach WebinarGeek today and reports the gap, if there is one.
    • Counts form sign-ups against registrations from the same source.
    What the Operator Does
    • Request the Lead Sync product on the LinkedIn app. LinkedIn reviews the request, and that is the slow part.

    Every Step

    1. Read how form sign-ups reach WebinarGeek today.
    2. If a gap exists, request access to the sync now, because the review takes time.
    3. Put the 60-day token expiry in a calendar when the token is made.

    Done When The gap is known, and access is requested if it is real.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Access is requested early.
    • The token is renewed before day 60.

    Common Mistakes

    • Building before the review is approved.

    Owner The operator decides, operations buildsTime 30 minutes to decideSystem Landing page site, Google AnalyticsSafety Read

    Why It Matters

    Available One post a month that answers a question the buyer already asks, ending in an invitation to the next webinar, keeps earning between events. It is also raw material for the newsletter and the social batch. It is judged by one number: clicks to the registration page divided by views. The steps are in 5.16 and the operating view is in 4.20.

    What the Operator Does

    2. Choose the first question from a real pain point on the buyer card.
    3. Agree the gate in advance: under 1 percent click-through means change the call to action, and 3 percent or more means keep going.

    13.13 Decide Whether to Repurpose One Pillar Into a Week of Posts

    Owner Operations, OperatorTime 30 minutes to decideSystem Metricool, Canva, ClaudeSafety Read

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Proposes the cut points and drafts the captions for approval.
    What the Operator Does

    Every Step

    1. Name the pillar to cut first: a webinar recording or the month's blog post.
    2. Confirm the approval gate is unchanged.
    3. Read registrations per post after three batches before changing the mix.
