    The Lessons in This Section

    • The webinar is the right first funnel. A new shape must earn its place by fixing a named weak link.
    • The High fit shapes reuse assets that already exist: the application, the call, the books, the partner pattern, the declined-applicant draft.
    • Test one new shape at a time, small, with a deciding number and a date.
    • Anything marked Available or Potential is not running. It needs a plan card first.
    Part 14

    The Later Stage: Scale, Automate and Grow

    How the funnel grows without getting heavier: a spec, proven connections, a weekly rhythm, one experiment a week, a 52-week engine with its rules, a weekly scorecard, and hosted automation.

    Master Playbook

    15 task cards2 sectionsReviewed by Operator as owner

    What Later Means

    This is the part for after the funnel runs reliably. The first thirteen parts explain how the funnel works and how to run one webinar. This part explains how it grows without getting heavier: how to put Claude in charge of the routine work, how to find and fix the weakest step every week, how to look after everyone who did not buy, and how to move the automation off a single laptop.

    It follows the shape of the GrowthClub "hand it to the agent" stage, adapted to what FINTECH Circle actually runs.

    1NowRun through the chat and the connector. Operations does the login steps. Plan card before every change.
    2NextCode in a private GitHub repository. Claude Code makes reviewed changes. Landing page and lead tools built.
    3LaterScheduled jobs run without a laptop: nightly cleaning, daily reports, reply sweeps, alerts.
    4GrowthMore funnel shapes, weekly experiments, content as the biggest source, a 52-week engine for everyone who did not buy.

    STATUS: PLAN, NOT ALL BUILT   AS OF: 2026-10-17

    The first stage is how things run today. The second is the move to GitHub and Claude Code (12.2). The third is the scheduled, hosted running described in 14.9. The fourth is where the funnel widens: more shapes (Part 13), content as the biggest source, a 52-week engine for everyone who did not buy.

    14.1 Write the Funnel Spec

    Owner Operations, ClaudeTime 2 hoursSystem Consolidated Document, repositorySafety Go

    Why It Matters

    Facts that live in five places drift. A price worded one way on the page and another in an email goes live unnoticed. The fix is one file that holds every fact once, and one rule: change the spec first, never the tool directly. From then on, the page, the emails and the campaigns copy from the spec.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Reads every knowledge file and asks only about what is missing or contradicts itself.
    • Writes the spec and restates it for approval line by line, before touching anything live.
    What the Operator Does
    • Answer from what is true today, not what is hoped. "I do not know yet" beats a made-up answer.
    • Correct the restated spec, then approve it.

    Every Step

    1. Ask: "Read every knowledge file. Ask me only about what is missing or contradicts itself. Then write the funnel spec with each price, date, link, promise, cohort and time once, and restate it for my approval."
    2. Answer the questions. The usual conflicts are the cohort date, the module count and an old price.
    3. Read the restated spec hunting for the same fact worded two ways.
    4. Approve. Record the spec's place in the Consolidated Document, with a status line.
    5. From now on, a change starts as a change to the spec, and Claude applies it everywhere that fact appears and lists what it changed.

    Done When A change to one line in the spec reaches every place that carries it, with a list of what moved.

    What the Spec Holds Once

    • The webinar title, date, time in Europe/London, broadcast id and registration link
    • The three prices, deposits, the next cohort and its application deadline
    • The modules and the count (open decision D1, 28.4)
    • The five invite titles and the one-line offer sentence
    • The booking links and the application link
    • The operator's title and the voice rules
    • The list of tools in use and what each owns

    What Good Looks Like

    • Every fact written exactly as a reader should see it, with currency and time zone.
    • Where a fact is not yet known, the spec says so and names when it will be decided.

    Common Mistakes

    • Approving the restatement after a skim. It is the one cheap chance to catch a misunderstanding.
    • A quick fix inside a tool, so the spec and the live page disagree.

    14.2 Connect Claude to Every Tool, and Prove It

    Owner OperationsTime Half a daySystem Connector, Claude CodeSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    An unconnected tool is a blind spot: Claude guesses its numbers, and a guessed number becomes a fact in next month's review. The proof that a tool is connected is not that a key is in place. It is that Claude's answer matches the number the tool itself shows.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Reads each tool and quotes a figure that can be checked in the tool's own screen.
    What the Operator Does
    • Compare each answer to what the tool shows. Tick a tool as connected only when they match.
    • Keep one key per tool. Put keys in the secret store, never in a chat.

    Every Step

    1. For each tool, ask for one checkable number, as in the table below.
    2. Open the tool's own dashboard and compare.
    3. Record the result in the change log: tool, the question asked, the answer, match or mismatch.
    4. Fix any mismatch before relying on the tool. The usual causes are a read-only token, a stale cache, or the wrong account.
    5. Re-run the check whenever a key is rotated.

    Done When Every tool in use has a recorded matching test.

    ToolAsk ClaudeCheck against
    TantraList the campaigns for the last seven days with their yes, maybe, no and waiting counts.Tantra's own campaign page and the calendar RSVPs
    InstantlyList campaigns with their real status and bounce rate.Instantly's campaign list
    GHLRead contacts from the last seven days with tags.The GHL contacts view. A 401 means retry, not a dead token.
    WebinarGeekRegistrations and attendance for the latest broadcast.The broadcast statistics
    Google SheetsUnused leads on the latest WEB tab.The tab itself
    DashboardRead the generated time and whether today's refresh was complete.The page itself and the status line it shows

    What Good Looks Like

    • Every call is logged, and Claude refuses to send, launch or delete without a typed word.
    • One key per tool, never one all-powerful key everywhere.

    Common Mistakes

    • Ticking a tool because its key is stored, before the test answer matched.
    • Sharing a folder that still contains the keys file.

    14.3 Launch a Small Test Run Before a Big One

    Owner OperationsTime 2 hours to launchSystem All channelsSafety Send now

    Why It Matters

    Until strangers go through a new page or sequence, it is a guess. A big first launch makes being wrong expensive, and judging a channel a few hours in kills things that were working. A small, tagged, QA-checked run gives the dashboard a real row to learn from.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Runs the pre-launch checks and reads back each test contact's tags and source.
    What the Operator Does
    • Choose the smallest audience per channel that still gives a readable run.
    • Set the day the numbers will be read, after the run has finished.

    Every Step

    1. QA first. Check every page at phone, tablet and desktop widths (375, 768 and 1280 pixels), complete one real test registration, and check the dashboard columns fill.
    2. Tag every link with its source, and check one test contact per channel shows the right source.
    3. Launch the smallest version of each channel in the same window, all pointing at one registration page, so channels are compared on the same page.
    4. Do not read anything until the run has finished. Numbers read after a few hours kill things that were working.
    5. Mind the warm-up. Cold email and calendar invites wait until new mailboxes have warmed for two to three weeks. LinkedIn runs inside its daily caps.
    6. Book the review as a recurring event.

    Done When The test run is live, the read day is set and the review is in the calendar.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Start with people who already know FINTECH, such as past registrants, while new mailboxes finish warming.
    • Every buyer traces back to a channel through its tag.

    Common Mistakes

    • Sending to the full list on day one, so a mistake costs the whole list.
    • Starting cold email before warm-up ends and burning the sending domains.

    14.4 Find the Worst Step

    Owner Operations, OperatorTime 30 minSystem Dashboard, equation modelSafety Read

    Why It Matters

    Change five things at once and nobody can tell which one moved the number. The cure is to name the single step where the funnel leaks most, and put the week's work there and nowhere else.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Fetches the five numbers and compares each rate with the last run and the rest of the chain.
    What the Operator Does
    • Pick one step, even when two look weak. If torn, take the earlier one: it feeds the later one.

    Every Step

    1. Read five numbers: registration rate, show rate, call-to-action click rate, applications and calls, and customers.
    2. Compare each rate with the last webinar, not with an ideal. A step that dropped since last time is a candidate: something changed.
    3. Rule out traffic first. A high cost in one channel means moving effort, not rewriting pages.
    4. Enter the numbers in the Funnel Equation Model (Part 1, The Funnel Equation) to see each stage's change.
    5. Find the row below and swap only the thing it names.

    Done When One step named, not three.

    The dashboard showsUsually meansSwap this
    Sends go out, few visitsWrong list or weak hook: a traffic problemThe invite title, the cold email, or the list
    Visits, few registrationsThe page is not earning the clickThe landing page headline and hero
    Registrations, low show-upReminders are not landingOne reminder, or its timing
    Attendees, few call-to-action clicksThe offer is not landingThe offer slide and the button wording
    Clicks, few applications or callsFriction after the clickThe application form or the booking page, or the follow-up email
    Applications, few paymentsPrice, trust or timingThe call, the deposit, the downsell

    What Good Looks Like

    • Rates are compared, never totals. A big count can hide the lowest rate in the funnel.

    Common Mistakes

    • Naming three steps and fixing none.
    • Blaming reminders when people turn up but do not click the offer.

    14.5 Run One Experiment a Week

    Owner Operations, ClaudeTime 60 min a weekSystem Dashboard, spec, change logSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    Without a split and a log, a lucky week becomes a permanent change. One controlled swap a week, judged on the dashboard, improves the funnel from evidence. And because fixing the worst step makes a different one the worst, it is a habit, not a project.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Proposes one variant of the element the worst step names, splits the next run in half, and logs it.
    What the Operator Does
    • Choose the one element and the number that decides it, before the run.
    • Make the keep or revert call.

    Every Step

    1. Ask Claude for one variant of the element the worst-step table named.
    2. Split the next run in half. Each half carries its own tag, so the dashboard counts them separately.
    3. Name the deciding number before the run, so no one can pick whichever metric flatters the result afterwards.
    4. When the run finishes, read both. If the gap is only a handful of people, run it again before calling it.
    5. Keep the winner, revert the loser in the spec, and log the change, the date, the expected number and the result.

    Done When Both halves counted separately, and an entry in the experiment log.

    The First Test at Every Stage

    StageTest this firstThe number it moves
    1 Leads and 2 TrafficThe invite title (V2 against another), or the country mix, one change at a timeYes and maybe rate, per segment
    3 LandingThe headline and hero, or the form lengthRegistration rate
    4 NurtureOne reminder's timing, for example WhatsApp one hour before the startShow-up rate
    5 WebinarThe offer slide, or the wording of the call-to-action buttonsApplication and call rate
    6 Apply, call, payThe follow-up email, the application form, or a deposit before the callCalls held, payments
    GrowthThe replay-first email, or the downsell versionBookings from follow-up

    What Good Looks Like

    • One change per variant. Two changes leave it unclear which one worked.
    • A new worst step appearing is the loop working.

    Common Mistakes

    • Ending a test early because one half looks ahead after a day.
    • Keeping the winner live without updating the spec.
    • Two experiments on the same step at once.

    14.6 Set the Operating Rhythm

    Owner Operator, operationsTime 90 min a weekSystem Calendar, dashboardSafety Person

    Why It Matters

    A funnel stops improving the week the review stops happening. One fixed slot a week keeps it running, and the rest of the cadence runs around it.

    How It Works

    What the Operator Does
    • Pick the weekday and block 90 minutes, every week, as a recurring event.
    • Read last week's numbers before running the content batch.

    Every Step

    1. Weekly ritual: read last week's numbers, write three lines (keep, change, repeat the mechanism), run the content batch with this week's webinar and must-cover topics, strike and keep ideas at the gate, review and approve scheduling.
    2. Keep, change, repeat the mechanism. Keep the formats and topics with the most registrations. Change the weakest and try a new hook, format or call-to-action position. Repeat the mechanism, never the angle: what made the best post work, carried into a new angle.
    3. Judge a post by what it moved down the funnel: registrations first, then clicks, then reach. Likes come last.
    4. How much data is enough. A few posts a week is a weak signal. Keep the topic mix balanced until a pattern holds for three batches.
    5. Skip nothing. The used-content registry only stays fresh when every batch writes back.

    Done When The slot is in the calendar and last week's numbers are read before every batch.

    Daily, automatedDashboard rebuilds. Alert if a step rate falls sharply.
    Weekly, the operator and ClaudeRead last week, confirm the worst step, launch one experiment, run the content batch.
    MonthlyRe-pull cost, rebalance effort toward the cheapest channel, retire losing variants, refresh the deliverability picture.
    QuarterlyRevisit the offer, the persona and the cohort calendar. Still the right ones?

    What Good Looks Like

    • Early in the week leaves time to review and schedule before the posts start.

    Common Mistakes

    • Reading reach alone. A post with half the reach and four registrations beat it.
    • Calling a winner on a handful of clicks.

    14.7 Write the Scale Plan

    Owner Operator, operationsTime 45 min a monthSystem One pageSafety Person

    Why It Matters

    Five lines turn the dashboard into next month's decisions: what a customer costs, where effort goes, what to test, what to sell next and what keeps customers. Without them, effort follows habit and customers leave after one purchase with nothing above it to buy.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Rewrites the five lines each month from fetched numbers.
    What the Operator Does
    • Fetch lines 1 and 2 from the dashboard and payments, not memory. Name the next offer up and the first win.

    Every Step

    1. 1. My cost per customer is ___ and a customer's value is ___. (The dashboard's tool cost is a floor, because Tantra, Apollo and hosting are not costed.)
    2. 2. My cheapest channel per customer is ___, so next month's effort moves toward it. Channel attribution is an open gap (28.4, OQ-20) and must close before this line can be fetched.
    3. 3. My worst step is ___ and this week's experiment is ___.
    4. 4. My ascension offer is ___: the rung above what they just bought. Today that is Flagship or Elite above Digital, and the Summit and angel network beyond.
    5. 5. My retention mechanism is ___: what produces the first win, and by when. For a new member, the cohort WhatsApp group and the first module date.

    Done When Lines 1 and 2 contain fetched numbers, not estimates.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Customer value against cost: around three times is healthy, below one means every customer costs more than they return. A rule of thumb, not a target.

    Common Mistakes

    • Estimates in lines 1 and 2, so the model only confirms a guess.
    • Leaving line 5 vague, with no first win and no date.

    14.8 Build the 52-Week Engine

    Owner Operations, OperatorTime Build over a quarterSystem GHL, WebinarGeek, Tantra, LinkedInSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    Most people who registered did not buy. They are not lost: they are the most likely buyers of the next cohort. A funnel that stops after the webinar throws that audience away. The 52-week engine keeps everyone who did not buy warm for a year, and anyone who replies comes back into the pipeline.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Builds the audiences from the contacted history and the tags, drafts each message in the operator's voice, and reports who replied.
    What the Operator Does
    • Decide which channels are used and how often. Approve every message. Keep consent in view for each channel.

    Every Step

    1. Segment by tag. Everyone who did not buy stays warm through the state tags: registrant, attended, watched replay, not watched, and purchased. Each tag triggers its own follow-up.
    2. Cohort emails to attendees, seven of them, from replay and apply through to the next webinar.
    3. No-show sequence at one day, one week, two weeks and one month.
    4. A re-invite to every webinar for no-shows and past registrants, the cheapest traffic the funnel has.
    5. LinkedIn content keeps the whole audience in view between webinars, and the matched audience (4.6) brings paid reach to the same people.
    6. A regular insight email. A short, genuinely useful note on board governance, positive in tone, with one call to action. Only to people who can lawfully receive it.
    7. Later: WhatsApp nurture only with documented consent, and an AI check-in call to high-value non-buyers, both tested small first.
    8. Anyone who asks to be removed is suppressed everywhere, immediately.

    Done When Each tag has a follow-up, each follow-up has an owner, and replies return to the pipeline.

    Who Is Contacted, and When

    AudienceWhat they getFrom
    Attended, did not applySeven cohort emails from replay to the next webinarWebinarGeek, moving to GHL
    Registered, did not attendReplay, then call, then insight emails at +1 day, +1 week, +2 weeks, +1 monthWebinarGeek, moving to GHL
    Declined applicantDigital-tier invitation, in two versionsGHL (draft)
    Everyone not suppressedA re-invite to each new webinar, and LinkedIn contentTantra, Instantly, LinkedIn
    CustomersCourse access, onboarding, cohort group, ascension offersGHL

    What Good Looks Like

    • Every message has one call to action and the suppression sweep runs first.
    • The engine feeds Stage 1 again: replies and referrals come back as new traffic.

    Common Mistakes

    • Treating a tag as proof of consent. A tag says what someone did, not what they agreed to.

    14.9 Host the Automation 24/7

    Owner OperationsTime 1 to 2 weeksSystem Cloud scheduler, hosted functions, secret storeSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    Today the daily dashboard rebuild and the weekly deliverability report run on one Mac, and only when it is on and awake. That is fine while the funnel is being proven. Once it is proven and the team wants it hands-off, the jobs should run on a schedule in the cloud, independent of any computer or person. This is the final stage, not the first.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Moves each job to the host and writes its schedule, then checks the first scheduled runs against the runs from the Mac.
    • Builds the plan card for anything that would reach people and alerts a person instead of sending.
    What the Operator Does
    • Decide when the funnel is proven enough to move. Approve the cost and the host.

    Every Step

    1. Choose the host. The documented plan uses three Google Cloud pieces: a scheduler (the clock), hosted functions or containers (the worker), and a secret manager (the vault that replaces the local keys file). FINTECH already runs Workers on Cloudflare, so Cloudflare's scheduled Workers are an alternative to compare. Decide once, with a plan card.
    2. Move the keys from the local keys file into the host's secret store. Never into a repository.
    3. Move the jobs one at a time. Start with the read-only ones: the dashboard rebuild and the deliverability report.
    4. Set the schedules and run old and new side by side for a week. They must agree.
    5. Wire the alerts to email or chat for any failure.
    6. Add the sends last. Anything that reaches people stays behind a typed word until the whole routine has run clean for a quarter.

    Done When The read-only jobs run in the cloud, agree with the runs from the Mac, and alert on failure.

    A Daily Routine, Hosted

    1MorningPull new leads
    2CleanVerify, dedupe, apply exclusions
    3PlanBuild the wave as a plan card at safe volume
    4CheckDeliverability, DNS, bounces
    5CollectRSVPs and attendance
    6ReportClassify replies, rebuild the dashboard
    7AlertTell a person on any failure

    Each step runs as a read or a plan. Sends are never part of the unattended run: the routine builds the plan card and alerts a person.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Trigger the move only when the funnel is proven and hands-off running is wanted. Until then keep it where it is: the tool APIs do the work either way, and hosting only changes where and when it runs.
    • Two timers, not one: a run, and a guard that makes sure the run happened.

    Common Mistakes

    • Moving before the funnel is proven. Hosting an unproven process makes mistakes run faster.
    • Giving the hosted job permission to send without a gate.

    14.10 Set Guardrails for Unattended Running

    Owner Operations, OperatorTime Half a daySystem Repository, secret storeSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    Every serious mistake in this workspace has been a stale-knowledge failure, not a reasoning one: a campaign verified as a draft at 12:08 went active at 12:26 and sent 200 emails, and the stale claim was repeated for hours. The more that runs unattended, the more the guardrails matter.

    Every Step

    1. Separate reading from acting. Unattended jobs read, report and prepare plans. Acting waits for a person.
    2. Log every call with the tool, the request and the result, and read the logs on a schedule. Nobody reads the Worker logs on a schedule today (28.4).
    3. Cap what a job can spend or send per run, per day. A hosted job that loops cannot send more than the cap.
    4. Add a kill switch: one named way to pause every scheduled job.
    5. Keep one client per environment. Keys, data and service accounts are never shared across clients.
    6. Re-read before asserting. Any status stated to a person is read in that same turn.
    7. Rotate keys on a schedule, and whenever anything is pasted into a chat.

    Done When Reading and acting are separated, logs are read, caps and a kill switch exist.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Failures alert a person quickly, with the cause, not just the fact.

    Common Mistakes

    • Giving an automated job a key that can do more than it needs.

    14.11 Decide Who Does What as Volume Grows

    Owner OperatorTime 1 hourSystem TeamSafety Person

    Why It Matters

    One person can run the funnel through the chat at today's volume. As webinars, content and calls grow, roles need to separate, so the quality of each is protected and no single person is the only one who knows how a step works.

    Every Step

    1. A content owner on the team who runs the weekly batch and the design and scheduling. Susanne is the content owner (5.18).
    2. An appointment setter who reviews applications and books the calls.
    3. A call-taker, who may be the operator at first, and later a rotation of several people on a shared calendar.
    4. An operator who runs the cycle, the waves and the checks, and keeps this playbook current.
    5. One owner for the infrastructure: domains, mailboxes, DNS and the health report.
    6. Write each role's weekly tasks as the cards in this playbook, so a new person starts from them.

    Done When Each role has a named person and a list of the cards it owns.

    What Good Looks Like

    • A new person is productive in days because the steps are written down.

    Common Mistakes

    • One person holding every login and every step in their head.

    14.12 The 52-Week Grid and Its Rules

    Owner Operations, OperatorTime Build over a quarterSystem GHL, Tantra, WebinarGeekSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    The 52-week engine (14.8) needs a plan, or it becomes whatever gets sent when someone remembers. A grid fixes that: five lanes, one touch per lane per week, and a checkpoint at weeks 1, 13, 26 and 52. Potential Email is the lane FINTECH already uses in part; the other lanes are options to add one at a time. The grid is the reference model.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Writes the first four weeks of the email lane and the weekly letters after them, in the operator's voice.
    • Builds the three entry rules from the tags, and reports each checkpoint.
    What the Operator Does
    • Choose which lanes to switch on and in which order. Approve every message.
    • Read the list at each checkpoint and decide: keep, change or shorten.

    Every Step

    1. Five lanes, one touch each per week. Email carries the main rotation: a welcome, a pillar lesson, a case study, a founder note, a how-to, a re-engagement, and a wrap-up each quarter. WhatsApp is a one-line twin of that week's email. SMS is only for the time-critical. The AI newsletter is one themed issue a week, drafted by Claude from the same context and edited by a person. Retargeting ads show a fresh creative to a refreshed audience each week; for FINTECH the option is a LinkedIn matched audience (4.6).
    2. Four checkpoints, at weeks 1, 13, 26 and 52. At each, read the list: who is opening, who replied, who booked a call, who was removed. Change what is not working.
    3. Three tracks. Entry depends on what the person did (see below). The rules are written once, as tags.
    4. Four useful sends for every one that asks. A call to action in every message turns a nurture into a sales list and shortens its life.
    5. Point every invitation at something that exists: the next webinar, a replay, a booking link or a new case study.
    6. Shorten when the cycle is short. If buying usually takes weeks, collapse the grid to 12 weeks. For an annual contract, build the year around the renewal date.

    Done When The grid shows which lane carries what in every week, the three entry rules are written, and the four checkpoints are in the calendar.

    What Good Looks Like

    • One lane is switched on at a time and proved before the next.
    • Each checkpoint ends with a decision, not just a report.

    Common Mistakes

    • Switching on all five lanes at once.
    • Putting a call to action in every send.

    14.13 The Weekly Letter: Rotation, Nine-Word Email and Leaving Quietly

    Owner Operations, ClaudeTime 60 to 90 min to set upSystem GHL or email tool, ClaudeSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    The email lane (14.12) is where most of the 52 weeks happen, so its rules matter most. A welcome series that teaches the method one step at a time comes first. After it, one letter a week, on a fixed rotation, from a fixed day, with a clean way for people to leave. Available The rules below are the reference model.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Writes the welcome series and drafts each weekly letter a day or two before its slot, using the month's theme.
    • Counts unopened emails and lists who is due for removal.
    What the Operator Does
    • Edit and approve each letter. Choose the send day and time once.

    Every Step

    1. Welcome series first. Email 1 thanks them, names the problem and lists every step of the method the series will walk through. It turns a list of emails into a course people want to finish. Then rotate three kinds: a step email, a case study (only results the customer approved in writing) and a tool how-to.
    2. Then the weekly letter, on the 12-topic rotation below.
    3. The nine-word email is for an old list never followed up. Run it first, as a reactivation: one short line asking if they are still interested in the result they wanted, tested against an AI-personalised version. Anyone who opens joins the welcome series.
    4. Leave quietly. Remove anyone after 20 unopened emails in the weekly letter. In the reactivation series, anyone silent after 10 sends is removed. Every email carries a one-click unsubscribe.
    5. One fixed send day and time. Never move it, so readers learn when to expect the letter.
    6. Four useful sends for every one that asks for something.

    Done When The welcome series is approved, the first weekly letters are scheduled in one fixed slot, and the removal rule is written down.

    What Good Looks Like

    • Each letter teaches one step, with one example from the brand's own proof.
    • A sender who never moves their send day builds a habit in the reader.

    Common Mistakes

    • Turning every email into a pitch.
    • Keeping contacts who never open. They damage delivery for everyone else.

    14.14 The WhatsApp Twin of Every Email

    Owner Operations, OperatorTime 1 to 2 hours to set upSystem Tantra WhatsApp, GHLSafety Go

    Why It Matters

    Potential A short WhatsApp message beside each weekly email lifts the chance it is read. A WhatsApp number is also easy to get blocked, so the rules matter more than the copy. FINTECH does not run this today; the 52-week engine (14.8) lists WhatsApp as a later step, only with documented consent.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Writes the twin for each email, chooses pointer or compressed mode, checks it is under 400 characters and says which mode it used.
    • Adds only opted-in contacts when each twin is due.
    What the Operator Does
    • Connect the WhatsApp number once. Approve the twin with its email. Answer replies like a person.

    Every Step

    1. Consent first. Only people who ticked WhatsApp on the registration form receive a twin. The tick box saves the consent with the contact. A tag is not consent.
    2. Choose the mode per email: pointer for long emails, compressed for short ones.
    3. Keep it small. Under 400 characters, one idea, one link, one twin per email.
    4. Send it an hour after the email, never in the same minute.
    5. Always a way out. Every twin ends with how to stop. A reply of STOP ends WhatsApp for that person and is recorded.
    6. Answer replies like a person. They count as engagement.

    Done When The first two twins are written, approved and scheduled next to their emails, and a STOP reply was tested.

    RuleWhy
    Opt-in onlyNo consent, no message. This is the main reason numbers get blocked
    Under 400 charactersRead on a phone between other things
    One idea, one linkA second link splits the click
    An hour after the emailA reminder, not a competitor
    STOP always worksRequired, and recorded

    What Good Looks Like

    • A twin is a nudge, not a copy of the email.
    • SMS stays for the time-critical only.

    Common Mistakes

    • Messaging people on WhatsApp who never agreed to hear from the funnel.
    • A twin that is a pasted email, too long and too often.

    14.15 The Weekly Scorecard

    Owner Operations, OperatorTime 20 min a weekSystem DashboardSafety Read

    Why It Matters

    A funnel stops improving the week nobody reads the numbers. The scorecard is the one page that is read in the weekly slot: a handful of numbers, each against last time, each with a verdict. It replaces a long dashboard tour with a decision.

    How It Works

    What Claude Does
    • Fetches every number from the dashboard and the tools, compares each with the last run, and proposes a verdict.
    • Marks a verdict as weak when the sample is small.
    What the Operator Does
    • Agree or change each verdict. Name the one thing that gets this week's effort.

    Every Step

    1. Open the scorecard. Every number shows this week, last week and the change.
    2. Give each number a verdict: scale, hold or fix.
    3. If two numbers are fix, take the earlier step: it feeds the later one.
    4. Write three lines: keep, change, repeat the mechanism (5.15).
    5. Record the decision and the number that will judge it, before the run.

    Done When Every number has a verdict, one step is named, and the experiment and its deciding number are written down.

    What Good Looks Like

    • A blank number stays blank. It is never filled with a guess.
    • Rates, not counts. A big count can hide the lowest rate.

    Common Mistakes

    • Calling a winner on a handful of clicks.
    • Reading the page without writing a decision.

    Readiness Checklist for Hands-Off Running

    • The funnel has run end to end for several webinars with the same process
    • The funnel spec is approved and every tool's test answer matched
    • Experiments run weekly, with a log
    • The code is in a private repository with two owners and a review flow
    • Keys are in a secret store, not a file, and none has ever been committed
    • Read-only jobs have run in the cloud for a week and agree with the local runs
    • Alerts reach a person, and a kill switch exists
    • Sends remain behind a typed word

    The Lessons in This Section

    • Change the spec first and let Claude apply it everywhere.
    • A tool is connected when its answer matches the tool's own screen.
    • One worst step, one experiment, one number, every week.
    • Everyone who did not buy is a future customer. Keep them warm and lawful.
    • Host the automation last. Reading is automated before acting is.
    • The 52-week grid is five lanes and four checkpoints. Switch lanes on one at a time.
    • A twin is a nudge, sent an hour after the email, only to people who opted in.
    • Read one scorecard a week and give every number a verdict.

    17.8 Glossary

    Plan card
    The reviewed summary Claude shows before any change
    Wave
    One Tantra calendar campaign of about 1,000 invites
    Stamp
    Marking a lead as used in the outreach sheet, only after its campaign is confirmed ready
    Broadcast
    One scheduled showing of the webinar in WebinarGeek
    Connector
    The service that lets the chat read and act on the live systems. It speaks MCP, a standard way for an AI assistant to use tools.
    API
    The door a tool opens so another program can read or change things in it, using a key
    Service account
    A robot login that acts for people or mailboxes without a person signing in
    SPF, DKIM, DMARC
    Three public records that prove mail really comes from the domain and say what to do when it does not
    Suppression list
    Everyone who must not be contacted, shared across channels
    Worker
    The small cloud program that links WebinarGeek to GHL and keeps tags in sync
    Webhook
    A message one tool sends another the moment something happens
    RSVP
    A Yes, Maybe or No reply to a calendar invite; counts as interest, not registration
    Warm re-invite
    An invite to past registrants who did not attend
    Context bucket
    The nine documents that hold everything the content writer needs
    Used-content registry
    The running list of every angle already posted
    First comment
    The comment below a LinkedIn post that holds the registration link

    17.16 The Dashboard: Schedule, Stages, Provenance and Corrections

    STATUS: CURRENT, FROM THE DASHBOARD DOCUMENT VERIFIED 2026-09-15 AND THE PRESENTATION NOTES OF 2026-09-23   AS OF: 2026-10-18

    The dashboard document in the Fintech folder is the single source of truth for the dashboard. If it and the dashboard's own daily build disagree, the build wins and the document is a bug. This section is the playbook's copy of what a person needs to run the dashboard, check it and avoid its known mistakes. It holds no live figure, because a figure written here would go stale. Read the figure from the dashboard.

    Where It Is Served

    SurfaceStatus
    dashboard.fintechcirclepro.comThe default page. Share this link. Rebuilt and redeployed by the daily run. It is a Worker serving every path with no login, and asks search engines not to index it.
    The older design on the Workers addressA fallback, still rebuilt daily. Retire it once the new page is signed off.
    The Claude ArtifactDeprecated. Its share link is pinned to an old build, so viewers see stale numbers forever. Never share it.

    The dashboard is public by decision, on a domain the team owns, so anyone with the address can read it. It is marked so search engines do not list it.

    The Daily Schedule

    • 12:00 India time (07:30 UK): the full rebuild, ending in the two Worker deploys.
    • 13:15 India time: a guard that re-runs everything if today has no OK status, and does nothing if the rebuild is still running.
    • A scheduled job that was written but never loaded fires nothing. Check that both agents are loaded, not only that they exist.
    • A sleeping Mac skips the job and runs it once on wake, sometimes hours late. Judge freshness from the last-run file, never from the clock.

    Did It Run?

    Read the one-screen last-run file first: status, duration, whether the live page deployed, and which stages failed. The same facts are in a machine file with per-stage timings. When today's run was not clean, the page shows a Partial refresh banner naming what failed. A failed deploy has no banner, because viewers never received the new page. It appears as a notification and in the last-run file. The render refuses to publish a zeroed page.

    Field-by-Field Provenance

    Every figure on the page has one source and one rule for what counts. Read the figure from the page, and use this table to know what it means.

    FigureSourceWhat counts
    RevenueGHL paymentsCompleted transactions at or above a floor that excludes test probes. Owner and test payments and duplicate orders are excluded. Deposits count, with the unpaid balance shown as committed, not received.
    CustomersGHL payments, merged by identityPeople, not orders. A deposit and its balance are one customer. One person paying under two addresses is one customer. Three counts are correct at once: total, webinar-attributed and outreach-sourced.
    Outreach-sourced customersThe conversion tableA conversion goes to the last webinar whose outreach list holds the person and whose date is on or before the conversion. Someone contacted after paying is not outreach-sourced. People are matched on identity, not email alone.
    Webinar sign-upsWebinarGeek, per broadcastRegistered is the broadcast's own subscription count. Attended is live plus replay viewers. Public-replay viewers are audience, not attendance.
    Registrants, self-registeredWebinarGeek page and the custom landing page onlySign-ups through the calendar bridge or a bulk upload are interest, not self-registration, and are never added to the RSVP counts.
    RSVPs per webinarThe 20 sender calendarsYes, Maybe and No. The Tantra campaign list drops completed campaigns, so it is not the source for old events.
    Outreach setTantra, master-sheet stamps and that webinar's emailed Instantly leadsBeing in the master outreach sheet counts as contacted. An Instantly lead counts as contacted only with a last-contact time.
    Cold-email replies and opensInstantlyReplies are the vendor's own and under-report. Opens are absent on purpose, because link tracking is off.
    Calls bookedGHL calendarThe calendar that holds the bookings is not in the listed calendars, and its id is built into the daily refresh. Never conclude no events from the listed ones.
    Call-to-action clicks, applications, calls (per webinar)Typed in by the operator after each eventNo API exists. They show a dash until entered.
    Tool costsTyped in by the operatorA floor. Tools without a confirmed price are named, not counted as zero.
    Bounce rate and suppressionInstantly and the suppression listJudge by rate per campaign, not by count.
    Sending-domain healthDNS lookups per domainScoped to domains that hold a live mailbox. A subdomain with no record inherits its parent's policy.
    SegmentsThe participation masterShow wins over appearances beside the index. A pooled rate is not evidence.

    Provenance Badges and the Honesty Rules

    • Every figure label carries a badge: live, operator, derived or awaiting input. A reader can tell a measurement from a typed estimate.
    • A blank means not available. A zero means someone measured zero. The page has no path that turns an unknown into a zero.
    • No number is written in the page code. Typed figures live in input files that are re-read on every render, so a correction is a file edit and a re-render.
    • A ratio is computed only when both sides are known. Cost per registration needs cost and attributed registrations. The CRM does not record the lead channel, so no channel ratio is shown.
    • Totals name what they exclude.
    • Brand colours are not data colours. The sun, sky and dusk hues are call-to-action and chrome only. Status colours are reserved and always paired with a word.

    Manual Tasks, and What Under-Reports if They Are Skipped

    TaskWhenIf skipped
    Build the outreach set for the webinarThe day after it airs (30 to 40 minutes)The conversion table under-reports that webinar. The daily run now rebuilds a missing set itself.
    Enter call-to-action clicks, applications and callsAfter each webinarThose tiles show a dash. Clicks can never be automated.
    Rebuild the participation masterAfter new outreach or webinar dataFirmographics and attribution degrade. It is the oldest input left.
    Add webinar notesAfter each webinar, when anything went differentlyThe panel says no notes recorded.
    Update tools, costs and lead purchasesWhen an invoice arrivesCosts stay estimates.

    Before Trusting the Page, Check These Reconcile

    1. Funnel totals equal GHL for customers and revenue.
    2. The ramp's 21-day totals equal the webinar panel's own figures.
    3. The windowed subscriber count equals the broadcast's subscription count.
    4. No webinar reads 0/0/0 after it has aired.
    5. The live address serves the same Generated stamp as the local build.

    The Corrections Log: Mistakes That Already Put Wrong Numbers on the Page

    Every one was caught by the operator, not the pipeline. They are listed so nobody repeats them.

    GroupThe mistake and the rule it left
    Counting peopleA customer is a person, not an order. Match on identity, not email alone. Exclude owner and test payments and duplicate orders. Fix the merge in one place, because the funnel and the conversion table both read it.
    Vendor interfacesAn Instantly lead listing filters on the singular campaign field, and the plural forms are silently ignored. Account-level analytics return account totals, not a campaign's. Instantly's contacted count accumulates across steps, so never divide it by leads. Loaded is not contacted. Match a campaign by id, never by name. WebinarGeek offers no call-to-action data. One webinar id serves several broadcasts, so split cohorts by creation time with the boundary on the day after the previous broadcast, and key subscriptions on their own id. A page of results that fails to load is retried, not allowed to stop the daily refresh. Tantra sits behind a firewall that blocks anonymous automated visitors, so every Tantra call identifies itself.
    ClassificationMatch job titles as whole words, never as part of a word, because the letters of one title sit inside another. A pooled conversion rate is dominated by the biggest send, so look at wins over appearances.
    AttributionRegistrants mean the WebinarGeek page and the landing page only. Public replay viewers are audience. Conversion buckets must partition the population. There is no hardcoded cold or LinkedIn split, and putting one back is a regression. Utm values exist on every subscription and are empty.
    StalenessA cached file that the render prefers over an API is a staleness bomb, so check the write path as well as the rebuild. A vendor failure must never become a zero: raise, and print a dash with an unavailable-not-zero notice. A webinar aired after the last participation-master rebuild reads zero unless backfilled. A metric definition change must be backfilled across history, or it renders as a business decline. A change in the basis of a series, such as all-time against featured-webinar, makes a delta lie. Any rewrite of a file the funnel reads must be prepared in full before the old copy is replaced, because a crash halfway is data loss. The render must survive the empty state between one webinar airing and the next being scheduled.
    DNSA subdomain with no DMARC record inherits its parent's policy, so a presence check raises false alarms. A policy of none with no report address is unenforced and unobservable. A report address on another domain needs that domain's permission record, or no reports arrive.
    PublishingA scheduled job must be loaded into the scheduler, not merely present. The scheduler does not see the same tools a person's session does, so every tool it calls is named in full. The second daily check follows the rebuild finishing, never a clock time. A rebuild is skipped only when the content is unchanged, not because one already ran today. The pass or fail verdict comes last in the run, and the health record is written before the page is built. The artifact share link is pinned to one build and must not be shared.

    25.6 The CRM Pipelines as Configured

    STATUS: READ LIVE FROM GHL ON 2026-10-18. RE-READ BEFORE QUOTING   AS OF: 2026-10-18

    GHL holds two pipelines. Both are empty of opportunities, so revenue and progress are read from payments and contact fields instead (16.12). The stages below are the configured ones.

    PipelineStages, in order
    Marketing PipelineNew Lead, Hot Lead, New Booking, Visit Attended, Sale, Left a Review
    Sales PipelineCall Booked, Call Reminder Sent, Call Completed, No Show, Follow-Up Sent, Won

    What this means. The Marketing Pipeline reads like a stock template for a booking business, and its stage names do not match this funnel. The Sales Pipeline fits the call stage. Neither is populated. The funnel's own stages in this playbook are registered, attended, applied, call and paid. A decision is needed on whether to rename the Marketing Pipeline stages to those, and whether to start moving contacts through the Sales Pipeline by workflow. Until then, no report should be built from pipeline stages. Whether the call's 52-week stage exists as a pipeline is not known from this read.

    25.7 Connector Settings and Reach

    STATUS: CURRENT. RE-CHECK A CONNECTOR'S TOOL LIST IN SETTINGS BEFORE RELYING ON A WRITE   AS OF: 2026-09-28

    Each connector's tools can be set to Always allow, Needs approval or Blocked. Blocked means blocked: the chat does not look for a workaround. A blocked action is still possible for a person in the tool's own screen, or for the operations pipeline after a typed "send now". The block stops the chat doing it by accident.

    How Connectors Work

    • A connector belongs to a user or the organisation, not to the Project. Each person enables it and signs in themselves, then switches it on per chat.
    • A custom connector must be a remote service reachable over HTTPS. Local-only tools, such as Tantra's own local server and the password vault, cannot be used from the chat.
    • A connector address that contains a key (Instantly) is a secret. It is never pasted into a chat or a document.
    • If a connector a task needs is not on, the chat names it and stops. It does not substitute another system.

    Required Tool Settings

    27.1 How the Log Works

    STATUS: HISTORICAL; APPEND-ONLY   AS OF: 2026-10-20

    HISTORICAL This is what happened when the system was run. The Master Playbook says how it works. The Current State says what it looks like today. The Event Runbook says how to run one webinar. The Log records one event at a time, after it is over.

    Rules for the Log

    • One record per webinar, written after the event in the post-event steps of the Event Runbook (26.4). Never edited to match a later view of the past; a correction is added with its date.
    • The dashboard is the system of record for the figures. A record here is a dated copy of a finished event. Read the dashboard for anything that must be current.
    • Nothing is guessed. A field the page does not hold reads "Not recorded". Do not fill it from memory.
    • A lesson earns a place in the Master Playbook only when it changes a rule. Then the record says which section changed. Otherwise it stays here.
    • Do not copy a record into the Master Playbook. A reusable mechanism is explained there as an example; the history stays here.
    Figures Snapshot

    Figures in these records were copied from the dashboard's data files generated on 20 October 2026 (10:53 and 10:57 UTC). Source: the dashboard data and conversion files. Owner: Unassigned.

    Words for Missing Information

    WordMeaning
    Not recordedThe source does not contain the information.
    Not verifiedThe information may exist but was not checked.
    None recordedThe source was checked and records none.
    Not applicableThe field genuinely does not apply.

    Most fields below read Not recorded, which is a statement about the sources and not a finding that nothing happened.

    27.4 Pooled Analysis: Webinars 1 to 9

    STATUS: HISTORICAL RESULT; HOLDS UNTIL THE ANALYSIS IS RE-RUN   AS OF: 2026-09-18

    HISTORICAL The pooled analysis of the calendar channel across webinars 1 to 9. The standing rules it produced are in Part 1, under Why This Funnel Fits This Audience. The evidence is kept here.

    From the analysis of webinars 1 to 9 (calendar channel): 240,319 invites produced 1,304 yes and 970 maybe replies, a base yes rate of 0.543%. These are conclusions that hold until the analysis is re-run.

    QuestionFindingDecision it supported
    GeographyThe UK is the only market that beats the average in every webinar (9 of 9, 0.617% yes, 1.18 times the base). The Netherlands, Switzerland, Singapore, France, Hong Kong and Norway are consistent losers.Move volume from the losers to the UK. Worth about 14% more yes with no extra sends.
    Seniority"Head of" titles perform at least as well as C-suite and won every webinar they appeared in; Partner is below average.Buy Head of alongside C-suite. Drop Partner, VP and Manager.
    Company sizeNo predictive value (0.91 to 1.24 times, inconsistent).Do not filter on headcount.
    CopyInvite title V2, "The Strategic Framework to Stop Advising and Start Governing in 2026", is the best of five (1.17 times). V3 and V4 are below average.Weight the next wave toward V2.
    FatigueYield fell about four times from webinar 2 to webinar 9 while volume rose about four times, because the same people were reached again.Fresh leads and warm re-invites matter more than any copy change.
    Why Germany Stays Out

    Germany reads above average when pooled (1.13 times) but wins only one or two of five webinars, so it stays excluded.

    One open question

    A group of 2,154 invites at large firms converted at 3.39%, six times the base, and does not appear in any bought list on file. If it was a warm or referral source, it outperforms every bought segment. Identifying it is worth the time.

    27.5 How to Add a Record

    After each webinar, in the post-event steps of the Event Runbook (26.4), ask the chat:

    Add a record to the Event Log
    Add a record to the Event Log for webinar [N], held on [WEBINAR DATE]. Read the dashboard for registered, attended, applications, calls, sales and revenue and quote the time it was generated. Read the campaign notes and any problems from this event's campaigns. Write Not recorded for anything you cannot read. Do not change any earlier record. Then tell me whether any lesson changes a rule in the Master Playbook, and which section.

    This changes a document, not the funnel: it needs a plan card but no safety word that reaches people.

    Part 28

    Decision Register

    Permanent decisions, current actions, open questions and historical items, kept apart, each with an owner, a source and a date.

    Decision Register

    28.1 How the Register Works

    STATUS: CURRENT; REGISTER OF DECISIONS, ACTIONS AND OPEN QUESTIONS   AS OF: 2026-10-20

    This register holds every decision and open item in one place and keeps the four kinds apart. A permanent decision is context for everything else. A current action has a known next step. An open question needs an answer first. A historical item is kept so the reasoning is not lost.

    KindPrefixMeaning
    Permanent decisionsPDIn force until a new decision replaces them. They explain why the rest of the playbook reads as it does.
    Current actionsCASomething to do, with a known next step and a role to do it.
    Open questionsD, OQAn answer is needed before anything can be done. D1 to D14 keep the ids they had in the old table.
    HistoricalHDecided or resolved. Not an instruction.

    Each item carries its id, the question, why it matters, status, owner, source, the decision or action needed, the consequence of leaving it open, the date opened and the date resolved. Owners are roles. Where no role is known the owner is Unassigned. A date is given only where a source states one. Dates are never inferred from file dates, build dates or audit dates: Not recorded means the source has no date for it. The older numbered items (OI-1 to OI-26) are listed in the Also known as field, so earlier references still resolve.

    Rule
    Nothing else in the playbook restates an open item. Other parts point here, so there is one place to update.
